Similarities

Coding Similarities

Type of Similarities Cited

• Regardless of one’s own gender, when asked to imagine a computer scientist, people typically report imagining a male.2

• These gendered beliefs may detrimentally impact females’ computer science self-efficacy, one’s personal beliefs about their ability to achieve a goal.

• By elementary school, females are less interested in and less confident in their computing abilities in comparison to their male peers.1,4,5

• However, some females imagine computer scientists as other females, which could positively benefit their computer science self-efficacy.3

Research Question:

• Whether and how do females’ gendered beliefs about the identities of computer scientists affect their own self- efficacy about coding?

Hypotheses:

• We predicted that female children who drew female computer scientists would have greater computer science self-efficacy • Further, we predicted that female children with greater computer science self-efficacy would describe similarities related to coding.

Imagining a Role Model: Female Children’s Computer Science Self-Efficacy

Stephanie McCarty, Paige Smyth; Naomi Polinsky, Jose Sotelo, David H. Uttal

Northwestern University

Introduction Results

Discussion

Participants & Methods

• 17 6- to 9-year-old females who participated in a large, virtual research study with their parents.

• Children completed two tasks: o Computer Science Self-Efficacy task: survey measuring children’s beliefs about their personal coding ability and the characteristics of other children who code (max = 161).

o Draw-a-Computer-Scientist Task: 5 minutes to draw a picture of a computer scientist. Then children were asked to report similarities between themselves and the person they drew.

• Similarities were coded as "coding similarities" if a child cited anything coding-related as a similarity between themself and their computer scientist.

• Girls who draw female computer scientists & girls who report having coding similarities with their drawn computer scientist seem to have stronger computer science self-efficacy than their female peers.

• Responses could be influenced by scientists and adults present in the moment (e.g., researcher gender, parent occupation).

• Potentially self-identification with characteristics and interests of computer scientists may boost girls’ computer science self-efficacy.

• More representation of women in computer science fields could positively alter young girl’s conceptualization of who belongs in computer science fields and expand the cultural narrative of the computer science identity

nurj_title: Irish Language Revitalization in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland
text:
Irish Language Revitalization

Shannon Lally, Northwestern University

Background____________________

Research Questions_____________

Methods______________________

Results_______________________

Discussion____________________

Future Research_______________

References_______________

Irish language subjugation began when England invaded Ireland in 1169 CE. In order to assert their dominance, English rulers passed laws forbidding the use of the Irish language. Irish people began using Irish as a way to differentiate themselves from their colonizer. The increased Irish nationalism as a means of decolonization culminated in the Irish War of Independence fought from 1919-1921. The island was then partitioned into the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, where the conflict continues.

How effective have Irish language revitalization movements been in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland? What accounts for the difference between these regions? How do colonial relationships affect the success of language revitalization movements?

In addition to library research, the most recent census data from both regions were used to produce maps of the percentage of Irish speakers per county. The difference in the percentage of speakers in each region over time was found and mapped in order to represent the efficacy of language revitalization movements in both regions.

Acknowledgments_________

Every county in the Republic of Ireland saw a decrease in the percentage of speakers. Three counties in Northern Ireland increased in the percentage of Irish speakers, and the rest of the counties decreased at a lower rate than counties in the Republic of Ireland.

Despite governmental support, all counties in the Republic of Ireland decreased in the percentage of Irish speakers. On the other hand, Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, had an increase in Irish speakers in half of their counties. This evidence indicates that governmental intervention in language revitalization movements is not a primary indicator of success. Furthermore, the counties in Northern Ireland that saw an increase in Irish speakers were also counties that experienced the most conflict during The Troubles. The historical success of anticolonial nationalist movements in promoting the use of the Irish language in addition to the ongoing anticolonial nationalist struggle in Northern Ireland indicate that this conflict is a predictor of Irish language revitalization success.

Additional research is needed in order to determine how language legislation impacts the amount of speakers long term, as well as how Brexit will affect the identity struggle and language use in Northern Ireland.

label: The Revolutionary Act of Staying Indoors
nurj_title: The Revolutionary Act of Staying Indoors
text:
ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20

Northwestern University

The Revolutionary Act of Staying Indoors

Thomas Kikuchi

Asian Languages and Cultures Senior Seminar 397

Professor Paola Zamperini

12/4/2020

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 Introduction

There is a certain condition that exists in modern Japan that plagues people’s lives and causes their world to come to a halt.  Here, the mere thought of leaving their room is unthinkable, let alone going to school or working. They fill their time with games and other mindless entertainment, continuing to live on in their world away from society. Such is the

Hikikomori, or as it roughly translates to acute social withdrawal.  By nature, it is hard to say just how much this condition plagues Japanese people, as they seclude themselves in their rooms, hidden from the world.  However, somewhere along with this narrative, the media has portrayed

Hikikomori as mostly young adult men.  Even in academia, the ratio of male to female

Hikikomori is reported as 4:1 (Teo, 2010).  Due to the inherent nature of this condition, it is difficult to make a definitive conclusion as to whether or not this bias is true.  Regardless of this ratio, societal understandings of a condition that is 4 times more prevalent among men reveal much about the underlying gender expectations that Japanese men face.  Therefore, these heavily skewed societal understandings of Hikikomori and will alter how women who are in similar positions are portrayed.

Definitions of a Hikikomori

It is first important to define Hikikomori to get a full understanding of its uniqueness from other psychopathologies.  In his literary review, Alan Teo cites the Ministry of Health,

Labor, and Welfare for Japan on their criteria.

1. A lifestyle centered at home

2. No interest or willingness to attend school or work

3. Persistence of symptoms beyond six months

4. Other mental disorders have been excluded

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 5. Among those with no interest or willingness to attend school or work, those who maintain personal relationships (e.g., friendships) have been excluded (Teo, 2010)

During this social withdrawal, they typically do not leave their room, and have no close and intimate contact with people, except for some exchanges with family members. What’s important to note is that people may exhibit these tendencies in various ways that make it hard to predict and generalize behaviors. There are cases where people may communicate exclusively through the internet or some cases where people may step outside, though during times when they feel like they can go unnoticed by society. Notice the emphasis on other mental disorders being excluded; meaning that while Hikikomori may display other symptoms of other mental illnesses, that something about their condition is uniquely different than other diagnoses. By definition, the diagnostic material does not specify gender and does not yet recommend different types of treatment.  Therefore, there must be some societal explanation that would explain where such a distinct narrative on the gender difference in Hikikomori.

Psychopathology of Hikikomori Based on Gender

A study done in 2019 by Yong and Nomura reveals that dropping out of schooling or work is heavily associated with Hikikomori.  This may be due to childhood trauma that stems from bullying or the ultimate failure to achieve societal expectations.  It’s important to note the importance of good schooling, which many believe leads directly into a high-paying job and the association of this to masculinity.  If we follow the perspective of the male Hikikomori, the argument here is that their relation to manhood has been taken away from them.  A review in 212 by Vandello and Bossan calls this phenomenon precarious manhood, as they describe the criteria as follows:

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 1.Manhood must be earned (in the context of society, this would be a high-paying job)

2. Manhood can be taken away at any point in time.

3. You must display this manhood for others to see (stressing the importance that manhood is a social construct and is only sustained through social approval).

Many Hikikomori develop their social withdrawal tendencies in the early 20s and indicating their failure to transition from childhood to adulthood.  For the Hikikomori male, when they shut themselves in their room, this is their way of reclaiming that adulthood and defining masculinity for themselves.

But for women, it is more likely that their struggles continue to go unnoticed.  In their study, Yong and Numura also cite that while they found a gender difference between men and women Hikikomori, other studies are not so conclusive (Yong, Numura, 2019).  Especially in rural areas of Japan, the ratio of men and women who are Hikikomori is very similar.  In another survey by Yong, et al., they found a distinction in the association of men and women

Hikikomori, “Furthermore, after adjusting for all tested variables as possible confounding factors, being jobless and having fewer outdoor frequencies were associated with being a hikikomori man, and being a homemaker and having no social support were associated with being a hikikomori woman.”  Clearly, the way in which Hikikomori present themselves is very different, with significant emphasis on jobs for men and homemaker for women.  While still pertaining to their social roles, it is the case that Hikikomori women’s struggles are “invisible,” and thus lack the support and space in society to have their voices heard.

Hikikomori in Anime

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 It’s important to talk about anime as this is one such form that Hikikomori will consume.

The concept of animation being able to depict anything to the creator’s ability opens an entire world full of creative possibilities.  Though, as it seems to be in the case of Hikikomori, the stereotype of Otaku also gets linked to them.  Otaku is seen to be very materialistic and also overindulge in purchasing anime paraphernalia.  Things like figures, posters, manga, mousepads, games, etc. all have a purpose in allowing these consumers to purchase a lot and fill their room to the brim.  In some ways, it offers escapism, but at the same time, it isolates people even more and collects into a suffocating pile of consumerist trash.  Of course, each case of Hikikomori is different and unique, but given the stereotype that often is associated with Hikimori about being anime lovers, it is worthwhile to analyze how someone who is a Hikikomori might view themselves through this lens.

Caption: Image that advertises the anime for Himotou Umaru-Chan.  Besides the brown-haired character, every other humanoid figure in the frame is Umaru, though notice the distinction between her two forms.  She has many more expressions in her Chibi form and emphasizes her self-indulgent nature when she is in this form.

Himiotou Umaru-Chan is one such anime that presents the resistance from society for a woman to express her antisocial tendencies in an attempt to sell her deviances as cute and commodifiable.  Umaru is a younger sister, a high school girl, and most importantly, a self-

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 indulgent gamer.  Her character represents an interesting dichotomy; in public, she has perfect looks, achieves perfect grades, and is always humble and gracious making her the ideal girl.

Though, when she comes home after school, she transforms into a cute chibi version of herself who will stay up throughout the night to play games, eat unhealthily, and keep up on all of the anime shows.  In this form, she is helpless, in both physical form and mental capabilities, and all she knows how to do is play games and eat convenience store snacks.  Instead of going outside to get her own food, she relies on her brother to provide for her and either cook or pick up snacks for her on his way home from work.  Her ideal social standings juxtaposed with such a self- indulgent nature all point to the impossibility of her character, which creates the appeal of the show.  Even though she seems to be the most capable, she still relies on her brother to provide the most necessities to her.  In her chibi-state, this helplessness enables viewers to feel a sense of superiority to her through her cute demeanor and soft design.  This means that the things she says and her desires can be dismissed as something of a childish desire and not be read into much further.  Yet when we consider how these qualities in women are undesirable, we can further see the more problematic tendencies of this representation.

In one scene where Umaru-chan is left to attend her apartment alone, we see her in a more naturalistic and regressive state.  She can fully eat any snack she wants and drink as much cola as she can, all while playing her favorite game without her brother watching over her telling her when to go to bed.  Instead of throwing a party or going out to social events, the emphasis of worry is focused more on if Umaru can properly take care of herself, drawing on her dependency on her older brother.  When he finally returns from his business trip, we see her rush to him and confess how, despite being able to stay up as late as she wanted, she missed her brother and the dependent relationship is reinforced.  For a Hikikomori to be sustainable, they will need the

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 support of someone, even though the relationship is skewed.  However, Umaru herself cannot be classified as a Hikikomori.  For one, she is designed as a high school girl, and she still goes to school, achieves perfect grades even.  For another, she has a group of friends who she hangs out with throughout the show.  However, it’s important to note that these things all take place in another form, her ideal form.  This is what she wears when she is seen by people who she doesn’t know, and when she comes home, that is her other form.

The idea that Umaru cannot be represented as one person in one form, and that the tendency to play games and eat junk food has to be represented in a more digestible and cute form of a young high school girl plays on the idea of the impossibility of society to accept that women are allowed to express antisocial tendencies.  For more or less, Umaru is still expected to produce, and only has the night time to be comfortable.  There’s another dynamic to the show that is people finding out about her “true” nature at home.  One character, Kirie, befriends

Umaru in her “true” form, referring to her as sensei, as a sign of respect and admiration.

Umaru’s character represents Japanese society’s reluctance to cast women in roles of those who are shut-ins and enjoy games, because of the assumption that women need to be desirable to men.  It’s not enough to just represent these problems in anime, but create it in a cute and marketable way that appeals to a wider male audience.

Conclusion

With animated depictions of women like this, creators can get the ideal version of a woman at the expense of minimizing someone’s problems and experiences.  Some numbers estimate that the amount of Hikikomori present in Japanese society today may be in the millions and that this problem will continue to rise if things are not done.  Is this just an act of reclaiming one’s gender identity, or is it also a problem that continues to be overlooked by the masses?

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

12/5/20 Society’s tendency to create desirable depictions of women and create them into a marketable form of media only further alienates and alters the experiences of said population.  In that same vein, for men, it creates an even more isolating and pressured instance of providing for society.

Again, the gender-role of being a provider has fallen onto men.

It’s important to note too, there is a prevalence of Hikikomori in other countries as well.

Social isolation is a common theme among many late-stage capitalist societies.  Japan, however, has taken a different approach to tackle this concept, as it is more talked accepted in society as a condition.  Other countries, for example, do not have the same kind of language or understanding for social isolation (Kato, 2011).  This is a condition that is reactionary to a larger issue within a society that asks us to turn our bodies into a producing machine.  Our sense of worth is determined by our proximity to capital gain, and when that sense of value is lost, how are we to ever gain it back?

People’s self-worth should not be based on their relation to goods but their relationship with others.  We have effectively removed that by reinforcing stereotypes against many identities, including gender.  As we reconcile with how to properly address sexism within our society, it should also reflect our healthcare and how we care for people.  Yet, we are so focused on only those who produce, men, and the phenomena that they suddenly remove all of the desire to want to work.  In this way, we are overlooking the problems of other identities and effectively bias our understanding and treatment.  In this way, if we value the lives of those most vulnerable and overlooked, we can begin to change the ways of thinking and how societies are run.

Humans are not meant to be alone, rather grow together.

ALC 397 Senior Seminar

Thomas Kikuchi

Radical Caring

A Qualitative Study on the Role of Frontline Workers in Eradicating Gender-Based Violence in

Asian American Communities

Chloe Wong Weinberg School of Arts and Sciences

Advisor: Prof. Shalini Shankar

Department of Anthropology

- Sun Hee*

“I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, so I had been working on my own healing journey for a number of years. When the

Children’s Advocate job came up, I was at the crossroads of thinking about my career… having this job come up that seemed to blend together my desire to put energy outwards instead of just focusing on inner healing for myself, this was really crucial.”

*All names and organizations in this presentation are pseudonyms to protect the identities of my interlocutors.

What is Gender-Based Violence?

“an umbrella term for any harmful act that is perpetuated against a person based on socially ascribed (i.e gender) differences between males and females. It includes acts that inflict physical, sexual or mental harm and suffering, threats of such acts, coercion, and other deprivation of liberty. These acts can occur in public or in private” (Inter-Agency, 2010).

21-55% of Asian women in the US report experiencing intimate physical and/or sexual violence during their lifetime, based on a compilation of disagregated samples of Asian ethnicities in local communities (APIGBV, 2015).

Radical caring is the amalgamation of individual and organizational motivations,along with personal responsibility, to care for survivors.

— Rudrappa, 2004

Frontline workers are direct service professionals who “comfort, advocate for, and assist victims and survivors of gender-based violence”

— Wies and Haldane, 2011

Women of Asian Descent Were 6 of the 8 Victims in Atlanta Shootings

THE ATLANTA SHOOTING AND THE DEHUMANIZING OF ASIAN WOMEN

To live through this period as an Asian-American is to feel trapped in an American tragedy while being denied the legitimacy of being an American.

Atlanta shootings show Asian women’s vulnerability in the workplace

A Century Of Objectifying Asian Women: How Race Played A Role In Atlanta Shootings

STRUCTURAL VIOLENCE AGAINST ASIAN

AMERICAN COMMUNITIES

Imperialism Racism

“White sexual imperialism” -

Sunny Woan

(2008)

State-sanction ed bigotry and hate (ex. The

Page Act of

1875)

Asian American

Critical Race

Theory (AsianCrit)

Story, Theory, and

Praxis (Curammeng, Buenavista, and

Cariaga, 2017)

Q#1

How do frontline workers view their work relative to their racial and ethnic identities?

RESEARCH QUESTIONS

Q#2

How can radical caring, and Asian American Critical Race Theory be used as frameworks of understanding the labor of frontline workers?

THEORY & METHODOLOGY

Asian American Critical Race Theory

Story, Theory, and Praxis

Ethnographic

Fieldwork

6 weeks at a domestic violence agency in Chicago

Documenting lived experiences as it is impacted by gender, race, etc.

Key Informant

Interviews

14 interviews with frontline workers from 5 agencies across Chicagoland

Feminist Ethnography

Researcher Positionality

Individual

Community

Relationship

Societal

Biological and personal history factors of frontline workers

Close relationships between frontline workers and survivors

Settings in which healing and caring relationships occur

Combatting the broad structural factors that lead to violence

SOCIO-ECOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR VIOLENCE PREVENTION

INDIVIDUAL LEVEL

“Growing up in a very collectivistic culture, you hear a lot about things like, “If a man beats you, it’s okay.” I’ve heard it and seen it to be very normalized and it has always bothered me. I have seen the manifestations of domestic violence in my relatives. Two of these girls were actually my nieces… They used to be very upbeat and friendly, very jolly.

After all these years, I was quite shocked, like what the hell happened to you, not only physically but emotionally.”

- Munira

Themes:

● Personal History of Trauma (Sun Hee)

● Shared Immigrant Identities

○ First-Generation Immigrants ● Resonating with Culturally-Specific Agencies

CONCLUSIONS

Complex Interactions between Personal, Social, and Professional

Factors Translate in

Radical Caring

The professional advocacy of Asian American frontline workers is intertwined with their lived experiences, life histories, and intimate knowledge of communities.

MOVING FORWARD

Asian American feminist voices are crucial in identifying the political connectedness of their everyday experiences.

Deep coalitions should be formed with care providers within academic conversations of gender-based violence.

Thank you.

Questions?

Know The Different Types of Loans

And How to Manage Them

Private vs Federal Student Loans

Let’s start with the basics, there are two types of student loans: private and federal student loans. With your first thought you might be thinking, “Does it really matter? They're basically the same, either way, I'll be taking out money that I'll have to pay back.” In hindsight, you'll learn that these two have their own advantages and disadvantages. To start, let’s look at what these two are at their most basic level.

Federal loans are granted by the government, specifically the Department of Education. These loans will either be subsidized or unsubsidized, something you can learn more about in the next section. Federal loans have set interest rates, decided by Congress, that won't change over the term of your loan. The repayment term for federal loans are set at 10 years but can be extended if you choose to look into different plans. To apply for a federal student loan, you'll have to fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). The FAFSA determines if you qualify for a federal loan, taking into account what your family can pay or your expected family contribution. The FAFSA is something you'll be using a lot in terms of applying for student loans and financial aid purposes. Federal student loans also have better options if you're struggling with repayment by giving you 270 days before default versus the 120 days for private loans, many helpful repayment plans, and more!

Private student loans can be a little trickier, as they can have many other options. A private student loan is any loan that is not provided by the government. These loans will be issued by a bank, credit union, or any other private company. Unlike federal loans, you'll have to pay interest on these through school and have fewer benefits than some federal loans that pay your interest while in school. The interest rates on private loans tend to be higher and can be extremely high, some being over 18.00%. The repayment options on these loans may be limited and they don't offer loan forgiveness programs. Credit scores and a possible cosigner may be required to take out a private loan as well. You may be thinking, “Why would I ever take out a private loan?" In some cases, they're just necessary. Private loans can be beneficial when you need a bigger loan amount or don't qualify for a subsidized student loan. Interest rates vary, but it may be a good option if you plan on refinancing once you get an awesome paying career after school.

Subsidized vs Unsubsidized Student Loans

Student loans can be extremely complicated and intimidating. Hopefully by the end of this, you'll have a better understanding of two of the major types of student loans. When applying for a federal student loan, they'll be either direct subsidized or direct unsubsidized. Private loans are a whole different beast, which we'll also dive into. But first, let’s focus on federal loans as they are the most common. Subsidized and unsubsidized loans (sometimes called Subsidized Stafford Loans and Unsubsidized Stafford Loans) have their similarities and differences. Knowing about each one is important when deciding how you'll tackle paying off your loan in the long run and how the interest works for each.

A subsidized student loan is a loan that the government will pay interest for while you're in school. This means that if you apply for a principal loan of $20,000 as a freshman, your loan will still be for $20,000 after four years because the government paid for the interest costs. Not a bad deal, right?! If you put your loan into deferment or forbearance after graduation, they'll also pay the interest on your loan. Another great thing about subsidized loans is the fact that no payments are due until six months after you graduate, commonly known as the grace period, allowing you some time to find a job - which is a huge stress reliever. The downside of a subsidized student loan is that they're only for students who have financial struggles. If your parents make over a certain amount of income each year, then you won't qualify. You can find out if you're eligible for a subsidized loan by filling out and submitting the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). A maximum loan amount for a borrower is $23,000 so you may have to borrow more through unsubsidized federal loans or a private loan. Sadly, graduate students don't qualify for subsidized loans.

Abstract

Spontaneous Auditory Neuron Activity

Shreya Sriram1, George Ordiway1 & Jason Tait Sanchez1,2,3

1Roxelyn and Richard Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders, 2Knowles Hearing Research Center, 3Department of Neurobiology, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL. USA

Synaptic connections between neurons is typically established through spontaneous activity in vertebrates. Spontaneous activity is the occurrence of neuronal events – such as intrinsic action potentials (APs) or postsynaptic currents – in the absence of external stimuli. Generally, when a neuron is isolated in a brainstem slice, spontaneous activity is not seen because physiological conditions are not applicable. However, we have previously reported spontaneous intrinsic AP activity in a subgroup of neurons in the avian auditory brainstem (termed NMc). The goal of this project aimed to characterize spontaneous synaptic activity of NMc neurons. We identified spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) that were mediated by ionotropic AMPA receptors (AMPA-Rs) and GABAA receptors (GABAA-Rs).

Whole-cell voltage clamp recordings were obtained from domesticated chickens at embryonic (E) days E19-E21. Spontaneous postsynaptic excitatory currents (sEPSCs) were recorded by voltage clamping neurons near their resting membrane potential (-60 mV) for 2 minutes. Synaptic transmission through AMPA-Rs and GABAA-Rs were blocked depending on which synaptic currents were isolated and studied. sEPSC properties were recorded and analyzed before, during, and after bath application of CNQX (AMPA-R blocker), or PTX (GABAA-R blocker). NMDA-Rs were blocked with AP-V to isolate the other currents. Data reported are from 19 NMc neurons.

Method

Background

Funding: NIH, NIDCD R01 DC017167 & R03 DC013841 (JTS) School of Communication and The Knowles Hearing Research Center, Northwestern University

(A) NMc neurons receive multiple synaptic inputs onto their dendrites and soma, unlike traditional adendritic NM neurons which receive 1-2 large Endbulb of Held synapses. (B) NMc neurons are more excitable, have a lower threshold for AP firing and are more depolarized compared to traditional NM neurons. (C) Schematic of the neurotransmitters glutamate and GABA, and the postsynaptic receptors they bind to. Figure 1 (A & B) adopted from Hong and Sanchez (2018), Journal of Experimental Neuroscience.

Conclusions

1. sEPSCs of NMc neurons are mediated by AMPA-Rs and GABAA-Rs.

2. Frequency and amplitude of sEPSCs were not correlated with low voltage activated potassium currents (LVAK+), suggesting that spontaneous synaptic activity is not related to intrinsic excitability.

3. sEPSC frequency and amplitude were correlated, suggesting that more synaptic events have larger average amplitudes.

4. Spontaneous AMPA and GABA neurotransmission suggests that NMc synaptic inputs are complex and specialized.

Validating Genetic Tools to Isolate Individual ipRGC Subtypes

Madison Luce*, Ely Contreras, Tiffany Schmidt

Department of Neurobiology, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208, USA Introduction

Objectives

Conclusions

Future Experiments

Acknowledgements

• Light regulates the mammalian vertebrate visual system to affect both image-forming and non-image forming behaviors • Light is detected by the classic rod and cone photoreceptors, and by a newly discovered, third class of photoreceptors, intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) • The extent to which ipRGC subtypes differ in their gene expression and how each individual subtype contributes to visual behavior is unknown • To address this gap in knowledge, it is important to develop new tools which can genetically isolate individual ipRGC subtypes • The Schmidt Lab has developed a new Opn4FlpO mouse line (FlpO: flippase recombinase) to be used in an intersectional genetic strategy, to target subsets of ipRGCs

• Validate the newly developed Opn4FlpO mouse line as a tool in an intersectional genetic strategy to isolate, ablate, and manipulate ipRGC subsets Ø Does the line target and label all ipRGCs or merely a subset? Ø Does the mouse line label other non-ipRGC mouse lines?

• The Opn4FlpO line can be crossed with single- reporters, RCE:FRT and Ai65F, to label ipRGCs with a fluorescent protein • The Opn4 staining confirmed that the Opn4FlpO mouse line labels ipRGCs; however, not all GFP- labeled cells co-immunolabeled with Opn4 Ø These cells are likely M4, M5, and M6 ipRGC subtypes • The cross with the RCE:FRT line labels more cells than the Ai65F reporter mouse line

• Investigate the identity of the non-Opn4, GFP- labeled cells Ø To do so, I will immunostain for other markers of ipRGCs, such as SMI-32 • Inject Cre and FlpO dependent viruses into the retinas of Opn4Cre; Opn4FlpO mice to further characterize the intersectional genetic strategy

This work was funded by the NIH grant 1DP2EY027983 for T.M.S., as well as a Sloan Research Fellowship and Klingenstein-Simons Fellowship in the Neurosciences to TMS. I would like to thank the Schmidt lab members for their support.

The Impact of Framing on Decision-Making in the Context of COVID-19

Abigail Furdak Northwestern University Department of Economics

Background

• People can make different decisions based upon the same set of facts depending on the framing, or phrasing and presentation, of that information1 • Previous research found that people have a higher appetite for risk when information is framed negatively2

Methods

• Goal: create a more realistic framing study by applying concepts to COVID-19 • Participants were asked if they would go out to dinner during the pandemic • 503 responses were collected through online surveys • Each participant was told the risk of dining out, framed 1 of 3 ways:

Negative Frame

There is a 2.75% chance that you will become infected with COVID-19

Positive Frame

There is a 97.25% chance that you will be safe from COVID-19 Relationship Frame

There is a 2.75% chance that you will expose your household to COVID-19

•All subjects were asked if they would dine out given 2.75%, 5.50%, and 8.25% risk levels3 •Subjects also provided demographic information:

Pre-existing

Conditions

Political Affiliation Sex

Age Living Situation Education

Research Question Does framing, or scenario portrayal, influence people’s decision-making during COVID-19?

Results

Figure 1: Share of Respondents Opting to Dine Out for Each Frame and Infection Probability

COVID-19 Infection Probability

Key Findings 1. Receiving the positive frame increases the probability of dining out relative to receiving the negative frame 2. Receiving the relationship frame decreases the likelihood of going out compared with receiving the negative frame

Discussion

Implications of results: • Employ relationship framing to inspire risk- aversion and encourage people to take precautions • Use positive framing to spur economic activity if pandemic outlook or treatments improve Suggestions for future research: • Control for income or socioeconomic status • Create a more diverse participant pool • Collect survey responses at multiple stages during a future pandemic

• Regression models were performed to evaluate the statistical significance of findings and to control for demographic variables • Key Finding 1 was statistically significant at the 5.50% and 8.25% infection risk levels • Key Finding 2 was significant at all 3 risk levels • Framing increases or decreases the probability of dining out by 0.10-0.15 where significant

Conclusion

Framing influences decision-making in the context of COVID-19. • Receiving positively framed information increases risk-seeking behavior compared with receiving negatively framed information • Receiving the relationship frame increases risk- aversion compared with receiving the negative frame

Machine Learning to Identify Cells in Zebrafish-Skin Patterns

Harita Duggirala    (Computer Science, 2024)

haritaduggirala2024@u.northwestern.edu

Broad Motivation deccanherald.com

Zebrafish deccanherald.com

Zebrafish (Danio rerio) share a similar genetic structure to humans. Their black pigment cells (melanophores) are related to the originating cells for melanoma in humans.The skin patterns of zebrafish are comprised of horizontal stripes of different colored pigment cells. Accurately quantifying the cell size of various pigment cells in relation to their location on the skin is a crucial step towards better understanding cell behavior.

Motivation for My Project

Determine the size and distribution of black pigment cells (melanophores) in the stripes.

Approach: Machine learning to extract cells from fish images in an automated process

Challenges

●Machine learning methods are often a black box ●Fish pictures are taken under various lighting conditions & microscopic lenses (see below)

Objectives

●Automatically extract black cells from a large set of fish images ●Quantitatively describe how different machine learning methods influence resulting measurements

Method

●Identify black cells manually in small set of images using Ilastik ●Utilize batch processing to generate predictions of black cells for larger set of images ●Quantitatively describe effects of using different initial training sets on accuracy of cell prediction

Role of Training Set on Results

Our results show that using different images for training during machine learning has: ●Minimal effect on our predictions of cell size ●Significant effect on the number of cells we extract

Future Research

●Compare accuracy of different image processing software to determine optimal method for extracting cells from fish images ●Isolate and determine the individual effects of different lighting and microscopic-lens conditions on the accuracy of our cell predictions

Acknowledgments

●Close-up images of cells courtesy of Hans Georg Frohnhöfer and Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard (Max Planck Institute for Developmental Biology) ●The study resulting in this presentation was assisted by a grant administered by Northwestern University's Office of Undergraduate Research. However, the conclusions, opinions, and other statements in this presentation are the author's and not necessarily those of the sponsoring institution. ●Thank you to Dr. Alexandria Volkening for your mentorship and support for this project.

label: Food as Power, Growing as Resistance
nurj_title: Food as Power, Growing as Resistance
text:
Abstract In an interview with Elizabeth Hoover, Muckleshoot nutrition educator Valerie Segrest remarked, “When our foods cease to exist, so do we as a people.” For Indigenous peoples, food takes on meanings beyond simple sustenance; it serves as a conduit between us and the land we occupy with its own complex histories, acting as both an agent of cultural significance and a metric of power. To analyze this Indigenous understanding of food, I will explore the contributions of the federal nutrition assistance programs in the disruption of Indigenous food systems and, more specifically, how the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR) undermines foodways and Native nation sovereignty as a consequence. This assessment will be juxtaposed with a narrative representation of the cultural history and modern power dynamics surrounding a single native seed: manoomin. Through this chronicle, I aim to emulate the style of Robin-Wall Kimmerer’s Braiding Sweetgrass to demonstrate how plants can teach us about power, culture, violence, and healing. This narrative will position a region-specific story of one native plant against a broader discussion of culturally significant foods and Indigenous food sovereignty at a federal level. The combination of these two dialogues puts forth an understanding of the paradoxical position of food as not only a life-giving source but also a medium of colonial violence.

Who is manoomin?

“It’s almost a slogan that we say, ‘Let the food bring us together.’ In our community, sharing the bounty is one of the primary community connections—our foods are an opportunity to bring generations together and bind families around the dinner table and connect them to other families when they share their bounty … It’s easy for many Native communities to feel isolated from other communities or to feel a sense of remoteness, but gatherings like these show that’s just an illusion. We are all very connected and gatherings like this are key to keeping those bonds strong. ” -Ken Hoyt 1

In Anishinaabe tradition, as the Creator gathered the elements and began sculpting Turtle

Island, the last to be formed was Nanabozho, the Original Man. Part-man and part-spirit,

Nanabozho defined what it means to be human and did so through learning from those predating his existence: the plants, the animals, and the land. Through their teachings, he made Turtle

1 “Traditional Foods.” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, August 16, 2021. https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/ndwp/traditional-foods/index.html.

Island his home, a home which supported him in exchange for his reciprocal generosity. In his 2 journeys, Nanabozho oftentimes struggled as he stumbled along learning to live through the land.

Returning home from a hunt without having gathered food, Nanabozho noticed a duck sitting near his warming kettle. Upon his return, the duck flew away, leaving behind a bundle of wild rice floating atop the boiling water. The next day, Nanabozho traveled in the direction of the duck in hopes of understanding the source of this gift and was greeted by a plant who had found a home in water. This home, of course, was a wild rice bed; its resident was manoomin. It was 3 because of the kindness of the duck that Nanabozho learned the virtue that would be passed down through generations to come: rice is life.

Years later, the children of Nanabozho came to sow their own relationship with manoomin. As the Anishinaabe were residing in an area now known as the east coast, they were visited by seven prophets. Each of these spirits brought with them Seven Fires, divinations of the times to come. The Seven Fires acted as the compass, guiding the Anishinaabe away from impending violence and towards their new home, a land where “food grows on water.” Through 45 the prophecies, the Anishinaabe returned to the lands walked by their original ancestor and became Indigenous to a once-unfamiliar part of Turtle Island. Who is manoomin? For

Anishinaabe peoples, manoomin is an unraveling of time, intertwining legacies of history and modern foundations of community.6

6 Courtney Calia and Kathy Smith. What is wild? Manoomin (wild rice) harvesting w/ Courtney and Kathy. The Red Nation Podcast. Podcast audio. October 28, 2019, https://open.spotify.com/episode/2LrkFI9agQphbcVZck5JTr?si=1t_FXp4AT6GZT9f3KWDk2g

5 Kaminski, June. “7 Fires Prophesy.” Chi Manidoo: Great Spirit of my Anishinabe Ojibwe Ancestors, 2005. http://www.chi-manidoo.com/7fires.html.

4 “Prophecy of the Seven Fires.” Passamaquoddy at Sipayik. Pleasant Point Tribal Government. Accessed November 16, 2021. http://www.wabanaki.com/wabanaki_new/Seven_Fires_Prophecy.html.

3 LaDuke, Winona. “Wild Rice Moon.” Sierra 85, no. 5 (2000).

2 Wall-Kimmerer, Robin. “In the Footsteps of Nanabozho: Becoming Indigenous to Place.” Chapter. In Braiding Sweetgrass, 205–215. Canada: Milkweed Editions, 2013.

Thanks, Adam Smith

Through systemic land displacement, climate violence, and other manifestations of settler colonialism, the state currently known as the U.S. government and its subscribers have disrupted

Indigenous food systems and traditional agricultural practices since contact. In response to 7

Indigenous self-advocacy surrounding food insecurity, the U.S. government began to extend welfare programs to Native Nations in the 20th century, including Supplemental Nutrition

Assistance Programs (SNAP) outlined in the Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA) of 1933.

SNAP, however, proved unsuccessful in solving the so-called problem of Indian food shortages and similar legislation has been repeatedly passed to supplement this New Deal program since its inception. In 1973, under the Agricultural and Consumer Protection Act, Congress established the initiative which later came to be known as the Food Distribution Program on Indian

Reservations (FDPIR) to be administered through the United States Department of Agriculture

(USDA). This was primarily in response to a lack of substantive change in the food status on reservation lands, a shortcoming that governmental officials attributed to a lack of sufficient

SNAP offices.8

The Agricultural and Consumer Protection Act outlines steps towards bolstering federal assistance using the language of “commodity distribution” when describing the formation of the

FDPIR. This verbiage gestures to the inscription of the settler-capitalist idea of food as 9 commodity as a foundational feature of this food pathway. Gilio-Whitaker describes this

9 House of Representatives, “Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act of 1973” (2019).

8 Finegold, Kenneth, Nancy Pindus, Diane Levy, Tess Tannehill, and Walter Hillabrant. “Tribal Food Assistance: A Comparison of Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (FDPIR) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).” The Urban Institute, November 2009. https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/28396/412034-Tribal-Food-Assistance.PDF.

7 Gilio-Whitaker, Dina. “Food Is Medicine, Water Is Life.” Chapter. In As Long as Grass Grows: The Indigenous Fight for Environmental Justice, from Colonization to Standing Rock. Beacon Press, 2019.

phenomenon as settler-industrialism, the process by which colonizers strip previously existing economies and replace them with their own. What effects does this ideological imposition have 10 on the relationship between Indigenous peoples and their food? The answer is not particularly succinct but can be explored through discussions of the ways in which Indigenous peoples have responded and resisted FDPIR.

Manoominike Giizis and Lighting the Eighth Fire

“It's Manoominike Giizis, the wild rice making moon on a string of lakes in the heart of Ojibwe country. There is nothing so defining of Ojibwe people, perhaps as the wild rice harvest, and this year looks to be a good one--the rice falls gently into the canoes, laughter sounds across the lake, and boats pull in with men and women full of rice worms and smiles. ” -Winona LaDuke 11

August marks the beginning of the Wild Rice Making Moon, Manoominike Giizis, a celebration of history, community, and the gift of rice. After their migration to the Great Lakes region, Anishinaabe peoples trusted in manoomin and maple for sustenance during their time of uncertain foundations. The harvest of wild rice in the fall sustained them all throughout the winter; right as the rice grew depleted, the time for syrup harvesting cycled around to provide nourishment into the spring. The manoomin and maple trees work together, taking turns in conversation to keep the food system balanced. Through Manoominike Giizis, the people honor 12 this natural harmony and follow the example set by these plants, acting together in community to harvest, process, and store manoomin. The accompanying teachings are twofold: a keeping of culture and a dialogue of ecological knowledge. In this annual collective of sharing and learning,

12 Calia and Smith, 2019.

11 LaDuke, Winona. “Manoominike Giizis.” The Circle: News from the American Indian Perspective. October 1, 2009, sec. 1.

10 Gilio-Whitaker, 2019.

Anishinaabe keep their stories alive through generations and preserve what is now frequently referred to as sustainable agricultural practices.13

Manoominike Giizis does not only hold significance for Anishinaabe localized near their homelands. The last part of the prophecy of the Seven Fires is the lighting of an Eighth Fire– there will come a time when people seek reconnection, to “retrace their steps to find what was left by the trail.” Like the outstretching of roots, Manoominike Giizis reaches out to carry 14

Anishinaabe peoples back to their ancestral geographies, reminding everyone of their past and present relationship with the earth. Not only does the festival draw in Anishinaabe from across

Turtle Island but it also draws members of other Native Nations, serving as a representation of the multicultural identities and a unification of Indigenous peoples through shared harvest. Kathy

Smith, a member of the Keweenaw Bay Indian Community, reflects with adoration upon the lighting of the Eighth Fire: “We’re all going to come together and become one.” Manoominike 15

Giizis is, thus, not only about the preservation of tradition and history but also about reimagining and building a more equitable, unified landscape. Who is manoomin? Manoomin is a teacher through which we can understand the complex functions assumed by culturally significant plants for Indigenous peoples, providing context to the greater food sovereignty movement.

Aid Ain’t Equity

In a recent article, the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium (ANTHC) celebrated the expansion of FDPIR in Alaska—from 32 people at its inception to 827 participants in 2018. A 16

16 “Celebrating 10 Years of the ANTHC Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations.” Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, August 27, 2018. https://anthc.org/news/celebrating-10-years-of-the-anthc-food-distribution-program-on-indian-reservations/.

15 Calia and Smith, 2019.

14 “Prophecy of the Seven Fires.” Passamaquoddy at Sipayik. Pleasant Point Tribal Government.

13 “Akiing: Where The Wild Rice Grows.” Honor The Earth. Accessed November 16, 2021. https://www.honorearth.org/akiing_where_the_wild_rice_grows.

2009 study by the Urban Institute found that the national enrollment rate generally levels out around 80-90 thousand participants ; this is in comparison to the hundreds of thousands of 17

Indigenous people living below the poverty line on reservation lands. What mechanism 18 underlies this relative low rate of enrollment? One possible explanation is the lack of culturally significant foods available through FDPIR. FDPIR and other governmental food assistance programs rely heavily on Western foods such as beef, bacon, flour, coffee, salt, and sugar. The rapid forced adoption of a high-calorie European diet yet low in nutritional value has been cited as a possible underpinning of the higher rates of chronic health conditions in Indigenous communities. This includes diabetes, which is one of the leading causes of death on 19 reservations and whose rates are about 15.9% across Nations as compared to the national average of 11.7%, but it may reach upwards of 33% in some communities such as the Navajo Nation.20

The formation of FDPIR and related programs can be understood as reactionary policies aiming to reverse some of the impacts of systematic land displacement, serving instead to strengthen the colonial relationship between the federal government and Native Nations.

Assistance programs characterized by malnutritious foods are, thus, a form of violence against

Indigenous bodies, erasing culturally significant foods and exacerbating health disparities. The low rates of enrollment in FDPIR may be viewed as a form of resistance to this ongoing colonialism; this protest is directly connected to the growing Indigenous reclamation of traditional foods through the establishment of sovereign food systems.

20 Gillio-Whitaker, 2019.

19 Hoover, Elizabeth. “‘You Can't Say You're Sovereign If You Can't Feed Yourself’: Defining and Enacting Food Sovereignty in American Indian Community Gardening.” American Indian Culture and Research Journal 41, no. 3 (2017): 31–70.

18 “Living Conditions.” Native American Aid. A Program of Partnership with Native Americans. Accessed November 16, 2021. http://www.nativepartnership.org/site/PageServer?pagename=naa_livingconditions.

17 Finegold et. al, 2009.

The Rights of Manoomin

“Seed sovereignty is to me when you have an understanding of your inherent right to save seed and pass it on to future generations, and that you are exercising it at that same time. It also means that you as a person or as a community are self-informed and dictate your relationship to seed; that says that there are seeds that really do not belong to anyone. They belong to us as a community in the commons but that we can define our relationship to that seed based upon our own values and not the values of anyone else outside of our community.” -Rowen 21

White

Cut from the tool book of colonialism, slow violence is a patiently calamitous force with the capacity to undercut the deepest rooted communities. It is characterized by a passive but intentional disruption of health, safety, culture, and knowledge. Such is the case of one 22 population, which found itself under threat of an encroaching colonial force by the name of

Bayer CropScience in 2006. Backed by Bayer, an invader quietly slithered into aboriginal habitats and inscribed itself over this native population, superimposing unto the land and threatening generations to come. Agrobusiness, however, is not the only perpetrator in this violence: academica-endorsed seed mutation working behind the smokescreen of scientific progress likewise serves as a longstanding threat to the conservation of manoomin.

No stranger to colonialism, Indigenous people and proximal agricultural organizations began to recognize this discreet erasure and brought it to the surface in the early 2000s. For

Bayer, this attention culminated in a lawsuit, accusing them of allowing their appetizingly named

“LibertyLink” rice to contaminate and threaten local rice beds. Having not yet even received

USDA approval for this genetically modified strain, Bayer lost the lawsuit, but the damage to

22 Nixon, Rob. “Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor.” Introduction. In Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2013.

21 Hoover, 2017.

native rice farms had already been thoroughly executed. As native seeds received this blow in 23 one area of the country, researchers at the University of Minnesota were being called out for the same attempted modification of manoomin in the Midwest. Winona LaDuke points to the importance of bringing “ethics into relationships with Indigenous people” in order to “stop the destructive patterns of research” characterizing the genetic modification of seeds. Genetic 24 modification directly threatens seed sovereignty and, consequently, cultural pervasiveness and brilliance. Who is manoomin? Manoomin is a survivor of colonial violence.

Sovereignty (As Defined by Someone Other than George W. Bush)

Blooming out of the dregs of failed FDPIR programs is an intertribal movement towards food sovereignty across the Native Nations. Operating under the understanding that a nation cannot be considered sovereign without a self-sustaining food system, food sovereignty is a direct dissension from the attempted power-grab central to federal food programs. Food sovereignty is not just a matter of power, however; it also proposes a complete restructuring of how food is gathered, emphasizing intergenerational responsibility and a rebuilding of relationships with the land. Restructuring Indigenous foodways offer a path towards self-determination and emphasizes communal participation, ensuring that every individual has a say in where and how their food is procured.25

One method for operationalizing this proposition is through the formation of community-based farming and gardening projects. In her ethnographic research, Elizabeth

25 “Traditional Foods,” 2021.

24 LaDuke, Winona. "WILD RICE AND ETHICS." Cultural Survival Quarterly, Fall, 2004, 15, http://turing.library.northwestern.edu/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/magazines/wild-rice-ethics/docview/1974 52713/se-2?accountid=12861.

23 LaDuke, Winona. "Manoomin, Seed Sovereignty and Genetics." News from Indian Country, Oct 30, 2006. http://turing.library.northwestern.edu/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/newspapers/manoomin-seed-sovereignty- genetics/docview/367455256/se-2?accountid=12861.

Hoover discusses this work in depth as well as the various ripples flowing from food sovereignty movements—most topically, the procurement of Native seeds (like manoomin), a revival of tribal health, and a restoration of reciprocal relationships with the land. Much like Native languages and other cultural elements put under attack, a continual push towards the preservation of heritage seeds assumes a large role in food sovereignty. This cultivation aims to liberate 26 seeds from patenting rather than perpetuating the hegemonic relationship with them asserted by agrobusiness. In terms of health impacts, as discussed in the documentary Gather, a return to

Native foods may have strong implications in restoring the health of Indigenous peoples and lowering rates of diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. Moreover, the effects of this movement 27 go beyond cultural and health impacts, galvanizing a complete and ideological shift of worldview. Diverging from the language of commodification central to federal food policy,

Indigenous food sovereignty is grounded in spirituality and rejects the notion of human-nature dualism. Through this affirmation, these localized food economies enable Indigenous peoples to create individual connections with the land and re-envision this relationship for future generations.

Tales of Tar Sands and Tyranny

“Rice is life, and it’s a part of that water. You know, they go hand in hand. So, without clean water, we don’t have rice. Without rice, we can’t eat. Without that, we have nothing. We have no food or water. So, what happens to our people? ” 28

-Courtney Calia

While agronomical and academic institutional forces have endangered the genetic makeup of manoomin, pipelines threaten to render the species’ home uninhabitable and, in

28 Calia and Smith, 2019.

27 Gather. Netflix, n.d. Accessed November 20, 2021.

26 Hoover, 2017.

consequence, the health and culture of connected communities. Horticulturally speaking, manoomin is unique in that it exists at the intersection of land and water, highlighting the interconnectedness of the two ecosystems. In the same way that Western contact spread an ontological separation of humans from other lifeforms, colonialism enforces a severance of land and water, the first being  imposed with the label of private property and the next being exploited as an imperial resource. Manoomin accentuates the importance of incorporating water into any 29 discussion of mending relationships to the land and, more directly, emphasizes how crucial waterways are to our food systems. It is unsurprising then that manoomin has emerged as central to the opposition of Line 3 and the continued work of Winona LaDuke.30

Building upon the doctrine Rights of Nature, a newfound notion that (some) landmasses are in fact living and should be protected and treated as such, the White Earth Band of Ojibwe ratified a law guaranteeing the Rights of Manoomin in December 2018. According to this legislation, manoomin has “the right to clean water and freshwater habitat, the right to a natural environment free from industrial pollution, the right to a healthy, stable climate free from human-caused climate change impacts, the right to be free from patenting, the right to be free from contamination by genetically engineered organisms. These outlined Rights of Manoomin 31 have been invoked by LaDuke and other water protectors in their fight against Enbridge and the now-operational tar sands pipeline. Born out of migration stories, the personhood of manoomin has evolved again and again: it is an agent of cultural significance, an organizer of communities,

31 “First ‘Rights of Nature’ Enforcement Case Filed In Tribal Court To Enforce Treaty Guarantees.” Stop Line 3. Stop Line 3, August 5, 2021. https://www.stopline3.org/news/manoominvdnr.

30 LaDuke, Winona. "Extending Wild Rice, the "Rights of Manoomin"." News from Indian Country, 03, 2019. http://turing.library.northwestern.edu/login?url=https://www.proquest.com/newspapers/extending-wild-rice-rights-m anoomin/docview/2226738208/se-2?accountid=12861.

29 “Mapping Chicagou/Chicago: A Living Atlas.” Issuu, September 17, 2019. https://issuu.com/settlercolonialcityproject/docs/20190910_sccp_mcc.

a subject of genetic erasure, and, finally, an emblem of resistance. Who, then, is manoomin?

Manoomin is a way of life – “our freedom. ” 32

Food as Power, Growing as Resistance

Using manoomin as a case study, it is evident that food takes on greater importance for

Indigenous communities beyond simple sustenance. Manoomin serves as a medium through which ancestral legacies are understood. As a cross-cultural unifier, it carries Anishinaabe peoples back to their homelands, creating a space through which tradition is preserved and futures are reimagined. Much like the people to which it holds significance, not only has manoomin been put under threat of erasure in the form of genetic modification but it also takes on roles central to direct action as in the case of Line 3. Grounded in this understanding, harvesting manoomin is itself an act of resistance; it is a rejection of the colonial undermining of

Indigenous ecological knowledge and ontologies, linking Anishinaabe ancestral perseverance to the modern assertion of sovereignty through the growing of traditional food.

32 LaDuke, Winona. “Honoring Manoomin and Fighting for Its Survival.” The Circle (Minneapolis, Minn.). 2021.

While food, in this way, can be considered as a tool of liberation, it can also serve as a channel for colonial violence. This can be seen in the implementation of federal food assistance programs and, specifically, FDPIR. This program, like many other federal programs operating under the guise of welfarism, forces reliance of the Native Nations on the U.S. government for necessities, undermining tribal sovereignty and amplifying colonial frameworks. This is without considering the actual effects of such federal nutrition assistance programs, which ultimately exacerbate Indigenous health disparities through the imposition of a European diet. Coming out of this paradoxical legacy as a source of resistance and tool of subjugation is a new understanding of what the food sovereignty movement means for Indigenous peoples. While water is life, food is power. After all, “you can’t say you’re sovereign if you can’t feed yourself.”

33 Hoover, 2017.

label: Medical Non-Compliance: A Structural Issue
nurj_title: Medical Non-Compliance: A Structural Issue
text:
Medical Non-Compliance: A Structural Issue

Introduction and Explanation of Problem

When patients fail to follow treatment plans or attend appointments, the medical institution blames the patient and labels them as “non-compliant.” However, the doctor-patient relationship has two sides and both need to be considered to fully understand noncompliance.

Clearly something is not working when medical providers prescribe treatment plans that their patients cannot reasonably access. Doctors, however, are only the tip of the iceberg. Medical institutions, primarily on a hospital and government policy level, need to restructure themselves to empower and encourage medical providers to adapt and respond to their patients’ barriers to medical access. As the only side of the relationship with institutional and infrastructural power, it falls on medical institutions to help bridge the medical accessibility gap created by social inequalities.

Therefore, it is more helpful to understand noncompliance as an unimplemented treatment plan and as a breakdown in the doctor-patient relationship, facilitated by the medical systems, rather than as a patient’s individual failure. Thus, employing a medical system lens of analysis rather than a strictly individual lens is best. Structural inequalities, such as poverty and cultural barriers, often fuel noncompliance. While the medical system cannot solve structural issues like poverty, it can adapt their treatment plans and medical routines so that medicine is more accessible to people experiencing poverty. Thus, medical institutions’ adaptation of treatment plans to their patient’s accessibility needs will increase medical compliance.1 Mama

Might Be Better Off Dead by Laurie Kaye Abraham primarily illustrates how poverty can impact

1 Further clarification: these changes will happen mostly on the hospital and governmental policy level and then manifest in doctor-patient relationships where they will have the most immediate impact on patients.

compliance whereas The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down by Anne Fadiman highlights the impact of culture.

Statement of Significance

Why does noncompliance matter? Whether it is framed as the patient’s problem or as a breakdown in the doctor-patient relationship, it results in patients not receiving the medical care that they need to get better, survive, and prevent future illness. In particular, noncompliance often most impacts people with marginalized identities who are already at higher risk for poor health due to the physio-emotional impact of discrimination, environmental racism, and so on. Thus, addressing noncompliance matters because it is critical to ensuring medical equity.

Why does changing society’s understanding of noncompliance matter? Society’s current focus on the patient’s fault rather than a doctor/medical institution’s fault is unhelpful because it fails to recognize and address the structural issues causing noncompliance. In fact, blaming patients’ for noncompliance can exacerbate medical noncompliance by deterring patients from going to medical appointments due to a fear of scolding or condemnation.

Example of Noncompliance and Poverty

Mama Might Be Better Off Dead by Laurie Kaye Abraham describes and analyzes the author’s ethnographic study of the Banes family’s experiences with medical institutions from

1989 to 1990. A poor, black family living in Lawndale, Chicago, the Banes’ medical experiences reveal how poverty, as well as racism and cultural differences, can negatively impact a patient’s ability to comply with their doctors’ treatment plans. Jackie Banes is the head of the family and the caretaker for her ill grandmother Cora Jackson whose diabetes resulted in the amputation of one of her legs prior to the study and her other leg during the study, leaving her dependent on

Jackie for care and decision-making. This section will analyze the two women’s interactions with

Mrs. Jackson’s treatment plan and medical providers, specifically focusing on how the family’s poverty severely restricted their ability to comply despite their best intentions.

A large and impactful barrier between Mrs. Jackson and her medical treatment was the financial inaccessibility of her treatment. For instance, Mrs. Jackson’s monthly pills cost roughly

$75 and were unreliably covered by Medicaid, forcing Jackie to ration her high blood pressure medicine. Furthermore, Mrs. Jackson needed transportation equipped for wheelchairs and transfer, which was an expensive task that Public Aid only covered intermittently and often forced Jackie to pay $70 out-of-pocket if she wanted a single day’s transportation. This prohibitively high cost then caused Mrs. Jackson to miss doctor appointments because Jackie could not afford them. For instance, Mrs. Jackson had to miss a critical appointment with her podiatrist about her blackening toe; partially due to the lack of medical intervention, it eventually required amputation. Thus, financial barriers to medical treatment can have devastating consequences when it causes lack of care and the escalation of illness.

The medical institution further exacerbated Mrs. Jackson’s transportation barrier by requiring frequent transportation. First, the office was unable to schedule multiple appointments on the same day.2 Second, the hospital often discharged Mrs. Jackson with critical appointments scheduled in the subsequent weeks for follow-up care and procedures because outpatient appointments were less expensive than inpatient ones. Her inconsistent ability to attend outpatient appointments significantly contributed to the eventual necessity of amputating her entire leg rather than just her foot. Thus, while Jackie wanted to take Mrs. Jackson to her appointments, she did not reliably physically have a way to get there: her non-compliance in this case stemmed directly from structural financial inequality rather than active choice.

2 However, Jackie was once able to advocate for a hospital admission rather than an outpatient follow-up appointment due to her transportation concerns, but that was an exception not the rule.

Mrs. Jackson’s noncompliance was fueled at least in part by structural barriers. Thus, if the medical institutions could adapt to the structural barriers keeping Mrs. Jackson from fulfilling her treatment, her compliance rates would most likely increase. This ethnography elucidates a couple of ways hospitals and government policy can improve. First, doctors can write three-month rather than one-month prescriptions, so that patients can have access to their medications even when they are intermittently uninsured. Alternatively, the government could create stable insurance programs for poor people. Second, hospitals can offer accessible transportation for medical appointments, align doctors’ schedules so that patients can have multiple appointments in one day, and offer more appointments inpatient when necessary.

Finally, medical clinics can increase their communication with their patients: “Middle-class pet owners get more prompts from their veterinarians” than lower-class people do from their doctors.

More phone calls and letters about upcoming vaccinations, recommended appointments and follow-ups and even changes in Medicare and Medicaid could all increase compliance. While all these changes would require a financial commitment, this example illuminates that helping patients navigate the structural barriers keeping them from healthcare will increase compliance, a long-term goal of medical institutions.3

Example of Noncompliance and Language / Cultural Barriers

The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down analyzes Anne Fadiman’s multi-year ethnography with the Lee family. The Lees were recent Hmong refugees from Vietnam, and their young daughter Lia had severe epilepsy. Fadiman followed her medical journey that was complicated by immense language and cultural barriers: Lia’s illiterate, Hmong-speaking parents only understood Hmong’s view of illness while her Western, English-speaking medical providers only understood Western medicine’s view of illness. This section will argue that a driver of the

3 Could also decrease long term costs because it would result in less expensive, emergent care.

parents’ noncompliance were these two barriers between the Lee family and their doctors and that doctors’ adaptation of their treatment plans to these barriers would have helped to increase compliance.4

There were many devastating ways that the language barrier harmed Lia’s medical care.

At the time of Lia’s first ER trip, the hospital did not employ a single interpreter, so her physicians had to practice veterinary care because they could not communicate with her parents.5

As a result, it was not until Lia arrived at the hospital still seizing that her doctors realized she had epilepsy, a delay that probably worsened her condition. Without interpreters, Lia’s doctors unhelpfully wrote down their instructions in English, illustrated by Lia’s first ER trip discharge information or when her first prescriptions “simply read ‘Take as directed.’” Later, social workers would create med charts with sun and moon stickers to denote morning and nighttime meds as well as different colored stickers to differentiate all of Lia’s meds with limited effect.

There were still missteps, such as when one social worker wrote “prune” on a piece of paper and expected Lia’s parents to purchase prune juice at the grocery store, and these accommodations could only be so helpful without explanations of the medicines’ and treatment’s purpose.

Even with interpreters, doctors struggled to substantively explain Lia’s diagnosis and treatment plan to her parents due to the fundamental differences between Western and Hmong understandings of the body and medicine. The Hmong community has little to no conception of internal organs: they do not conduct post-mortem autopsies as it would harm the soul’s spiritual progression after life. Thus, the translation of “X chromosome” alone was nearly 50 words.

5 Veterinary care is a concept adopted from veterinarians who are unable to talk to their animal patients and must, therefore, diagnose patients based on observable symptoms and test results. Because Lia’s doctors could not communicate with either her or her parents, the ER doctors had to conduct veterinary medicine.

4 To be sure, there were times that Lia’s parents explicitly did not follow the doctor’s treatment plan. Fadiman even acknowledges that the Lee family were noncompliant both due to lack of understanding of what to do and due to not wanting to give Lee the pills. My argument is that only focusing on the parents’ fault in noncompliance obscures the ways that Lia’s medical team could have also fostered medical compliance.

Alternatively, Hmong culture believes that the body and the spirit are inextricably intertwined, so physical health problems often have spiritual sources. Thus, the Lees prioritized Shaman’s work and animal sacrifice to help cure Lia, decisions that her doctors struggled to understand or accept. As one resident said, “‘The Hmong simply didn’t have the same concepts that I did,” so even when translators were available, they struggled to convey ideas across the cultural barrier.

The medical system can take many different approaches to responding to this cultural-lingual barrier: this essay will consider three, each more comprehensive and, therefore, probably more effective than the last. The first, and most obvious, approach for medical systems is hiring translators. At the time of the book’s publication, there still was not a budget line specifically for translators at the Lee’s local hospital; rather, the hospital hired “Hmong lab assistants, nurse’s aides, and translators” who then doubled as translators. Hiring employees whose sole purpose is translating for patients is a pivotal first step towards helping the patients understand their diagnosis and treatment plan, essential components for compliance.

The next level of doctor adaptation, as always empowered and enabled by institutional adaptation, is learning the basics of Hmong culture, so that the medical providers can communicate treatment plans in culturally competent ways and, thus, increase compliance.

Illustrating the need of this adaptation, Fadiman documents a set of Hmong parents who refused medical treatment for their child, and the doctor then researched the surgery rather than learning why the parents objected to the treatment and how he could change their minds.6 Alternatively, she noted an example of this adaptation’s success when a female, Hmong patient refused medical intervention, and the doctor knew to speak with her husband rather than the patient directly to gain consent. By respecting Hmong culture’s power hierarchy, the medical provider adapted to

6 Learning about Hmong culture is not a panacea to surmounting the cultural-lingual barrier between Hmong patients and their Western doctors, as noted by Fadiman when Neil and Peggy still struggled to communicate with Lia’s parents despite their research on Hmong. However, it can still be part of the solution without being a panacea.

their patient’s culture and changed a situation of noncompliance into one of compliance.

Importantly, a doctor's cultural adaptation can work, and it does not need to be strenuous.

The third and most comprehensive way that the medical system can accommodate its

Hmong patients is by hiring cultural brokers, the solution that Fadiman suggests in her book.

While translators translate the words spoken, cultural brokers help to translate the very ideas and concepts being discussed so that both the doctors and the patients understand and feel understood, truly accomplishing informed consent. This more robust interpretation is especially critical because Hmong culture and Western medicine view the world and health in fundamental different ways, established above. A cultural broker, for instance, would know that Hmong do not have a conception of most internal organs, explain that fact to the doctor so they are aware, and then do their best to phrase the issue in a way the Hmong could conceptualize. Similarly, they could explain to doctors why Hmong are so hesitant about blood draws and spinal taps and help Hmong patients understand the procedures and their purpose. Furthermore, they could help broker a compromise between Hmong culture and Western Medicine, helping doctors incorporate shaman and spiritual work into Western medicine. Fadiman noted that patients are often more likely to medically comply with Western medicine treatments if they are also able to practice their own healing rituals. Thus, there are many ways that the medical system can adapt to help accommodate their patients with cultural barriers, increasing compliance in the process.

Conclusion

Noncompliance is undoubtedly an issue and patients’ personal, individual choices certainly contribute to it. However, that analysis only considers one side of the doctor-patient relationship. It misses how medical providers, and by extension the medical systems where they are employed, also contribute to medical noncompliance by prescribing treatment and following routines that are structurally inaccessible to their patients for economic and cultural reasons. In these cases, the medical providers are setting their patients up for failure from the beginning.

This essay looked at two specific examples of structural barriers that limited patients from complying with their treatment plans: poverty and cultural-linguistic barriers. This paper does not propose that medical systems must solve poverty and cultural barriers toeffectively treat its patients. Rather, it argues that doctors and medical institutions must consider and adapt their treatment plans to the barriers that their patients face, which will require institutional and governmental level changes of policy and priorities to allow doctors this added flexibility. By offering more inpatient appointments, accessible transportation, interpreter services, cultural brokers, and so on, doctors will be able to meet their patients halfway. Only then can medical providers even begin to reasonably expect their patients to medically comply and follow their treatment plans. Overall health will increase, too, benefiting the doctors and their patients.

Reference Page

Abraham, L. K. (2019). Mama Might Be Better Off Dead: The Failure of Health Care in

Urban America. University of Chicago Press; First Edition.

Fadiman, A. (1998). The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down: A Hmong Child, Her

American Doctors, and the Collision of Two Cultures. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

nurj_title: The DMCA in Action: Copyright Law, Algorithmic Censorship, and Free Speech in The Internet Age
text:
The DMCA in Action: Copyright Law, Algorithmic Censorship, and Free Speech in the Internet Age

Brian Vogel

3/14/2022

INTRODUCTION
