In 1998, during the infancy of the internet, Congress began holding legislative sessions and committee meetings to construct the legal mechanisms necessary to regulate this brave new technology. One of the largest questions posed to the legislature was related to the liability of copyright infringing content on online spaces mediated by a third party. Online content never exists purely independently – a content-hosting platform is required to broadcast content through the world wide web. This left an important question of legal responsibility: if someone illegally posts copyrighted material, who is to become liable? The individual user who illegally posted copyrighted intellectual property, or the third-party content hosting platform that disseminates the infringing material? To answer this question, Congress established the Digital Millennium

Copyright Act (DMCA), an act that established the modern interface of legal structures that governs legality in online spaces to this day.

The DMCA lays out a series of hoops that content hosting platforms and users are required to jump-through in order to discern liability. The user is liable for copyright infringing material, but rather than immediate litigation, the remedy is for third party platforms to de-platforming the infringing material. This de-platforming is carried out by the content-hosting platform on behalf of the copyright holder, but these platforms have not escaped liability. If they refuse to take down any claimed material, these platforms then take on the liability for any copyright infringement, should the justice system decide if such infringement occurred. This fear of liability has incentivized platforms to wield content-removing tools with absolute and unchecked restraint, using automated filtering algorithms to remove all content with even the prospect of copyright liability, often without the instruction of the Internet Protocol (I.P.). holder.

This has empowered some bad-faith actors to abuse this system. This abuse comes in two forms:

reporting copyrighted material for a purpose other than remedying the copyright misuse, or claiming legal material as copyrighted, knowing that platforms will remove the content without doing due-diligence. Indeed, no such requirement for due-diligence exists in the DMCA, giving content hosting platforms all-powerful control over what types of online speech are “legal” or

“illegal”.

In the Trump era, when concerns over the truth and validity of what is said online became a well-known concern, the phenomenon of DMCA abuse became somewhat mainstream. I aim to investigate how the DMCA differs in intention from execution with regards to freedom of speech online. The particular angle this investigation seeks to tackle is related to the mechanization of DMCA claim management through algorithms. Too much content is posted each and every day for a human to analyze and verify that it is copyright compliant, so platforms employ algorithms to automatically filter content based on broad, indiscriminate criteria. The use and effect of these algorithms were a total blindspot of the DMCA, and their use has radically altered what is allowed to be said on the internet. I therefore sought to examine: How were copyright-law algorithms for content-hosting platforms exploited to control speech online between 2016-2020?

ANALYSIS

SECTION I

[omitted from condensed version]

SECTION II

Between the years 2016 and 2020, when the political climate was ripe for mistrusting any information disseminated online, the ways in which the DMCA was used as a tool to silence internet-based content became thrust into the spotlight. Much has been written of the DMCA’s potential to economically harm online content creators, but comparatively little has been written about how the very same law can be exploited to politically harm an individual.

Algorithms are pieces of code that are used to carry out a specific function1. Their use is varied, but where the DMCA is concerned, algorithms are used to recognize patterns on a volume incapable of individual human examination2. These content hosting platforms see incalculable amounts of content uploaded each day, which raises a problem with regards to being

DMCA compliant. According to DMCA Section 512, a content hosting platform is liable to be sued for copyright infringement if they maintain the infringing content on their platform after a claim has been filed by the holder of the copyright. Because of the sheer volume of content, it is impossible for groups of people to comb through all of the content and manually identify copyrighted material3. The platforms therefore employ algorithms to flag copyrighted material and remove it in order to avoid liability4. This system has two main problems however: first, the pattern recognition of these algorithms cannot match human pattern recognition, which leads to

DMCA-compliant content being filtered out on account of overzealous algorithms protecting the platform. Second, in order to minimize red tape and liability and maximize efficiency, copyrighted content is removed without the consultation of the holder of the copyright.

One of the through-lines in the presented examples is overzealous claiming of material via algorithms with little to no human oversight. Three of the five examples below deal with copyright claims that removed content that would have been deemed acceptable if a nuanced and

4 Nighat Mir, “Copyright for Web Content Using Invisible Text Watermarking,” Computers in Human Behavior no. 30 (January 2014): 648–53.

3Joel D. Matteson, "Unfair Misuse: How Section 512 of the DMCA Allows Abuse of the Copyright Fair Use Doctrine and How to Fix It," Santa Clara High Technology Law Journal 35, no. 2 (November 2018): 1-22.

2 Niva Elkin-Koren, "Contesting Algorithms: Restoring the Public Interest in Content Filtering by Artificial Intelligence," Big Data & Society 7, no. 2 (2020).

1 Xiaoqiang Ma, Jiangchuan Liu, and Hongbo Jiang, “On the Design of Algorithms for Mobile Multimedia Systems: A Survey,” International Journal of Communication Systems 24, no. 10 (October 2011): 1330–39.

properly-discerning human actor was to have considered the validity of these claims instead of an algorithm, whose only job is to automatically protect corporate interests. The absence of the intervention of a copyright holder makes the actions of these algorithms all the more egregious – since an algorithm cannot manually prove the person filing the complaint is the valid copyright holder, any claim – no matter how spurious – is treated as a valid concern, even if that is not the case. Both examples one and three are valid and protected forms of speech whose objector was not the copyright holder for the material called into question, but an unrelated third party. The algorithm therefore empowers neither the copyright holder nor the consumer, but instead empowers any bad-faith actor unscrupulous enough to exploit this system.

This system is ripe for exploitation because the DMCA offers little to no consumer protections. Platforms are free to utilize algorithms to censor content without the interest of the content creator nor the copyright holder, only the interest of the platform. The ability for the

DMCA to create exploitable systems of algorithmic enforcement has undoubtedly exposed the

DMCA’s shortcomings, which can be interrogated through the following examples:

Example 1: Officer James Knoblauch, a police officer in Oglesby, Illinois, was attempting to make an arrest at an office in LaSalle County. A civilian began to record the officer on her phone, and when Knoblauch turned around and noticed he was being filmed, he immediately pulled out his phone and began to play a Blake Shelton song at full volume in an attempt to trigger copyright detecting algorithms to keep the video of the arrest from being uploaded online.5

The noteworthy aspects of this example include the degree of knowledge exhibited by the actors, the absence of the intervention of a copyright holder, and the hierarchies present in this

5Tim Cushing, "Officer Claims Sheriff's Office Told Him To Play Copyrighted Music To Shut Down Citizens' Recording,". Newstex Blogs Techdirt. September 13, 2021 situation. First, this case is noteworthy in that all parties involved (the person under arrest not included) were aware of how copyright-filtering algorithms currently operate. The officer knew how these algorithms could be exploited, and the person recording the officer vocally calls out this deliberate tactic in the video footage. This is indicative of how widespread this phenomenon actually is, and its media coverage is only giving more ammunition to those with similar jobs and incentives. Second, the copyright holder is not present anywhere in the incident. Blake Shelton and his publisher, Universal Music Group, never filed a copyright claim against the video, and yet it was claimed and taken down. There is a possibility that the use of his song as a tool of suppressing police accountability may be against the interest of the copyright holder, but those interests were never taken into account. The final noteworthy aspect is that this incident exposes how the DMCA and the algorithms that uphold it can be used to reinforce hierarchies. Law enforcement being held above the common citizen, the use of an internet copyright law to maintain such a hierarchy is a pointed example of how these systems are codified into law in unexpected ways.

Example 2: In 2017, famous YouTube star PewDiePie released a stream of himself playing video games wherein he made several racist insults and casual pro-Nazi jokes. Members of the audience who were offended by such comments attempted to get the video taken down on the grounds that it violated YouTube’s guidelines regarding harassment and hate speech. When no remedy to this complaint materialized, the same people reported the video for copyright misuse, which led to the video being taken down almost immediately, and landing PewDiePie in a lengthy YouTube suspension6

6 Mona Ibrahim, “Firewatch Creators can Target PewDiePie with DMCA Takedowns, and it’s Perfectly Legal” Polygon (Sep 17, 2017)

This example is interesting in that the relatively positive outcome of the story also serves as an example as to why the systems relied upon to achieve this outcome are worrying. The

DMCA was utilized in preventing the proliferation of hate speech – it is a clear example of those with less power (the audience) leveraging the legal system to hold a party with a considerable amount of power (the wealthy YouTube star) to account. What is troubling is that copyright liability was the only incentive taken into account by the platform. It is an unfortunate example about the priorities of content hosting spaces like YouTube: harassment, hate speech, and violations of community guidelines were met with apathy, while the only complaint these platforms are willing to take seriously are those revolving around copyright and the DMCA. It is a clear value-judgment on the part of the law and the platforms that copyright liability is a priority over the health and safety of their user base.

It’s also an example of algorithmic abuse. The copyright claim immediately triggered a takedown algorithm, but after a several month battle, the content was evaluated to fall within the

“fair use” guideline of the DMCA, denoting the copyright claim as having been made in bad faith7. Hate speech is something that is tied to moral and social values, a concept that is challenging for an algorithm to recognize. No such value judgment needs to be made for copyrighted material however, especially when the legal security of a company is on the line.

This example shows that human resources need only be employed when non-legal issues arise, such as those of harassment, but no human resources are needed in cases concerning the DMCA.

The implications for algorithms and algorithmic censorship online in relation to free speech are of foremost importance. As established in section one, the very existence of

7 The “Fair Use” determination is a process that requires human intervention, given that it relies on pattern recognition not currently available in modern algorithm technology. When evaluating a subject for fair use, the platform needs to determine if the alleged infringing material is suitably “transformative” in relation to the original work, common examples being parody, education, and criticism.

content-filtration algorithms was never imagined by the authors of the DMCA because their scope for internet use was so limited. But the question remains as to whether the implementation of these algorithms was inevitable, or if the constraints and expectations established by the

DMCA propelled their widespread adoption. This analysis concludes that it is the latter. This is because the DMCA elevates the power of the Section 512 “notice and takedown” feature of the law above protections for the content creator by legally mandating Section 512, but only legally suggesting consumer protections. There are a few key consumer protections built into the

DMCA, such as the “fair use” protection, which defends consumers from copyright infringement if their content is suitably transformative from the original material. However, the way the

DMCA allocates legal penalties in such a lopsided way makes this nearly irrelevant in the face of algorithmic content filtration. YouTube or Facebook face consequences for hosting copyright content, but do NOT face consequences for removing content, regardless of fair use or the established precedents surrounding freedom of speech. This incentivizes harsh censorship that can be carried out by unfeeling, uncaring machines.

Example 3: In 2020, a Black Lives Matter protest held in Douglas County, Nevada was being live-streamed as a way to drum up support for the ongoing movement. Protesters numbered approximately 30-40 people, but counter protesters numbered in the hundreds. As the protest march proceeded into the streets lined with counter protesters, members of the counterprotest began to blast country music, and within minutes the livestream was terminated prematurely due to copyright infringement8

This example is consistent with the hierarchical evaluation presented in example one, but also illustrates a clear divide between freedom of speech on and offline. In this scenario, both

8 Kelly Penrose, “BLM Protest in Douglas County Draws Hundreds of Counter-protestors, Militia” Sierra Nevada Ally, (Aug 9, 2020)

protestor and counter-protestor are entitled to a right to assemble and express their freedom of speech, but those rights are no longer represented when this speech becomes digitized into its online form. This is consistent with Marceau and Chen’s legal analysis of how the DMCA inconsistently holds freedom of speech to a different standard online than off.9 The algorithmic regulation is also noteworthy in this case because the ability of censorship to occur in real time.

The ability to enforce a DMCA copyright ban was immediately effectuated during a live stream

– this is not a case where a piece of content was removed following its completion and posting, it was censored mid-creation, giving platform filtration algorithms the power to immediately censor speech in a chilling way. A piece of speech cannot be challenged in its entirety, but can be challenged before the completion of the speech based on alleged copyright misuse that was determined by an inhuman mechanism

Example 4: In 2016, a London-based children’s charity posted a negative review of construction company BuildFirm on a review forum called Mumsnet. Several days after posting the negative review, Google sent Mumsnet a notice and takedown order that her negative comment had been removed for violating DMCA policy. No copyright infringement had occurred. Instead, the review was copied verbatim into a separate web page entirely, which then retroactively copyrighted the bad review’s exact language in order to trigger the review as being flaggable for copyright misuse. It would later come out that employees of Buildfirm had done this maneuver deliberately. Google rejected the counterclaim by Mumsnet, and the review thread was removed entirely.10

10 Alex Hern, “Revealed: How Copyright Law is Being Misused to Remove Material from the Internet” The Guardian (May 23, 2016)

9 Justin Marceau and Alan K. Chen, “Free Speech and Democracy in the Video Age,” Columbia Law Review 116, no. 4 (2016): 991–1062; Their analysis is a legal exercise by which they take court precedent for various free speech cases and apply the given precedent to an online space, exposing how speech online does not align with constitutional law set about by the First Amendment

The implications for this particular example are threefold. The first implication is one of internationality and the consequences of the DMCA on a global stage. Despite the United

Kingdom having entirely separate copyright jurisdiction than the United States, Google – the company who hosts Mumsnet – is an American company, and is thus subject to regulation by the

DMCA, and American law. This essentially makes a huge section of the internet the legal domain of the United States, giving the U.S. unprecedented authority to control the flow of information on a global scale. The second implications of this case-study concern corporate and economic sabotage. The DMCA was not only used to limit the free speech of the charity in question, but it was done so with an economic motivation in mind. The BuildFirm scheme to copyright a bad review and use that as the basis for a DMCA claim was directly motivated by

BuildFirm’s bottom line. In the internet age when a bad review carries weight for the future success of a business, the freedom of speech of the actors involved is no longer an abstract political idea, but an economic force that poses a threat to certain companies.

Another implication is centered on the lack of due-diligence on the part of Google, and the lack of consequences for this mistreatment of internet-users. The remedy for an illegitimate

DMCA takedown is known as a counterclaim – a feature whereby the injured party can protest against the filtration of their content by filing a complaint to the content-hosting platform11. The ways in which these claims are handled varies from platform to platform, but because each platform is a private company, the regulation of the counterclaim function is internal. There is no external force that mandates counterclaims be taken seriously12. This gives content-hosting

12 Wendy Setzer, "Free Speech Unmoored in Copyright’s Safe Harbor: Chilling Effects of the DMCA on the First Amendment," Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, 24, no. 171 (Fall, 2010).

11 Alan Gocha, "A Modern System for Resolving Online Copyright Infringement Disputes: Administrative Rulemaking and adjudication, a One-Stop Fix to The Digital Millennium Copyright Act," IDEA: The Journal of the Franklin Pierce Center for Intellectual Property, 58, no. 131 (2018).

companies no real incentive to take these claims seriously. If they accept the counterclaim as valid in error, the platform becomes liable for copyright infringement, and verifying the validity of a counterclaim can be a costly process because it cannot be easily managed by an algorithm.13

Therefore, the only incentive companies have to take counterclaims seriously is to ensure the trust of their user base, which is not a strong incentive given the fact that most users will not switch to a competing platform over this type of controversy. There is also a degree of intersection between the first and third implication. The international nature of the incident means that if an individual in a foreign country wanted to bring a platform to court over their lack of due-diligence processing DMCA counterclaims, that remedy would not be available because the DMCA would be a law in a completely separate country.

The nature of this exploitation is another key implication. The DMCA – not just its algorithmic enforcers - is an incredibly exploitable law in a way that was not intended. Its exploitability is partially due to the universality of the internet; the internet is a tool used by a majority of people every single day, and that volume of use allows its user-base to become familiar with its mechanisms fairly quickly and fairly intimately. Both officer Knobloch and

BuildFirm were so aware of the law’s driving Section 512 mechanism that they were able to bend that mechanism to their own ends. Likewise, this controversy demonstrates that internet users do not approach the DMCA with the same skepticism for the law as is ordinary. Law is often regarded by a majority of the public as an arcane set of rules outside the scope of knowledge for the average lay-person14, but this is not so with the DMCA. The governing

14 Justin Marceau and Alan K. Chen, “Free Speech and Democracy in the Video Age,” Columbia Law Review 116, no. 4 (2016):

13 Zoe Carpou, "Robots, Pirates, and the Rise of the Automated Takedown Regime: Using the DMCA to Fight Piracy and Protect End-Users," Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts 39, no. 4 (2016): 551-590 mechanisms for a tool as important as the internet have made the widespread understanding of the law ripe for exploitation.

The intent of the DMCA is also affirmed by the transnational influence of U.S copyright law. This topic was arguably the most central ideal underpinning the DMCA. Congress was looking for a way to make the U.S the dominant force in the new internet landscape, and the system they devised whereby content-hosting platforms are the nexus for the legal viability of online content made that ideal a reality. If anyone – regardless of location – wants to post content, they need to be mediated by a U.S-based content hosting platform, and because the

DMCA regulates these platforms, it also regulates users across the globe.

Example 5: The Nicaraguan election of 2020 saw large protests against reigning President Daniel

Ortega. The state sponsored news media being unwilling to cover such protests, protesters turned to independent and international journalism to spread the word about the protests. The Ortega regime filed several false DMCA claims against reporting unsympathetic to his rule, falsely claiming the reporting was copyright infringing, leading YouTube to remove all coverage of the protest.15

This example is profoundly chilling in the way in which it demonstrates the power transnational corporations have over international politics. This case demonstrates how the abstraction of information through multiple mediums can disrupt the flow of information. The message of the protest is communicated through journalists, who communicate their journalism through content-hosting corporations like YouTube, who then broadcast that journalism through telecommunications networks. If any link in this chain becomes disrupted, the availability of information becomes compromised, and the fact that corporations with monied interests hold

15 Danae Vilchez, “YouTube Censors Independent Nicarguan News Outlets after Copyright Complaint from Ortega-Owned Media,” Committee to Protect Journalists; (May 6, 2020)

these links establishes a system where information can only be disseminated if that information is deemed profitable. Other noteworthy elements of this case include its international scale and political implications. The example falls in line with the precedent set by Google v. Equustek, demonstrating the intentional international reach of the DMCA – here though, the sovereign law of one nation is being upheld by the sovereign law of the United States, rather than being challenged16. The DMCA is therefore a political impediment, given its sweeping censorship capabilities on a global scale.

The previous examples demonstrate the fulfillment of the DMCA’s intent in a somewhat sinister way. The pre-eminence of U.S. law is undeniable: these are definitive cases where the

DMCA’s global reach is explicitly shown, but the context of that global reach is controversial. In both cases, the international reach of the DMCA was wasn’t used to protect U.S. copyright holders, but was instead used to attack some outside party, be it Mumsnet or independent

Nicaraguan journalists. The DMCA is not acting as a shield for U.S. markets on a global stage, but is instead used as a weapon to control international internet use with laws that constrain non-U. S. online action. This is a tightrope has yet to collapse, but remains precarious:

company’s suffer damage to their reputation when bad-faith DMCA claims exploit their platforms, and because this is an international affair, the profit motivation to let this occur is much weaker than a similar domestic infraction. These platforms are currently exchanging international reputation for international control, but the future of this transaction is uncertain.

Finally, the implications with regards to the establishment of user rights are defined by what rights each respective algorithm permits. The section two examples highlight that content filtration platforms are highly sensitive to music and quoted text. User rights extend in so far as

16 Robert Diab, "Search Engines and Global Takedown Orders: Google v Equustek and the Future of Free Speech Online," Osgoode Hall Law Journal 56, no. 2 (Winter 2019): 231-270 they can avoid these easily flagged categories, which is extremely tenuous given that, in situations of live recording or text-based commenting, any actor can take away the user’s right to post, regardless of the legality of said post. User rights are therefore constrained, left to the mercy of platforms too large and complex to guarantee these rights in any legally-recognized way.

CONCLUSION

The modern internet is a necessity to most people in The United States. Millions of businesses, livelihoods, and creative projects rely on content hosting platforms to function, which is a precarious position given that a single bad-faith actor or algorithmic misfire can damage or destroy anyone’s online contributions. The legal landscape of such a necessary space invests all-powerful authority in machines who are incapable of filtering content using the nuance and sensitivity required to accurately weigh the merits of copyright. Going forward, the framework of the DMCA needs to change. The internet no longer exists in the halcyon days of

1998, before Google, Facebook, and YouTube even existed, and the internet’s seminal governing law must reflect this fact.

I advocate for a legal mechanism that requires content hosting platforms demonstrate a greater degree of due-diligence when investigating copyright claims. I also advocate for the regulation of copyright-filtration algorithms, and suggest that future research be conducted into the specificities of these algorithms. The code for these algorithms is guarded by the platforms that utilize them, but any in-depth analysis of these codes would be invaluable to advancing this field of inquiry. This field is also in need of more meta-analysis. How many claims are done in bad faith? How many are made in error by an algorithm? How many counterclaims get ignored or under-investigated? These types of raw data would be especially useful in a future policy proposal. While these algorithms are a necessary function for a large, complex internet, they ought not to be the final, unchallengeable arbiters of who is allowed to speak in online spaces.

label: RAND and the Development of US Nuclear Thought in the Early 1960's
nurj_title: RAND and the Development of US Nuclear Thought in the Early 1960's
text:
RAND and the Development of U.S. Nuclear Thought in the Early 1960’s

80 years after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the world has yet to experience another atomic bomb. During the Cold War, however, the United States and Soviet Union (USSR) came dangerously close during the Berlin Crisis of 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. The heavily anti-communist Kennedy administration oversaw the successful navigation of these crises, all the while maintaining an uncompromised nuclear position and deterring the Soviet

Union from military action. At the behest of the Research and Development (RAND)

Corporation, the United States’s nuclear plans became more aggressive, confrontational, and malleable. In the early 1960s, the United States’ strategic nuclear policy shifted drastically in favor of flexibility and offensive capabilities due to the efforts of one institution: the RAND

Corporation.

The Kennedy administration marked a turning point in American defense thought. In

1958, the United States possessed an estimated 7,345 nuclear warheads. By 1964, that number quadrupled to more than 29,000.1 Military assistance to South Vietnam and the failed invasion of

Cuba lent evidence to a bold, new strategy: confrontation. The most important change in

American policy was ‘behind closed doors’, though. During the Berlin crisis of 1961, Kennedy and the Joint Chiefs of Staff secretly planned a nuclear first strike against the Soviets.2 The

Kennedy administration was convinced “that there was a ‘fair probability’ of success; it was ‘a plan to wage rational nuclear war.”3 This first test of Kennedy’s administration demonstrated a sharp departure from prior strategy. Not 10 years prior, General MacArthur was famously fired

3 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

2 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

1 Max Roser, Bastian Herre, and Joe Hasell, Nuclear Weapons (Our World in Data, August 6, 2013) https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons.

by President Truman for even suggesting the tactical use of nuclear weapons in the Korean War.

Kennedy’s serious consideration of nuclear first strike — and insistence that it could be successful — indicated a deviation from the conventional wisdom of mutually assured destruction, or that nuclear war would unquestionably result in worldwide desolation. The principle of mutually assured destruction was entirely defensive in nature, as it denied even the possibility of one side emerging victorious, thereby removing an offensive incentive. Moreover,

Kennedy’s openness to an offensive strike required a greater degree of flexibility in the event of nuclear conflict — the President needed to be able to successfully initiate both a small, targeted first-strike and a retaliatory second-strike. His actions during the Berlin Crisis implied that not only was nuclear war probable, but also winnable. So impactful was the administration’s plan that Secretary McNamara altered the Single Integrated Operational Plan (SIOP-63) to include

Kennedy’s suggestion of a potential first strike aimed at strategically paralyzing Soviet nuclear capabilities.4

In 1959, the U.S.’s first operational intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) enabled the successful implementation of a militant and adaptable nuclear strategy. ICBMs permitted the

United States to drastically increase its nuclear delivery system; payloads could be deployed up to 8,700 miles away without the same logistical issues which plagued bomber-based nuclear weapons. Despite Soviet claims of ICBM superiority, “by 1959 there was a missile gap… widening steadily in favor of the United States.”5 American ICBM buildup coincided with the general increase in nuclear weapons seen during the Kennedy administration, indicative of an aggressive shift in U.S. strategy. General Curtis LeMay — Chief of Staff of the Air Force from

5 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random House, 2009), 401.

4 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

1961 to 1965 — was a chief proponent of the new ICBM program, and regarded it as “the ultimate weapon.”6 LeMay relished in the thought of “reduc[ing] the Soviet Union to cinders,” a sentiment shared by many in the American government.7 Enthusiasm for nuclear offense and confrontation was evident, and the ICBM helped the ideas of persons such as LeMay and RAND come to fruition. The introduction of the solid-fuel Minuteman ICBM to the Strategic Air

Command in 1962 further enabled American destructive capabilities. Uncoincidentally, Kennedy

“had come into office railing about a ‘missile gap’ that was giving the Soviets a dangerous edge,” and the initial Kennedy plan for a general nuclear strike against the “Sino-Soviet Bloc” relied heavily on ICBMs.8 The United States of the early 1960s was ready to fight — and win — a nuclear war against the Soviet Union if necessary.

Established in 1948 by Curtis LeMay and others, the RAND Corporation provided analysis and research to the United States military and played an integral role in the new aggressive nuclear strategy of the United States. After Kennedy took office, McNamara hired a list of defense experts from the RAND Corporation to help shape the future of nuclear policy.

Among these were Carl Kaysen and William Kaufmann, and they exercised significant influence over America’s new nuclear strategy. Kaufmann found that despite Soviet claims of a significant

ICBM stockpile, they had only eight operational missiles.9 But, instead of assuaging fears of

Soviet nuclear capability, Kaufmann saw an opportunity. He believed that through an isolated attack, the Kennedy administration “could knock out the whole Soviet nuclear arsenal” and

9 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

8 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

7 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random House, 2009), 415.

6 Neil Sheehan, A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate Weapon (New York, NY: Random House, 2009), 415.

effectively win a nuclear war.10 Kaysen’s — and newly-recruited RAND consultant Henry

Kissinger’s — subsequent agreement with Kaufmann again alluded to a fundamental change in defense thought: that a nuclear war was winnable, and that aggression would be advantageous to the United States. Kissinger specifically instructed National Security Advisor McGeorge Bundy

“to submit a plan for graduated nuclear response,” in a memo on July 7, 1961.11 Bundy informed the President of RAND’s suggestion, and Kaysen “took charge of organizing the first-strike plan.”12 RAND not only had a direct connection to the Kennedy administration and the development of the new flexible first-strike plan, but also directly influenced the administration’s nuclear policy during and after the Berlin Crisis.

Arguably the most famous employee of RAND was Herman Kahn, who in 1960 published On Thermonuclear War — a controversial book discussing the possibility of atomic warfare. Also in 1960, Kahn published an article entitled The Nature and Feasibility of War and

Deterrence in which many of the same principles were discussed, namely how the United States could ‘win’ a nuclear war with the Soviets. Kahn argued that the United States must “stand up to the threat of fighting a [nuclear] war and to credibly threaten to initiate one.”13 Kahn correctly assessed that deterrence hinged upon the United States’ willingness to execute a nuclear strike and suffer casualties of its own. For U.S. nuclear strategy to work, the Soviets needed to believe the United States was capable of vast destruction at any moment. Implied in his article was the complete failure of mutually assured destruction, or that nuclear combat did not necessarily result in immediate worldwide ruin. The United States could possibly launch a successful first

13 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960), 39.

12 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

11 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

10 Fred Kaplan, JFK's First-Strike Plan (The Atlantic, October 2001) https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/.

strike on the USSR, as Kennedy prepared to do after Berlin. But, in the event of a Soviet first-strike, the United States needed second-strike capability, or the ability to deliver a lethal blow to the Soviets no matter how well-planned the initial attack — an idea echoed by many at both RAND and in the Federal government. This second-strike was to be tripartite; B-52’s carried nuclear bombs, submarines (SSBN’s) carried ballistic missiles, and mainland missile silos housed ICBM’s. The general principle was to disperse American nuclear capability in order to best preserve the United States’ ability to strike back in the event of an attack.

Kahn’s work at RAND concurred with the nuclear buildup of the Kennedy administration, and perhaps the former explained the latter. Kahn and RAND’s message was clear: the United States “must look much more dangerous as an opponent than as a collaborator” to the Soviets.14 This was an ‘aggressive defense’, so-to-speak; in the minds of those at RAND, more nuclear weapons meant a greater second-strike deterrent. And, even in the event of an attack, Kahn’s plan gave the United States the greatest chance of victory — a sentiment realized in the Kennedy administration’s first-strike proposal in 1961. Kaysen, Kaufmann, and

Kissinger’s proximity to President Kennedy, the National Security Council (NSC), and the

Department of Defense (DoD) certainly supported this theory. But some of the most convincing evidence came from Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara. By the mid-1960s, McNamara

“had come to believe that the U.S. deterrent capability, the nation’s strategic offensive forces, not the damage-limiting strategic defense forces, protected American society.”15 Moreover, he believed that a smaller, pointed nuclear strike benefited the United States more so than all-out

15 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in U.S. Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22. https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.

14 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960), 42.

warfare.16 His beliefs were similar to those of Kahn: that offensive capabilities served to protect the balance of peace, and reflected Kaysen, Kaufmann and Kissinger through advocating for a flexible, strategic nuclear response. McNamara implemented the RAND mode of thinking in the

1961 plan under Kennedy. The McNamara-RAND label of nuclear warfare was “calculated,

[and] deliberate” through extensive use of precise statistics to determine success; McNamara held that a U.S. strike — either preemptive or retaliatory — required at least 55 million Soviet deaths.17 Kahn similarly explored the possibility of widespread Soviet urban evacuations, in which only five to 10 million Soviet citizens would be killed in a U.S. retaliatory strike — a number insufficient for both deterrence and nuclear victory.18 Though defense was important,

McNamara reflected Kahn’s use of offensive nuclear capabilities to ensure that a) The United

States could ‘win’ a first-strike scenario; b) the Soviets would be deterred by a devastating second-strike; or c) neither side would use nuclear weapons for fear of mutually assured destruction.

RAND’s plan — though radical — was both innovative and effective, a fact recognized by both the Kennedy administration and military personnel such as Curtis LeMay. People such as

Kaysen, Kaufmann, and Kissinger communicated directly with the NSC and DoD, and Secretary

McNamara implemented many of Kahn’s ideas. RAND’s plan for nuclear deterrence and potential victory hinged upon sufficient nuclear stockpiles and a demonstrable willingness to initiate nuclear warfare — it ensured a ‘peace through strength’. Though counterintuitive, this

‘offensive defense’ was successful. For instance, the Soviets might not have been compelled to remove missiles from Cuba if not for a credible threat of nuclear war with the United States. The

18 Herman Kahn, The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence (Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 1960), 9-10.

17 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in US Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22. https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.

16 Keith B. Payne, The Great Divide in US Deterrence Thought (Strategic Studies Quarterly 14, no. 2, 2020), 22. https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276.

evidence supporting RAND’s responsibility for the change in nuclear policy was overwhelming; the Kennedy administration and McNamara replicated the ideas of Kaysen, Kaufmann,

Kissinger, and Kahn and made them official policy. Almost 80 years after Hiroshima and

Nagasaki, no nuclear conflict has occurred. Perhaps, then, RAND deserves credit for preventing a nuclear war during a time of great international volatility — the early 1960s.

References

Kahn, H. (1960). The Nature and Feasibility of War and Deterrence. RAND Corporation.

Kaplan, F. (2001, October 1). JFK's first-strike plan. The Atlantic. Retrieved March 2022, from https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2001/10/jfks-first-strike-plan/376432/

Payne, K. B. (2020). The Great Divide in US Deterrence Thought. Strategic Studies

Quarterly, 2(14). https://doi.org/https://www.jstor.org/stable/26915276

Roser, M., Herre, B., & Hasell, J. (2013, August 6). Nuclear weapons. Our World in Data.

Retrieved March 2022, from https://ourworldindata.org/nuclear-weapons

Sheehan, N. (2009). A Fiery Peace in a Cold War: Bernard Schriever and the Ultimate

Weapon. Random House.

label: TRAP Bills, Abortion
nurj_title: TRAP Bills, Abortion
text:
Methodology

In order to determine how Louisiana lawmakers discuss Targeted Regulation of Abortion

Providers (TRAP) legislation, this study examines and codes video footage showcasing the

House and Senate committee meetings where TRAP bills were deliberated. This study consists of a total of six TRAP bills and 12 corresponding videos, as each TRAP bill was argued both in a

House and Senate committee. Notably, most TRAP bills were sent to the Health and Welfare

Committee to be discussed, and that committee appears the most throughout the study. Although other abortion-related laws were introduced and passed within the time frame of this study, these six TRAP bills were my sole focus as they posed the greatest threat to abortion clinics in

Louisiana. The study spans from 2014 to 2020, corresponding to the year that House Bill 388, an admitting privileges law, was passed and the year it was struck down by the Supreme Court in

June Medical Services L.L.C. v. Russo.1 I watched these hearings and paid special attention to the language choices used by lawmakers when they discussed abortion, women, fetuses, and the

Supreme Court, which resulted in an open coding of the footage. This careful inspection and coding were used to highlight any societal gender-based stereotypes present in the passing of these TRAP bills, examine the Louisiana legislature’s attitudes about the Supreme Court, and obtain an insight into law-making in a pro-life state.2

Results

The first bill in this study, introduced in 2014, was House Bill 388. HB388 established admitting privileges for physicians who performed abortions, mandating that any abortion physician must be able to admit patients to a nearby hospital. As mentioned above, this bill was

2 A 2019 study found that 60% of Louisiana residents believe abortion should be illegal in most or all cases. “The State of Abortion and Contraception Attitudes in All 50 States,” PRRI (blog), accessed March 7, 2022, https://www.prri.org/research/legal-in-most-cases-the-impact-of-the-abortion-debate-in-2019-america/.

1 “18-1323 June Medical Services L.L.C. v. Russo (06/29/2020),” https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/19pdf/18-1323_c07d.pdf.

struck down six years later by the Supreme Court in June Medical Services v. Russo (2020).3 The next two TRAP bills— House Bill 488 and House Bill 815 — were introduced in 2016. HB488 mandated that abortion physicians must be board-certified, or if they are currently enrolled in a residency program, must obtain on-site supervision from a physician who is board-certified.4

HB815 regulated the ways in which abortion clinics could dispose of fetal remains after abortions were completed, requiring abortion providers to sign contracts with funeral homes to either bury or cremate the fetal remains.5 Senate Bill 325, introduced in 2018, established criminal penalties for abortion clinics that intentionally destroyed records, performed an abortion on a minor, or completed patient forms in advance of a patient’s appointment.6

The last two bills in this study, House Bill 484 and House Bill 133, were both introduced in 2019. HB484 imposed regulations on the storing of medical documents — mandating that physicians, medical directors, and owners of an abortion clinic would all be responsible for the retention of records. Additionally, the bill established longer retention periods and imposed penalties for violations.7 HB133 expanded the meaning of “abortion” to include medical abortions, mandating that the abortion pill could only be dispensed at a licensed facility.8 All six bills were signed into law within a few months after their introductions.

My analysis is split up into several key themes that emerged from the 12 legislative hearings on TRAP bills — negative treatment of opposition, the woman-protective argument,

8 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 133 by Representative Frank Hoffmann,” 2019 Regular Session, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=19RS&b=HB133&sbi=y.

7 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 484 by Representative Raymond Crews,” 2019 Regular Session, https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=19RS&b=HB484&sbi=y.

6 Louisiana State Legislature, “Senate Bill 325 by Senator Milkovich,” 2018 Regular Session, http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=18rs&b=SB325&sbi=y.

5 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 815 by Representative Julie Stokes,” 2016 Regular Session, http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=16rs&b=HB815&sbi=y.

4 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 488 by Representative Katrina Jackson,” 2016 Regular Session, http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=16rs&b=HB488&sbi=y.

3 Louisiana State Legislature, “House Bill 388 by Representative Katrina Jackson,” 2014 Regular Session, http://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?s=14RS&b=ACT620.

descriptions of fetuses, descriptions of women, and mentions of the Supreme Court. Throughout all 12 hearings, 23 individuals spoke in favor of these TRAP bills, while 15 voiced their opposition. House Bill 388 notably had the greatest number of people wishing to give testimony, as it was arguably the most detrimental to Louisiana women’s access to abortion. On top of supporting linguistic themes within the existing literature and highlighting the Louisiana legislature’s attitudes about the federal legality of abortion, this study also offers an insight into law-making in a conservative and anti-abortion state.

Negative Treatment of Opposition/Pro-Choice Sentiment

Throughout all 12 hearings, it was apparent from the attitudes of the Louisiana legislature that pro-life sentiment was the norm, and any TRAP bill that did not explicitly scoff in the face of the Court’s rulings, therefore inviting costly lawsuits, would be passed with little to no opposition. The Louisiana legislature expressed pride in their pro-life stances, as demonstrated when Rep. Pope (R) began his introduction to SB325 by saying, “I think it’s been very very evident throughout the last years that this committee has taken a very strong stance against abortion.”9 Upon hearing this, the chairman of the House, Rep. Hoffmann (R), responded with an emphatic, “No doubt.”10 Similarly, in his opening remarks on HB133, Rep. Hoffmann claimed,

“We are very proud of Louisiana being a pro-life state.”11 This pro-life bias was especially apparent in the treatment of pro-choice voices during these legislative sessions. Although not all hearings included pro-choice voices, when opposition did present itself, opposers of TRAP bills were noticeably silenced and critiqued at a greater rate than anti-abortion activists.

11 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:02:29-1:02:35).

10 Ibid., (1:39:16).

9 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Committee on Judiciary C Meeting 04/17/18,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2018/04/041718JUDC_0, (1:39:07-1:39:15).

The most notable examples of this occurred in discussions of HB388. While pro-choice lawyer Ellie Schilling explained her opposition of the bill, she was interrupted by Rep. Simon

(R) with a question of, “Can we wrap this up please?” When she agreed and began to finish her sentence, he repeated, “You have one more minute, ma’am.”12 Notably, this was the first time in this hour-long discussion where the aspect of time constraint had been mentioned. The representative also told a second opponent of the bill, Sylvia Cochran, to “wrap it up” before she was finished speaking.13 Another significant interaction with this bill occurred when Carrie

Wutten, a representative for Louisiana Progress Action, stated strongly that each legislator in the room would be complicit in the deaths of Louisiana women who would inevitably die after being forced to obtain an abortion illegally.14 In response, Rep. Simon angrily exclaimed, “We face decisions like this daily, and for somebody to come here and make a statement like that is just absurd…none of us take it lightly. And I speak on behalf of my members that we don’t appreciate that type of talk around here.”15 Lastly, when Rep. Simon read out the red cards in opposition of this bill at the end of this discussion, he seemed entirely uninterested and even refused to correctly state some of the names. As he read the cards, for example, he said,

“Bethany VanCamping…uhhh…Louisiana Students for Reproductive…Whatever,”16 which elicited a chuckle from Representative Jackson (D).

In the Senate discussion of HB388, Ellie Schilling claimed that it would be difficult for an OBGYN in a rural area to find a hospital within 30 miles where they could obtain admitting privileges. Sen. Nevers (D) responded by asking for documentation to back up that statement, a

16 Ibid., (3:53:57-3:54:08).

15 Ibid., (3:49:07-3:49:32).

14 Ibid., (3:43:26-3:43:59).

13 Ibid., (3:28:47).

12 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW, (3:02:48-3:02:57).

question that had not been asked of anyone else so far in this discussion.17 When Schilling responded by saying that her statement was based more on common sense than statistics, claiming that rural areas have less hospitals in general, Sen. Nevers countered by saying, “Well, I just, you know, because you’re sworn to tell the truth and–and you know, when you sign the witness card, I just wanted to be sure that if you–that you tell us if you have data that supports that statement or not. And right now, you don’t have that data.”18 This quote from Sen. Nevers was quite shocking, as no anti-abortion advocates had been asked to provide specific data to back up their claims in this discussion, even after several proponents of HB388 were proven to have misrepresented Louisiana’s existing admitting privileges laws earlier in this senate discussion.19

These clear examples of bias from the Louisiana legislature suggest that with morality policies such as abortion, it is extremely difficult for legislatures to be impartial.

Describing Abortion: The Woman-Protective Argument

The woman-protective argument that Siegel chronologizes in her work appeared commonly in the Louisiana legislature’s debates on TRAP legislation — it was mentioned in every video included in this study.20 Anti-abortion advocates relied heavily on this argument to promote adding additional regulations to Louisiana abortion clinics. Imposing stringent regulations on abortion clinics was framed as a necessity due to the dangers of abortion procedures. In reality, abortion is a remarkably safe procedure, with the World Health

Organization calling it a “safe and simple health care intervention” as long as it is performed legally and with proper sanitation.21 The protective paternalism that emerged in Greubel’s study

21 World Health Organization, “Abortion,” accessed March 11, 2022, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/abortion.

20 Reva B. Siegel, “The Right’s Reasons: Constitutional Conflict and the Spread of Woman-Protective Antiabortion Argument,” Duke Law Journal 57, no. 6 (2008): 1641-1692.

19 Ibid., (2:14:22-2:14:52).

18 Ibid., (2:24:00-2:24:16).

17 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (2:23:38).

was also present during these discussions, with many anti-abortion advocates promoting

Louisiana TRAP bills on the basis that the state has the right to protect women from incompetent physicians who would fall under Greubel’s definition of “bad players.”22

Anti-abortion advocates utilized the “bad players” argument in several ways, highlighting cases of supposed malpractice within Louisiana abortion clinics as well as using the case of

Kermit Gosnell to argue that women need protection from malicious physicians. Gosnell, the

Philadelphia abortion doctor currently serving a life sentence for running an unsanitary clinic and murdering three infants born after failed abortions, was mentioned a total of 10 times throughout these 12 legislative hearings.23 Greasley points out the logical fallacies of using Gosnell as an anti-abortion argument, as making legal abortion harder to access will most likely result in a greater quantity of illegal abortion cites and subsequently a greater amount of dangerous abortions performed.24 Louisiana’s legislature and anti-abortion advocates clearly disagreed with

Greasley’s argument, using Gosnell to advocate for stricter regulations on abortion providers.

Ryan Verret, representing Louisiana Right to Life, highlighted the Kermit Gosnell case in his advocacy for HB488, using Gosnell’s clinic as an example of “the tragedy that abortion imposes on women and unborn babies.”25 Verret was one of many anti-abortion advocates who used the Gosnell case to extrapolate and describe all abortions as highly dangerous. In several legislative hearings, connections were made between the Delta Clinic of Baton Rouge and

Kermit Gosnell, with Deanna Candler notably naming Eileen O’Neill, who left the Delta Clinic

25 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/30/16,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2016/mar/0330_16_HW, (17:28-17:33).

24 Kate Greasley, “The Pearl of the ‘Pro-Life’ Movement? Reflections on the Kermit Gosnell Controversy,” Journal of Medical Ethics 40, no. 6 (2014): 419–23.

23 Sarah Hoye, “Gosnell Sentenced to Life in Third Baby’s Death,” CNN, https://www.cnn.com/2013/05/15/justice/pennsylvania-abortion-sentences/index.html.

22 Amanda Greubel, “Benevolent Sexism in the Targeted Regulation of Abortion Providers (TRAP): A Case Study of Texas House Bill 2,” Sex Roles (2021): 650-660. Greubel defines “bad players” as “doctors and clinics who commit egregious harm in their practices of abortion” (655).

and “surrendered her medical license, claiming that she had Post Traumatic Stress

Disorder…After that, she went to practice without a license in the Philadelphia abortion clinic of

Kermit Gosnell.”26 While many other claims about the dangers of abortions were impossible to corroborate, the grand jury report on the Gosnell case does include this information on O’Neill, who was subsequently sentenced to six to 23 months of house arrest on conspiracy and corruption charges.27

The “bad players” argument manifested itself through descriptions of malpractice in

Louisiana abortion clinics, as well as claims of abortion clinics’ alleged connections to the sex trafficking industry. In his advocacy for SB325, Sen. Milkovich (D) accused abortion facilities of falsifying their records, adding that these facilities were allegedly concealing “abortions performed on minors and potentially abortions performed to support the sex trafficking industry.”28 The Senator offered no tangible proof to back up this intense claim. As the

Committee on Judiciary C meeting went on, Sen. Milkovich brought up the Delta Clinic in Baton

Rouge as an example, alleging that “women would be screaming, and they would not give them proper medical care…they were re-using the instruments over and over and over again and they were filthy.”29 These vivid and repugnant descriptions of the Delta Clinic are arguably descriptions of torture, with Sen. Milkovich essentially claiming that abortion physicians at this clinic knowingly abused their patients. In a similar way of thinking, Richard Mahoney, an independent citizen, also attacked the Delta Clinic, stating, “The Delta Clinic pre-signed and

29 Ibid., (3:03:37-3:04:05).

28 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Committee on Judiciary C Meeting 04/17/18,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2018/04/041718JUDC_0, (2:57:45-2:57:59).

27 R. Seth Williams, District Attorney, “Report of the Grand Jury,” Pennsylvania, https://operationrescue.org/pdfs/GrandJuryWomensMedical.pdf; Emad Khalil and Vince Lattanzio, “Tearful Gosnell Associate: I Just Wanted to Give Care,” NBC10 Philadelphia, https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/national-international/gosnell-associate-gets-house-arrest/1963884/.

26 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:48:56-1:49:25).

pre-checked the forms before they even saw their victims.”30 While Sen. Milkovich heavily implied that women who visited the Delta Clinic were abused, Mahoney explicitly referred to these female patients as victims, framing the clinic as an evil antagonist.

Rep. Crews (R) introduced HB484 by explaining that it was born out of necessity after an abortion clinic, Bossier City Medical, “unlawfully shredded patient records after the state documented that it failed to notify law enforcement of a 14-year-old girl’s reported rape. So, she reported rape, and then these records get shredded.”31 Rep. Crews’ word choice heavily suggests that the abortion clinic was knowingly complicit in the sexual crime committed through their shredding of the patient records. Rep. Crews similarly ended his testimony by saying, “This really is a women’s and sadly a child’s bill. We’re trying to stop trafficking and predatory practices and without records, what do you do?”32 His language establishes a sense of urgency, implying not only that abortion clinics are complicit in the continuation of sexual crimes, but also that clinic records are imperative to solving sex trafficking crimes. This implication that abortion clinics are perpetrators of crimes was taken a step further by Richard Mahoney, who stated that he was testifying against “the egregious medical malpractice and child molestation cover-up by the abortion cartel for 38 years in this state.”33 Mahoney’s strong statement was not backed up by any evidence, but his statement dramatically furthered the woman-protective argument by explicitly defining abortion clinics as criminal organizations.

The most common occurrences of the woman-protective argument were generalized statements of the dangers of abortions, with a heavy focus on the procedure’s possible health

33 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:43:35-1:43:46).

32 Ibid., (6:17:58-6:18:04).

31 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Wellness Committee Meeting 04/24/19,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (5:55:42-5:56:06).

30 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (1:43:45-1:44:00).

complications. Kathy Kliebert, representing the Dept. of Health and Hospitals, highlighted the

“clear health risks associated with an abortion,” such as “pelvic infection, blood clots, and other serious complications like perforation of the uterine wall, which is reported in 1 out of every 500 abortions” in her discussion of HB388.34 Dr. Damon Cudihy, a board-certified OBGYN, claimed that surgical abortions “have several known complications that are inherent in the procedure itself, not necessarily the result of an incompetent physician, or any sort of malpractice.”35 Dr.

Cudihy’s language provides a twist on the above portrayals of protecting women from evil or incompetent physicians, as he stigmatized abortions by maintaining that even the best physicians cannot save women from experiencing dangerous complications. In both discussions of HB133,

Dorinda Bordlee, the Senior Counsel of Bioethics Defense Fund, used imagery from a film to add a vivid description of the dangers of medical abortions, saying, “If any of you have seen the movie ‘Unplanned,’ it kind of opens up with that scene and how painful that is where she’s passing that baby at home in the shower.”36 Bordlee’s use of this film provided a visual to go along with the medical descriptions of abortion complications, furthering the classification of abortions as painful and dangerous procedures.

Accompanying their descriptions of abortion dangers and complications, many anti-abortion advocates made broad and factually incorrect claims about the deadly nature of abortions. Kathy Kliebert stated in her defense of HB388 that Louisiana “has a strong history of enacting strong laws to protect the lives of women and children.”37 Cindy Collins, the founder of

37 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW, (1:59:16-1:59:21).

36 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:04:32-1:04:41).

35 Ibid., (2:07:45-2:07:59).

34 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW, (1:59:31-1:59:52).

Louisiana Abortion Recovery, used her testimony to further this notion, exclaiming, “Women deserve the care that they need to save their life.”38 Dorinda Bordlee also claimed, “Abortion is a violence against women that commonly takes their lives.”39 Bordlee took the deadly abortion argument one step further by claiming that abortion is not only “violent,” but that abortion-related deaths are common-place. In discussions of SB325, Mike Johnson, an independent citizen representing himself, went on to describe Louisiana’s Delta Clinic by saying that this facility “risked the lives of every woman who went there for an abortion.”40

As proven in the beginning of this section, abortions have a very low complication rate, and dying from an abortion procedure is extremely uncommon. The above rhetoric was clearly meant to inspire fear of abortion clinics and physicians — a motive that may have disastrous consequences for Louisiana women. Influencing the women of Louisiana into losing trust in abortion clinics will not stop abortions, but might convince women to seek more dangerous, at-home methods of abortion. After all, why would women pay hundreds of dollars at an abortion clinic if doing so could result in the same complications they would receive from opting for a cheaper, street-market abortion method? Low-income women who desire an abortion for their own valid reasons might end up choosing cheaper, illegal methods of abortion if they believe that clinics cannot give them a higher standard of safety.

The Woman-Protective Argument: Mental Health

While most descriptions of the dangers of abortions were physical, mental health also played a notable part in this discussion, with anti-abortion activists maintaining that abortion inflicts mental trauma and distress upon women. In support of HB388, Cindy Collins stated, “I

40 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/08/18,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2018/may/0508_18_HW, (1:35:01-1:35:05).

39 Ibid., (2:19:56-2:20:02).

38 Ibid., (2:18:50-2:18:56).

have been helping women recover from the trauma they’ve experienced due to abortion for the past 28 years.”41 Collins returned to testify in support of HB133 and made several other statements that described abortion as mentally dangerous to women, saying, “We have many broken women in our state…and the damage to women is increasing also.”42 Collins’ description of women who obtain abortions as “broken” highlights the psychological emphasis on the woman-protective argument —anti-abortion advocates focus on possible feelings of regret following an abortion, implying that women who make this choice suffer a great psychological burden afterwards.

When a pro-choice opponent argued that a previously cited abortion-related death had not actually resulted from the abortion pill but from an unconnected drug overdose, Rep. LeBas explicitly mentioned this feeling of regret, alleging that, “Sometimes, when you deal with these people and they begin to suffer and have second thoughts, sometimes they revert to drug overdoses. The drug overdose may have been due to the abortion in that way.”43 Through his immediate speculation that this drug overdose must have occurred as a result of post-abortion depression, Rep. LeBas reveals the main mental health assumption of anti-abortion advocates — that it is extremely rare for a woman to feel good about her decision post-abortion. In the Senate discussion of HB388, Sen. Nevers asked the question of, “What’s the percentage of mental complications that we have following an abortion?” Alice Chapman, a medical student at LSU, responded by saying that she was aware of a study which “found better outcomes for women who sought an abortion and were able to obtain their abortion than they did for women who

43 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW, (2:54:18-2:54:46).

42 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 04/24/19,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2019/apr/0424_19_HW, (1:08:12-1:08:37).

41 Louisiana House On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 03/18/14,” https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2014/Mar_2014/0319_14_HW, (2:15:22-2:15:32).

sought an abortion and were unable to obtain it.” Sen. Nevers responded negatively to the mention of this study, stating, “Well that’s in your opinion. I–I mean, I’ve heard just the opposite, so I don’t know which one’s right. I mean, if we had the data, we could see it.”44 Not only does this short interaction provide further support for the showcased earlier in this study, it also highlights how real, tangible data is mostly ignored by the Louisiana legislature in favor of anecdotal evidence that favors their political opinions.

44 Louisiana State Senate On-Demand Video, “Health and Welfare Committee Meeting 05/07/14,” https://senate.la.gov/s_video/videoarchive.asp?v=senate/2014/05/050714h~w, (2:32:40-2:33:30).

label: The Relationship Between Image and Spectator: The Case of the Advertisement
nurj_title: The Relationship Between Image and Spectator: The Case of the Advertisement
text:
Sanders 0

The Relationship Between Image and Spectator: The Case of the Advertisement

Jean Sanders

Art, Literature, and Contemporary European Thought

Professors Isabelle Alfandry, Marc Crepon, and Michael Loriaux

December 12, 2019

Sanders 1

At one time in history, advertisements were confined to the print page. In contemporary society, we are surrounded by them everywhere we look. Advertisements did not truly enter the private sphere until the first television advertisement aired in 1941.1 In less than a century, advertisements have firmly invaded almost every aspect of our lives. They remain ubiquitous on the print page, on billboards on the streets, and on televisions in our homes. Now, they are even held in our hands. Furthermore, they are now pointedly targeted, as corporations use personal data to tailor advertisements to specific subsets of the population. As they become omnipresent, it is more important than ever to examine them closely with a critical lens. Advertisements are images that serve a specific and unique role, firstly because of the type of image that they are.

Herbert Read writes that “the artist cannot in any effective way avoid the economic conditions of his time; he cannot ignore them, for they will not ignore him.”2 This is certainly true: Marx describes art as being a part of the superstructure of an economic system.3 Images can be processed, understood, and analyzed through the lens of their role in the economic system under which they were created. However, advertisements are images that have an even closer connection with their economic system. In modern times, art can be used as a tool to propagate an economic system and a political ideology, like in the case of Soviet Socialist Realism in the

20th century. In this case, these images must be understood and analyzed not just through their status in culture and society, but also in close connection to this economic system. Although it is often the purpose of works of art to change the way that people think, in the case of advertising

3 Isabelle Alfandary, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” (class lecture, Topics in Comparative Literature: Critical Modernity: New Forms, New Experiences, l’Université Sorbonne-Nouvelle, Paris, France, November 11, 2019).

2 Herbert Read, “What Is Revolutionary Art?” (ART THEORY, accessed December 3, 2019, http://theoria.art-zoo.com/what-is-revolutionary-art-herbert-read/)

1 Daniel Ganninger, “The World's First Television Commercial,” Medium (Knowledge Stew, July 14, 2019), https://medium.com/knowledge-stew/the-worlds-first-television-commercial-4f0b73f27b07#:~:ta rgetText=)

Sanders 2 this purpose is more explicit: to exert influence over people’s beliefs and desires. Furthermore, the role of the spectator of the image is changed when a spectator is viewing an advertisement because the spectator is also firmly inhabiting the role of a consumer. There are many conflicting ideas about the relationship between spectator and image. Writers such as Jacques Rancière have attempted to de-emphasize the power of the image in order to accentuate the individuality of the spectator, while other thinkers such as Walter Benjamin and Guy DeBord have argued that the image is a dangerous and powerful tool with the capability to affect masses of people in the same way. Depending on how the relationship between spectator and image is defined, the critical value, transformative properties, or revolutionary ability of images changes as well.

DeBord’s explanation of this relationship emphasizes the power of the image and places the image as the very object which mediates relationships in society, which he calls “The Society of the Spectacle.” Some would argue that images are an incredibly powerful tool in the process of the fetishization of commodities. However, Rancière has an opposite stance in reaction to these and argues that the dissensus of the contemporary aesthetic regime means the image does not have the power others have assigned to it. There is a pre-existing body of literature from the

20th century that examines the role of an image and the relationship between spectator and image for many different types of images, but none of them focus on advertising. However, the ideas put forth about whether or not images have the power to affect the masses, what type of freedom spectators have, and the mechanisms by which images are persuasive can be utilized to examine the case of the advertisement. How can the relationship between spectator and image inform the relationship between consumer and advertisement?

This paper will argue that the relationship between consumer and advertisement cannot be analyzed on an individual scale because advertisements are proven to have the ability to

Sanders 3 change the attitudes and actions of society as a whole. A de-emphasis of the power of the image ignores this persistent effect on society, and the mechanism by which an image persuades not just individuals, but masses of people, is clearly at play in the case of the advertising image.

In The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, Benjamin traces mechanically reproduced images, or works of art, from lithography to photography to the sound film. Not only is advertising certainly a mechanically reproduced form of artwork, but it is also one that

Benjamin would say is similar to the film in that it is “completely subject to or, like the film, founded in, mechanical reproduction.”4 Benjamin’s point of view for critically analyzing mechanically produced art is also useful because he writes that “the question of whether photography is an art” is a futile one, and the “primary” question should be “whether the very invention of photography had not transformed the entire nature of art.”5 In outlets like Forbes and The Harvard Business Review many articles have posed the question: Is Advertising an Art?

This paper will instead try to situate advertising within the pre-existing body of literature written about art, regardless of its status as art or non-art, and to examine in which ways advertising has transformative properties or critical value. In analyzing mechanically reproduced art Benjamin writes of the concept of aura:

“One might subsume the eliminated element in the term ‘aura’ and go on to say: that which withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art. This is a symptomatic process whose significance points beyond the realm of art. One might generalize by saying: the technique of reproduction

5 Ibid

4 Walter Benjamin, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” accessed December 4, 2019, https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/philosophy/works/ge/benjamin.htm)

Sanders 4 detaches the reproduced object from the domain of tradition. By making many reproductions it substitutes a plurality of copies for a unique existence. And in permitting the reproduction to meet the beholder or listener in his own particular situation, it reactivates the object reproduced. These two processes lead to a tremendous shattering of tradition which is the obverse of the contemporary crisis and renewal of mankind. Both processes are intimately connected with the contemporary mass movements.”6

Aura is a negative phenomenon in that it is only experienced when it is lost — when it is present, it is not noticed, but its absence, according to Benjamin, is felt and changes the nature of the artwork.7 When art is mechanically reproduced the aura is absent, because the aura is what constitutes the aesthetic experience as unique, and mechanically reproduced works are inherently not unique because there is no original and each copy is identical.8

One question seemingly posed by his piece is: what are the political and aesthetic consequences of the loss of aura? He writes that “mechanical reproduction of art changes the reaction of the masses toward art.”9 One of the ways that it does so is through the shift from contemplation to distraction. He writes:

“Reception in a state of distraction, which is increasing noticeably in all fields of art and is symptomatic of profound changes in apperception, finds in the

9 Walter Benjamin, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” accessed December 4, 2019, https://www.marxists.org/reference/subject/philosophy/works/ge/benjamin.htm)

8 Ibid

7 Isabelle Alfandary, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” (class lecture, Topics in Comparative Literature: Critical Modernity: New Forms, New Experiences, l’Université Sorbonne-Nouvelle, Paris, France, November 11, 2019).

6 Ibid

Sanders 5 film its true means of exercise. The film with its shock effect meets this mode of reception halfway. The film makes the cult value recede into the background not only by putting the public in the position of the critic, but also by the fact that at the movies this position requires no attention. The public is an examiner, but an absent-minded one.”10

The idea of the spectator as an absent-minded and distracted examiner who is not paying full attention to the image in front of them is also present in the spectator-image relationship when it comes to advertising. Television advertisements “engages the audience in low-involvement learning.”11 Due to the fact that the spectator is paying little attention to the advertisements on the television, they are engaging in “learning without involvement.” This phenomenon is described by Schudson in “Advertising as Capitalist Realism” when he writes:

“In such learning, people are not ‘persuaded’ of something. Nor do their attitudes change. But there is a kind of ‘sleeper’ effect. While viewers are not persuaded, they do alter the structure of their perceptions about a product, shifting

‘the relative salience of attributes’ in the advertised brand. Nothing follows from this until the consumer arrives at the supermarket, ready to make a purchase.”12

Just as Benjamin describes the spectators of films to be distracted examiners, as are the consumers in front of the television in that they are “relatively unwary. They take ads to be trivial or transparent or both,”13 which is precisely the reason why advertisements are successful. This is

13 Ibid

12 Ibid

11 Michael Schudson, “Advertising as Capitalist Realism,” Advertising &Amp; Society Review 1, no. 1 (2000), https://doi.org/10.1353/asr.2000.0023)

10 Ibid

Sanders 6 consistent with consumer behavior research, which shows that when consumers are distracted when they see a persuasive message, it is more likely to be effective because the consumer is not paying attention enough to engage in internal counter-arguing against the persuasive message.14

Advertising images have taken advantage of the distracted spectator that Benjamin speaks about in order to persuade them of their message.
