text:
Running head: GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 1

Gendered Messages in The Handmaid's Tale: Offred's Evolution, 1985 - 2017

Kayan Khraisheh

MIT 398: Feminist Media Historiography

10/10/2021

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 2

In 1985, Canadian author Margaret Atwood released a novel titled The Handmaid’s Tale, which follows the chilling story of a Handmaid named Offred. In the dystopian society of Gilead, there are very few remaining fertile women, as a result of environmental pollution and radiation.

The protagonist, Offred, is one of the few women left with the ability to bear children. Her duty as a Handmaid is to give birth to children from upper-class men. If she fails to do so, she is labeled an “unwoman” and destined to a horrible fate. Gilead’s oppressive system functions due to the imprisonment and brainwashing of women (Septiawati & Darma, 2014). Offred’s story is explicit and harrowing, and does not have a happy ending. It has been the subject of extensive feminist analysis. Atwood’s novel was adapted to the screen twice, first as a film in 1990, and later as a TV series in 2017. The three versions of this story differ significantly and have been received very differently by critics and audiences. There is an abundance of feminist and media discourse regarding whether these different versions of The Handmaid’s Tale are pro-feminist and empower women, or anti-feminist and promote sexist narratives.

While several scholarly articles analyze the individual media artifacts from a feminist perspective, few studies, if any, compare the three versions in terms of gender representations.

Therefore, in this paper, I will be analyzing the differences in the gendered messages conveyed in the three versions of The Handmaid’s Tale to date: the 1985 novel by Margaret Atwood, the

1990 film adaptation directed by Volker Schlöndorff, and the 2017 TV series by executive producer Bruce Miller. For the TV series, I will primarily focus on Season One, as the following seasons extend beyond the events of the novel. I will highlight the changes in feminist narratives with an awareness of the different contexts at the time of each artifact’s release. This paper will also examine the historical reception of these artifacts; special attention will be paid to the 1990

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 3 movie adaption which is greatly overlooked and lacks in popularity compared to the novel and the show.

This paper concludes that the three versions of The Handmaid’s Tale differ narratively - through the prominence of Offred’s voice, her agency, and her motives - but also in terms of visual portrayal. In the film, these changes reduce the complexity of her character and the emotional depth of the story, resulting in a negative reception by audiences and critics. However, in the show, the changes made suit the contemporary context while still resonating with

Atwood’s original portrayal.

Historical Contexts

Before diving into an analysis of gendered messages, it is necessary to look at the different historical contexts at the time of each artifact's release. This will help in understanding the reasons for the changes made from medium to medium. The novel by Atwood was released in 1985, near the end of second-wave feminism. Some scholars analyzing Atwood and her work have determined that The Handmaid’s Tale is a critique of second-wave feminism. Although

Atwood was politically active in advocating for human rights and social equality for women beginning in the early 1960s, her beliefs did not always align with those of second-wave feminists. She believed that second-wave feminists frequently advanced a single issue at the expense of all the others, rather than confronting the multitude of socio-economic issues that women faced; this meant that women with different goals were often at odds with one another, with feelings of resentment and distrust more common than feelings of unity (Callaway, 2008).

Atwood was also strongly critical of radical feminism, a branch of second-wave feminism which advocated for the annihilation of sex roles and a complete revolution in terms of gendered

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 4 oppression on all fronts. Atwood found this approach to be antagonistic towards men and thought that this kind of fear and aggression could undermine the successes of the women’s liberation movement (Callaway, 2008).

Thus, The Handmaid’s Tale is frequently perceived to be exploring a potential outcome of radical feminism. Atwood even said in an interview, “if practical, hardline, anti-male feminists took over and became the government, I would resist them” (Neuman, 2006). This can be tied easily to the events of the novel, as it centers on the protagonist’s exploration of rebellion in a society where women are enslaved and oppressed. In “‘Just a Backlash’: Margaret Atwood,

Feminism, and The Handmaid's Tale”, Shirley C. Neuman states that specific scenes within the novel - namely the birthing scene and the brothel - are manifestations of the call of radical feminists for a ‘woman’s culture’ (Neuman, 2006). Over the years, Atwood has grappled with the definition of feminism and whether she considers herself and her work to be feminist, as demonstrated by her various published interviews. In a 1982 interview, she described the term feminism as “one of the all-purpose words”, saying feminist positions can range from “people who think men should be pushed off cliffs to people who think it's O.K. for women to read and write” (Callaway, 2008). In another interview, she claimed that her definition of feminism is a

“belief in the rights of women... [as] equal human beings”, concerned with freedom of choice and distinct from notions of feminist or doctrinaire separatism (Neuman, 2006). While her understanding of feminism has evolved over the years, she has remained firm on her opposition to radical feminism.

Atwood claimed that she invented nothing in Gilead, as the events of the novel were directly influenced by events occurring in the world in the early 1980s. Atwood studied and

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 5 integrated the actions of governments including Iran, Afghanistan, the Philippines, and Romania.

Some of the aspects of the novel that were inspired by real-life occurrences in these countries include the use of electric prods in beatings, the murder of dissidents, the monitoring of women monthly for pregnancy, the linkage of women’s wages to childbearing, the outlawing of birth control, and more (Neuman, 2006). It is also important to note that in the United States, the

1980s were marked by Ronald Reagan’s presidency, and he ushered in a new conservatism to

American politics during his eight years in office. Abortion in particular was under attack in the

US, with abortion clinics being bombed, Medicaid halting the funding of legal abortions, and state laws being passed prohibiting even the supply of information about abortion (Neuman,

2006).

The Handmaid’s Tale film was released in 1990, just five years after the release of the novel, during a time in which feminism was entering a new phase. A number of film critics commented on the film’s plausibility considering the context. One critic stated: “It's not entirely unbelievable that a government of fanatical fundamentalists could come to power. (After all, it happened in Iran.)” (Jacobs, 1990). Most interesting is how vastly different the director’s interpretation of the film was from how Atwood perceived it. While Atwood appeared to oppose the idea of a war between the sexes and emphasized the political context that informed the society of Gilead, Schlöndorff stated that the film was about ''the war of the sexes much more than any religious/political war” (Johnston, 1990). He claimed that it was about women’s sexuality, and their fear of sterility and a loss of independence. Atwood responded by stating: “I don't think the book is that at all, and I don't think the film is that. He must have been very worried that people would think of it as just a political film” (Johnston, 1990).

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 6

As with both the novel and the film, the political context at the time of the TV show’s release in 2017 was politically charged, particularly considering the post-election atmosphere.

The year was marked by the start of the Trump era, during which President Donald Trump immediately issued a number of executive orders, many of which restricted the rights of minority groups. Reproductive rights were once again under attack, with restrictions being imposed on abortion and access to birth control, and the impending threat of legalized abortion being reversed (Mulkerrins, 2017). The #MeToo movement was also going viral in late 2017, with people all around the world speaking out against sexual abuse and sexual harassment. This social movement influenced a number of the decisions made in the show, particularly during the transition to Season Two, which extends beyond the events of the novel (Bhuvad, 2018).

Differences

There are numerous changes involving other characters and the establishment of Gilead that were made between the novel, film, and TV show. However in this paper I will focus on changes regarding the protagonist Offred, over time and across different media.

Offred’s Voice

The first key difference between the three media texts is the prominence of Offred’s voice. The novel is narrated by Offred’s perspective, and Atwood frequently includes long, expressive internal monologues that provide valuable insight into her perspective. Having access to her thoughts helps communicate how she defies social expectations and expresses rage towards her situation, but also how she has been brainwashed to believe certain things. In an article comparing the novel and the TV show, Saartje Gobyn asserts that, at the start of the novel,

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 7

Offred’s internal monologues are the only method through which she can express her resistance and defiance of the regime (Gobyn, 2019). One of many examples is when she watches the

Commander whose house she resides in and imagines spitting out the window or throwing something at him. “I don’t feel like being kind”, she says (Atwood, 1985, p. 59). There are countless other examples in which Offred outwardly behaves but inwardly scorns or criticizes the people around her. However, Gobyn explains, Offred’s internal monologues also highlight how she is “slowly but surely indoctrinated by the ideas that she was initially opposed to” (Gobyn,

2019). Her resistance lessens over the course of the novel, and she begins to behave more passively, a change which is only evident through the progression of her thoughts. Thus, Offred’s internal monologues are essential in understanding her character.

The film omits Offred’s internal monologues completely, with no substitute provided to replace this look into Offred’s thoughts. According to Gobyn, Offred’s internal monologue is the primary narrative technique used to represent her search for identity, her resistance, and the collapse of her resistance (Gobyn, 2019). The removal of such an important aspect of the novel strips away much of the complexity of Offred’s character. Additionally, the film has a fairly minimalist script, meaning not a lot is verbalized. Offred has nearly the same amount of lines as the other characters. One scene which demonstrates the impact of this change is the scene in which Offred takes notice of a Handmaid who is pregnant. In the film it is quite a short scene, no more than 20 seconds, and Offred speaks only a few words. Ofglen, Offred’s neighbor and shopping partner, says, “she must be a very happy girl”, in reference to the pregnant Handmaid, and Offred replies with, “praise be” (Schlöndorff & Pinter, 1990, 0:34:30). The tone of her voice is neutral and the look on her face is blank, failing to reveal her true thoughts and feelings. The

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 8 other Handmaids clap respectfully and smile, but do not speak. In the book, however, it is a fascinating scene that highlights how the women have endured months of indoctrination.

Although Offred does not speak out loud at all, unlike in the film, her thoughts are very expressive. She refers to the pregnant Handmaid as an “object of envy and desire” (Atwood,

1985, p. 29). This is followed by a description of how the Handmaid is victorious and flaunts her pregnancy in public, earning the jealousy of the Handmaids who have yet to become pregnant.

One other Handmaid hisses “showoff”, and in response Offred thinks, “this is true” (Atwood,

1985, p. 29). In the novel, Offred’s thoughts, her choice of language, and the way she reacts to people around her much more thoroughly communicate both her internal resistance and the extent of the brainwashing that she has been through. There are instances in which she criticizes the regime, and instances in which she does not resist and simply expresses a desire to survive.

As the film’s audience had to rely only on Offred’s actions and dialogue to form a judgment of her character, they likely surmised that she is obedient and conformist. Her character was viewed by many critics as passive and flat, and the omission of the internal monologues is probably a key reason as to why (Gilbert, 2015).

In the show, a crucial decision is made to include voiceovers to reflect Offred’s inner monologues. As with the internal monologues in the novel, they help to convey the extent to which Offred’s thoughts and actions can - or cannot - be policed. Offred is more spirited and rebellious in the show - which will be discussed in more detail in later sections - but she is externally obedient and subservient, at least initially. The voiceovers, frequented by sarcastic or witty comments, provide insight into her anger and frustration. An example is when she is grocery shopping with the other Handmaids, and they encourage her to take some oranges. She

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 9 obeys silently, but her voiceover reveals her true feelings: “I don’t need oranges. I need to scream. I need to grab the nearest machine gun” (VanArendonk, 2017). While Offred is more spirited in the show compared to the novel, this moment does not seem out-of-character, as it echoes some of the violent thoughts Offred has in the novel; for example, at one point she eyes a knife in the kitchen, thinking: “[it] is sharp and bright, and tempting. I would like to have a knife like that” (Atwood, 1985, p. 49). Gobyn argues that while the internal monologues in the novel highlight the collapse of her resistance, the voiceovers in the show do the opposite, communicating how she grows stronger and more rebellious as time passes (Gobyn, 2019). As a result of the creative choice to include Offred’s internal monologues as voiceovers, her voice is much more prominent in the show compared to the film, and her character is perceived as more three-dimensional and sympathetic, as it was in the novel.

Offred’s Agency

In the novel, Atwood strikes an interesting balance with Offred’s agency, as she is depicted as being both powerless and powerful. On the one hand, she is enslaved, separated from her husband and her daughter, and forced into being a Handmaid. She is also a somewhat passive character; although she has thoughts about rebellion, her priority is survival, and she does not actively support the resistance. On the other hand, she is treated with some level of respect and reverence due to her status as one of the few fertile women left. Moreover, Neuman warns us not to perceive Offred as an unmitigated heroine, as she indulges in “her own small exercises of power, however ignoble” (Neuman, 2006). In one scene, the young male guards lust after her, and she takes advantage of this, sauntering in front of them. She is dressed conservatively, in an ankle-length skirt with full sleeves, gloves, and wings to conceal her face. Still, as these men are

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 10 not yet permitted to touch women, and her red clothing easily identifies her and announces her

‘purpose’ to the public, she wields the power of sexual appeal. She simultaneously enjoys the power she holds and feels ashamed for baiting them, because she believes her situation is not their fault - they all have roles to play in Gilead’s system (Atwood, 1985). Another example of

Offred’s power lies in her influence over the Commander. After they have spent many evenings together, she discovers that she can use his desire for companionship to her advantage. She begins with small requests, such as hand lotion. As her confidence grows, she capitalizes upon her position, asking about the Handmaid that came before her, and about the political situation in

Gilead. His feelings and desire for her grow, which she notes: “It’s difficult for me to believe I have power over him, of any sort, but I do” (Atwood, 1985, p. 200). She also realizes that she holds a kind of power over his wife, Serena Joy, although she does not know it, by way of these secret evenings with her husband. While Offred’s character is inarguably powerless in some regards, she has moments of defiance both internally and externally, and her unusual position allows her to wield small amounts of power over those around her.

In the film, this is not the case. While the film features moments of how she uses her budding relationship with the Commander to her advantage, the scene with the guards is not included. Moreover, without Offred’s internal monologues and that look into her thoughts, a majority of her character’s depth is lost. As established, in the novel her moments of resistance typically occur internally, through her thoughts. As the film omits the internal monologues, her inner moments of agency and defiance are not communicated to the audience. This leaves them with the externally obedient Offred. Rather than a balanced depiction of Offred as both powerful and powerless, she primarily appears to be powerless and dependent on others. She seems to

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 11 passively accept her situation and does not attempt to fight or join the resistance. There is no sense of her anger at her unjust situation or her criticism of the regime, which were so prevalent in the novel. The one moment of agency she is given in the film is when she kills the

Commander, which does not occur in either the book or the show. This decision might have been made in order to fulfill the expectations of mainstream films: that the antagonist is defeated, the protagonist escapes her dire circumstances and finds freedom. It is important to note that Offred is instructed to kill the Commander by a member of the resistance and is provided with the means to do so - a knife. While this can be perceived as a moment of true agency in response to her oppressive treatment, I would argue that she is still being used as a pawn, just by a different group. Due to the lack of insight into Offred’s thoughts, there is little sense of how strongly the desire to kill the Commander came from her, or whether she was just acting as instructed. Had she decided to kill him by herself, in an attempt to find freedom, this might have had different implications.

Offred is a more headstrong and feisty character in the TV show. She exercises increased agency and participates in the resistance against Gilead’s regime. In later seasons she becomes a freedom fighter, but even in Season One which follows the events of the book, she plays more of an active role. Atwood recognized this, stating in an interview that “the Hulu team made their

Offred more active than my Offred” (Vineyard, 2017). One example is the Salvaging ceremony, in which Handmaids are given permission to attack and kill criminals accused of crimes such as rape. In the book, Offred is intensely disturbed by the viciousness of the women attacking the man and does not participate. In the show, she is one of the first Handmaids to attack the man.

Similarly, in the book, Offred encounters some Japanese tourists and struggles to answer their

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 12 question about whether she is happy. She remains silent. In the show, however, she speaks to one of the ambassadors and her assistant, asks for their help, and secures their assistance in delivering a note to her husband. One final example occurs near the end of Season One, when she is presented with a way to help the resistance (by collecting a package) and she makes an attempt to do so. As explained above, in the book she does not actively aid the resistance efforts.

Series creator Miller explained part of his intentions behind the transformation of Offred’s character, stating that the Offred from the book was a woman from a different time. He wanted

Offred in the show to represent a woman of her age in today’s world, an everyday hero that exemplifies the “heroism of just doggedness”, of getting up every time you are knocked down

(Stanford, 2019). As a result, he decided to juxtapose Offred’s internal and external monologues

- done in part through the contrast between her actions and her thoughts, conveyed through the voiceover - resulting in a combination of obedience and indignance (Dockterman, 2017). Thus,

Offred’s increased agency stems from the contemporary context, motivated by the desire for the show’s protagonist to resonate with the growing group of women speaking out against sexual abuse, gender oppression, and more. The change happens gradually, with Offred growing more defiant and taking on a more active role in later seasons. This means that Offred in the show is not completely different from Offred in the novel, but her underlying rebellious characteristics are closer to the surface. Rather than growing less resistant, she demonstrates increased determination in resisting the regime as time goes on.

Names

One key change made between the three media texts that plays into the idea of Offred’s agency is the name she is given. In the novel, the Handmaids are never referred to by their birth

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 13 names. The protagonist is known as Offred, meaning Of Fred - property of Fred. The reader never learns her actual name. Regardless of this fact, Offred’s real name is given a lot of significance. She thinks of it often, as something that was taken away from her. In one of her internal monologues she ruminates, “I tell myself it doesn’t matter, your name is like your telephone number, useful only to others; but what I tell myself is wrong, it does matter. I keep the knowledge of this name like something hidden, some treasure I’ll come back to dig up, one day. I think of this name as buried” (Atwood, 1985, p. 84). Sure enough, when she begins to trust her love interest, the chauffeur Nick, she confesses to him what her real name is, still without revealing it to the reader. “I tell him my real name, and feel that therefore I am known” (Atwood,

1985, p. 255).

In comparison, in the movie, Offred is referred to frequently by her birth name, Kate.

This erases the depth and significance surrounding the idea of ownership and agency, which I believe was a compelling aspect of the novel. In the novel, there is a powerful scene involving

Ofglen, one of Offred’s friends. Near the end of the story, Ofglen kills herself and a new

Handmaid takes her place. When Offred asks where Ofglen went, the woman replies, “I am

Ofglen” (Atwood, 1985, p. 268). This highlights how replaceable the women are, “a national resource” as Offred says in the book (Atwood, 1985, p. 67). This scene does occur in the film, but unfortunately it is not as impactful. It is a very short scene, barely 15 seconds long, and

Offred does not say anything in response to the new Ofglen’s statement. Her facial expressions are also neutral (Schlöndorff & Pinter, 1990). Moreover, the fact that Offred’s birth name is utilized by other characters reduces the significance of the scene, as it undermines the idea that all Handmaids are replaceable resources. This scene does not occur in the show, as the character

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 14 of Ofglen is given a backstory and a role in coming seasons. In short, I disagree with the decision made by the film director to provide Offred with a name. The idea of these women as property with no agency or freedom is more impactful when they lack a basic human right: a name of their own.

In the show, Offred’s birth name - June Osborne - is also revealed at the end of the first episode. This does in part reduce the significance around the concept of agency, as continuously referring to the Handmaids as property of upper-class men emphasizes their cruel treatment.

However, the show does at least create a sense of mystery and importance surrounding Offred’s name, which is something that the film does not do. The Handmaids use their birth names as a type of currency, sharing them amongst one another as a way to connect and secretly keep tabs on each other. While the show unfortunately did not adopt Atwood’s powerful use of names, the director at the very least ensured that the Handmaids’ names were a significant aspect of the plot.

Also, Gobyn perceives this particular change as indicative of Offred reclaiming her identity. This makes sense in the context of her argument that Offred grows more resistant in the TV series, thus reconstructing her identity and reclaiming her name, whereas she does the opposite in the novel (Gobyn, 2019). Additionally, the show adapts an important aspect of the book, which - in conjunction with the use of names - further emphasizes how the Handmaids are property. In the novel, numbers are tattooed onto each Handmaid to identify them, similar to how prisoners in

Nazi concentration camps had numbers tattooed onto their arms (Harrington, 2017). Offred states that the numbers “guarantee that I will never be able to fade, finally, into another landscape”

(Atwood, 1985, p. 67). In the show, the Handmaids are identified by ear tags, which also function as trackers. This change from tattoos to ear tags is reasonable considering that the show

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 15 is set in more modern times and involves a greater use of technology. Like the tattoo, the ear tags are a cruel and inhumane method of distinguishing the Handmaids and preventing their escape.

In Season Two, Offred removes the tag by cutting into her ear, losing a chunk of cartilage and causing blood to drip everywhere. In contrast, to identify the Handmaids, the film uses bracelets that are easily removed and leave no visible mark on the women. This is another way in which the film reduces the impact of what should have been a chilling story of gendered oppression.

Ending

Another change that will be highlighted is the ending of each respective media artifact, as they vary in terms of emotional depth and reflect Offred’s differing motives. In the novel, the ending is quite ambiguous. Offred is rescued from the household where she works by Nick and the Eyes - Gilead's secret police - although she has no way of knowing what they will do with her. The epilogue is the famous ‘Historical Notes’ ending, which takes place in 2195, approximately two hundred years after the events of the novel. A professor is lecturing about

Gilead, which fell long ago. He is unsympathetic and dismissive of Offred’s struggles. He says that her fate is unknown - she may have escaped, or she may have been recaptured or killed. It is never revealed what happens to her afterward. Although she suspected that she might be pregnant with Nick’s child at the time of her escape, she was not certain and it is never confirmed (Atwood, 1985). This epilogue is highly significant in many of the discussions regarding the novel, as it hints at the idea that a society like Gilead’s is not as far off or implausible as we may think.

In the movie, Offred is also rescued by Nick and the Eyes, but only after she kills the

Commander. She is shown to be living in a trailer in the mountains, pregnant with Nick’s baby

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 16 and hopeful for the future. Although her future is uncertain, there is less of a mystery surrounding it, and it is essentially a ‘happily ever after’ ending. The exclusion of the powerful

‘Historical Notes’ ending further strips the film of the novel’s deeper implications. As with the bracelets, this ending undermines the significance of all that Offred has been through. It has been referred to as an attempt to “mute tragedy or horror”; while this ending may be appropriate for a typical Hollywood film, it is not suitable for an adaptation of one of Atwood’s novels, which are known for their darker narratives and more open endings (Nischik, 2010). Additionally, one scholar claimed that this ending features a reintroduction of the male patriarch, which is an inappropriate conclusion to a story about the enslavement of women (Bodelson, 2006). This choice was likely made to appeal to audiences, as the ambiguous ending of the novel might not have been perceived as satisfying in a mainstream Hollywood film.

In the show, Season One ends on the same note as the novel, with Offred disappearing with Nick and the Eyes. The show then flashes forward and depicts the ‘Historical Notes’ ending, relatively similar to the one described in the novel, where scholars debate Offred’s unknown fate (Keaney, 2017). A number of other events unfold over the course of Season Two, until Offred is given the opportunity to escape Gilead. Instead, she chooses to stay. Over the next few seasons, Offred becomes more involved in the fight against the regime and eventually becomes a freedom fighter. This decision transforms Offred’s character and her desires; in the novel and the movie, she fluctuates between wanting to escape the oppressive regime and wanting to stay so that she can be with Nick. In the show, she actively makes the choice to stay and fight back. While the decision to let Offred stay and fight could likely be attributed in part to the desire to continue the show, it was also greatly influenced by contemporary feminist

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 17 activism. The same can be said for Offred’s increased agency and transformation from a passive character to an active one. Elisabeth Moss, co-producer of the show and the actress who plays

Offred, spoke in an interview about how relevant themes such as female empowerment and resistance would feature heavily in Season Two. Another actor on the show spoke about how the show has converged with the momentum of the #MeToo campaign and similar movements, and how the character of Offred would represent that (Chuba, 2018). As Offred’s transformation is gradual and her motives evolve over several seasons, it does not feel unnatural or out of character. Miller builds on Atwood’s initial characterization of Offred, slowly drawing out her more rebellious characteristics as time passes.

Offred’s Eroticization

One final difference is how Schlöndorff’s visual portrayal of Offred eroticized her in a way that neither Atwood nor Miller did. In “Redemptive Restrooms: Moments of Utopic

Possibility in Volker Schlöndorff's Film Version of The Handmaid's Tale”, Amery Bodelson explores how the film can be viewed through the lens of phallocentrism, in which the male sexual organ and the image of castrated women give meaning to the world. She explains that the male gaze is a film device used to capture the power dynamic between the sexes. In particular,

Bodelson says that the director eroticized the film’s poster and still shots, encoding “erotic visual clues that the novel never suggests” (Bodelson, 2006). For example, the film poster depicts a beautiful, youthful, tanned Offred, with flowing blonde hair and a red robe clutched to her naked body. Her eyes are submissively downcast, but she does not look troubled or afraid, which is strange considering that this is a film about the enslavement of women. Another example is the

German poster promoting the film, which features just the naked backside of a woman, with her

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 18 arms bound behind her back. This is an explicitly submissive pose, and the poster hints at masochistic eroticism. With her head and her feet cut out of the frame, she has been reduced to a sexual object (Bodelson, 2006). There are numerous versions of the book cover and the TV series poster, but none of them sexualize Offred to this extent. They typically portray Offred in her conservative Handmaid attire, looking pensive or defiant.

Another example of Schlöndorff’s eroticization that I identified is the ceremony scene, in which Offred must have sex with the Commander as his wife watches. In the novel, this is not

Offred’s first ceremony, as she has been a Handmaid to other families in the past. It is described quite dispassionately and the whole process is brisk and impersonal. She lies still and detaches herself from the situation until it is over. Once back in her room, she changes into her nightgown, uses some stolen butter as a lotion for her face and hands, and attempts to go to sleep (Atwood,

1985). The TV series mirrors the book closely in its portrayal of the ceremony. Offred lies passively on the bed, face blank as she likely disengages from the present until the ritual is over.

She also returns to her room afterward and attempts to sleep. In the film, however, this scene becomes akin to a violent rape scene. It is Offred’s first ceremony and she sobs and gasps throughout the process. Once she returns to her room, she lashes out as she cries, breaking a cup.

She then pulls off her clothes and presses her naked body against the window, gasping for air.

Although it is initially a long shot, the camera zooms in until Offred’s naked body is in the center of the frame. Nick, her future love interest, also catches sight of her in this moment (Schlöndorff

& Pinter, 1990). This is an example of the fetishistic camera work that Bodelson mentions in her article. By transforming the clinical ritual into a violent rape scene and including the close-up of

Offred’s naked body, Schlöndorff amplified the erotic cues for the male gaze (Bodelson, 2006).

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 19

Interestingly enough, in a 2017 Buzzfeed article, Anne Helen Petersen praises the TV series for its “female glance”, as opposed to the typical male gaze that is present in most mainstream media, including Schlöndorff’s The Handmaid’s Tale. As opposed to the obsessive male gaze, she states that the female glance is “constantly vigilant… it observes, with patient detail, the moments of a woman’s world that often go unnoticed” (Petersen, 2017). This highlights how the visual framing of the film (particularly in comparison to the show) drastically impacted audience reception, especially considering that the focus of the story is the sexualization and exploitation of women.

Reception

The novel and the TV show were both received positively by critics and general audiences. The novel was perceived by most as powerful, compelling, and well-written; it was nominated for and granted multiple awards between 1985 and 1987. A 1985 article in The

Toronto Star just a week after the novel’s publication claimed that it was “riding a wave of rave reviews” (Adachi, 1985). The excitement surrounding the novel was not limited to the weeks after its release; in a 1986 book review in the Los Angeles Times, Elaine Kendall declared Offred to be a “spirited and engaging narrator”, and stated that “the power of the book comes… from

[Atwood’s] deliberate subjugation of imagination to demonstrable fact” (Kendall, 1986). In other words, Kendall’s primary praise for the novel was that it was based on actual events occurring at the time, making it feel more realistic than fictional. The bold and shocking ideas contained within the book continue to spark discourse amongst scholars and academics until today.

The show similarly resonated with audiences all across the world; women in the US,

Ireland, Poland, Argentina, and more have donned the Handmaid’s costumes in sexual assault,

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 20 abortion, and anti-Trump protests, to name a few. The Handmaid’s Tale became a powerful symbol of resistance as a result of the show’s popularity (Gulf News, 2018). Critics have called the show “brilliant, terrifying television”, “a total stunner of a series”, and the “most chilling

Trump era series”, amongst other praise (Brittany, 2017). Other reviews have remarked on the show’s timelessness and allure; an IndieWire review called the show “a haunting confluence of tenses… one of the best shows of the year so far, at times hard to watch but impossible to ignore” (Miller, 2017). It made history as the first streaming series to win Best Drama awards at the Emmys and the Golden Globes (Katz, 2018).

In comparison, the film was incredibly unsuccessful, grossing less than $5 million against its $13 million budget (Gilbert, 2015). The movie’s lack of success is likely attributed to

Schlöndorff’s execution, as criticism of the film was mainly aimed at the director’s choices or the actors’ performances, rather than the actual premise of the novel. Indeed, a number of critics wondered why a film about women being dominated by men had been directed by a male rather than a female (Nischik, 2010). In a 1990 review in the Chicago Tribune, renowned film critic

Dave Kehr stated that the film “comes to seem less feminist than frankly misogynistic” (Kehr,

1990). In other historical newspapers from 1990, numerous critics found fault with the film, claiming that it was exploitative of women, stating that the audience was distanced from the plot rather than immersed into it, and even reporting that the preview audience found it humorous, as they were snickering during the preview (Johnston, 1990; Jacobs, 1990). This could partly be explained by a 1989 interview in which Schlöndorff explained that he believes the novel and the film share a “sense of humor” that is often overlooked, as the horrific events are often described as hilarious (Forsberg, 1989). However, evidently the horrific nature of the story did not come

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 21 across to audiences in this way if they felt distanced from the plot and unsympathetic towards the characters. While the book and the show both successfully (according to audiences and critics)

convey a chilling story of women forced into sexual servitude, the film lacks this emotional depth. The shock factor was more surface-level, featuring in the violence and the rape scene rather than in the story about severe gender oppression and sexual enslavement and its impact on

Offred.

Conclusion

In this paper, I explored the changes in gendered narratives communicated in the three versions of The Handmaid’s Tale. They differ narratively, with the novel and the film highlighting Offred’s internal resistance and unique moments of agency. The internal monologues, featuring as the voiceovers in the show, were essential in forming Offred’s identity and making her a sympathetic character. While the novel and the TV show demonstrate different progressions in Offred’s motives - she grows less rebellious in the novel, but more rebellious in the show - the changes made in the TV show highlight and build upon aspects of Offred’s character hinted at in the book, rather than taking away from her character or making her unrecognizable. The changes made suit the modern context, as Offred’s increased agency and active resistance reflect contemporary feminist activism and social movements at the time.

By omitting this narrative technique, the film portrays Offred as a more passive, obedient character who lacks complexity and depth. The novel and the show both communicate a powerful story of sexual enslavement, using various plot elements (the names, the tattoos/ear tags, and the ‘Historical Notes’ ending) to emphasize the idea of the Handmaids as property of

Gilead. Schlöndorff omits a number of these elements, opting for a more Hollywood-ized

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 22 approach, with Offred killing the commander and having a ‘happily ever after’ ending. In doing so, the film undermines Atwood’s messages, lessening the emotional impact of the story. One final reason why the film did not resonate with audiences in the same way that the novel did just five years earlier is Schlöndorff’s visual portrayal of Offred; by catering to the male gaze and employing fetishistic camera techniques, the film eroticizes Offred and reduces her to a sexual object.

There are many other differences made between the three texts that could be analyzed, including the costumes and the development of supporting characters such as Ofglen, Nick, and

Moira, Offred’s closest friend. (In the novel and the show, Offred and Moira have been friends since adolescence, whereas in the film they meet for the first time at the Handmaid's training center.) One other detail excluded from the film is the concept of Unbabies: babies suffering from birth defects or physical deformations that are ‘disposed’ of by authorities in Gilead

(Atwood, 1985). This subplot is very significant in the novel and the show, and can be linked to the historical contexts regarding abortion and reproductive rights.

“The personal is political” is a key phrase used in the women’s liberation movement, especially during second-wave feminism (Dore, 2014). As Neuman asserts, “nowhere is the personal more political than in Gilead” (Neuman, 2006). In Atwood’s dystopian society, every choice a woman makes is rooted in the political context, from the decision to be a Handmaid rather than suffer a fate in the Colonies, to their often violent actions during the Salvaging ceremonies. Released near the end of second-wave feminism, Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale is a cautionary tale that hits close to home for many, considering its generous use of real-life events as inspiration for the horrors of the story. Not only does it comment on gender oppression, it also

GENDERED MESSAGES IN THE HANDMAID’S TALE 23 envisions the implications of religion, race, and sexuality in a dystopian society. The film and TV series adaptations were similarly released in highly politically-charged situations, in which earlier accomplishments in the women’s liberation movement were being challenged. The film’s failure highlights how drastically the story’s themes can be misinterpreted, whether unintentionally or deliberately. Correspondingly, the success of the TV show over three decades after the novels’ release demonstrates how Atwood’s powerful exploration of radical feminism remains relevant across a range of historical contexts. As one of the key texts that has been analyzed by scholars in the fields of gender and media, it is essential to consider the different interpretations of the messages encoded within The Handmaid’s Tale, as it is a story that has resonated strongly with audiences for decades, and will continue to do so for years to come.

text:
Northwestern University March 17, 2021

Geospatial Evidence for Diversification Effects in Branch Banking Deposit Stability:

A Case Study in Fracking

JACOB WIESENTHAL

Abstract

The heterogeneity of regional economies in the United States provides branch banks with plentiful opportunities to mitigate risk through geographic diversification. This paper introduces natural geography to the discussion of diversification in branch banking in order to examine the dynamics of deposit stability in the context of an economic shock. By developing a microeconomic index of geographic diversity by county, I assess how the emergence of hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s impacted industry concentrations across five distinct regions. A regression discontinuity framework is applied to counties who concurrently began fracking operations and, as a counterfactual, the counties with which they share a border. Positive spatial autocorrelation of deposit variances between proximate branches is estimated to quantify the degree to which deposit stability is derived by location. Given the exogeneity of natural gas shale play discoveries, I construct a difference-in-differences model that identifies the directionality in which geographic diversity augmented the effect of fracking on deposit stability. My analysis reveals that geographically diverse branches mitigated the shock’s impact on deposits and in some cases even became more stable. I conclude that geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stability, and that both interstate bank consolidations and online banking services are uniquely positioned to leverage this diversification advantage.

Keywords: banks, geographic diversification, deposits, fracking

JEL Classification Codes: C3, C58, G11, G21, L71, Q33, R1

1 Introduction

Federally-insured banking in the United States is inherently shaped by the vastly diverse regional geographies of which it serves. Historically, intrastate branch banks have existed and adapted on a microeconomic level, optimizing each branch to synergize with the unique profiles of their local populations. With the passage of the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994, which enabled bank holding companies (BHCs) to acquire branches outside of their headquartered state, interstate banking was able to capitalize on this heterogeneity by inducing diversification through mergers and acquisitions. Hughes et al. (1999) examine the mass interstate consolidation of banks following the Riegle-Neal Act and identify significant gains in performance attributable to these mergers.1 Akhigbe and Whyte (2003) build on this theory and provide evidence that these gains are derived from a decrease in risk due to larger and more diversified branch portfolios.2

It is well understood that lending risk can be mitigated through the diversification of industries represented in a portfolio, and that doing so generally increases profitability. Demsetz and Strahan (1997) suggest that large BHCs are able to increase their leverage and charter more profitable loans because of a “diversification advantage” in which the heightened risk of such operations is counterbalanced by the stabilizing effect of diversified portfolios.3 However, there may also be diseconomies to interstate expansion in lending. Acharya, Hasan, and Saunders (2006) find evidence that a lack of localized lending experience, an inability to specialize, and potential complications in monitoring distant branches can offset the risk-based advantages

3 Demsetz, R. S., & Strahan, P. E. (1997). Diversification, size, and risk at bank holding companies. Journal of Money, Credit and

Banking, 29(3), 300.

2 Akhigbe, A., & Whyte, A. M. (2003). Changes in Market assessments of bank risk following the Riegle–Neal act of 1994.

Journal of Banking & Finance, 27(1), 87-102.

1References

Hughes, J. P., Lang, W. W., Mester, L. J., & Moon, C. (1999). The dollars and sense of bank consolidation. Journal of Banking &

Finance, 23(2-4), 291-324.

of lending diversification.4 Thus the effect on lending profitability through diversification-enabled leverage is understood to be contingent on the idiosyncratic management of BHCs.

However, unlike lending, geographic diversification as it pertains to branch deposits has not been the subject of sizable research following the rise of interstate banking in the United States. This paper seeks to reconcile the insights of previous literature on lending diversification with evidence concerning deposit stability as it relates to the geography of branch banks. In particular, I assess whether the geographic diversity of a regional economy is negatively associated with deposit variability in local branches, and by extension, whether geographically diversifying a portfolio of branches induces aggregate deposit stability for a bank.

Ascertaining an answer to these inquiries will complement our lending-based understanding of how diversification impacts bank performance. This is because the financial leverage of which diversification is found to enable may be the result of either increased stability in loan earnings or increased stability in the deposit bases on which leverage is measured. Maintaining a stable deposit base is critical to justifying enhanced leverage and is thus equally worthy of inspection.

Identifying the effects of geographic diversification on deposit stability is a more unidirectional problem than that of lending because, unlike loans, soliciting deposits from a more diverse clientele does not introduce significant diseconomies of expansion. Whereas information asymmetry and poor management may destabilize loan earnings, their effects are less profound in disrupting the stability of a branch’s deposit base. For this reason, evidence of diversification effects in deposit stability would, in combination with our lending-based understanding of interstate banking, suggest that geographically diversifying may be advantageous to branch banks in both lowering risk and increasing profitability.

Two key contributions to the econometric evaluation of this dynamic are made in this paper. First, geographic diversity is measured at a more microeconomic scope than in previous studies, adding precision to its description of regional economies. Second, deposit stability is assessed in the context of an economic shock (the emergence of hydraulic fracturing) in order to

4 Acharya, V., Hasan, I., & Saunders, A. (2006). Should banks be diversified? Evidence from individual bank loan portfolios. The

Journal of Business, 79(3), 1355-1412.

empirically test whether the effect of geographic diversity on stability is causal and significant.

1.1 Literature Review

Previous literature attempting to measure the implications of geographic diversification in banking has procedurally become more microeconomic but is generally limited to metrics of distance and quantity. Rivard and Thomas (1997) conducted one of the earliest studies to segment interstate banking presence by Federal Reserve Bank district in addition to a dummy variable representing whether a bank operates across states.5 Their results suggest that the advantages of geographic diversification in lowering risk are not only derived from an interstate presence, but also differ depending on which particular regions the bank’s branches are located in. This approach was expanded by Berger and DeYoung (2006) in estimating the efficiency of BHC branches by controlling for individual state fixed effects, as well as introducing a measurement of distance between each branch and the BHC’s headquarters.6 Deng and Elyasiani (2008) measure geographic diversification with an emphasis on this relationship between branch and headquarters, employing a Cobb-Douglas function of both distance and geographic dispersion.7 It should be noted, however, that while distance is a sensible predictor of difference, their connection is far from absolute. In a human geography as dispersed as that of the United States, it is not uncommon for greater distance from one city to, at some inflection, begin approaching another city more similar than any rural areas between the two. Therefore, there is an argument to be made that distance should not be relied on as a strict indicator of diversity.

Following Deng et al. (2007), a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is constructed to represent the state and Metropolitan

7 Deng, S., & Elyasiani, E. (2008). Geographic diversification, bank holding company value, and risk. Journal of Money, Credit and

Banking, 40(6), 1217-1238.

6 Berger, A. N., & DeYoung, R. (2006). Technological progress and the geographic expansion of the banking industry. Journal of

Money, Credit, and Banking, 38(6), 1483-1513.

5 Rivard, R. J., & Thomas, C. R. (1997). The effect of interstate banking on large bank holding company profitability and risk.

Journal of Economics and Business, 49(1), 61-76.

Statistical Area (MSA) level concentration of a bank’s branches.8

A key development in Deng and Elyasiani’s second iteration of the measurement is the accounting of deposit dispersion, in which the HHI is weighted by the deposits held by each branch. This method calibrates the measure of geographic diversification to reflect the relative importance of each branch to the bank, assigning less weight to small branches and more weight to branches which represent a majority of the bank’s deposit base. They find that the relationship between geographic diversification and enhanced firm value is most significant for expansion to more remote MSAs, suggesting that the inclusion of rural regions in this body of analysis may elicit critical results which are currently unattainable from the mostly urban context of the literature.

In addition to the inability of these studies to extrapolate their results to rural banking, they are also limited in scope by the geographically broad indices of states and MSAs. Subregional economic differences within these geographies may lend inaccuracy to considering all states or MSAs as aggregately comparable exposures to risk, a condition which is generally assumed by these studies. However, as a more meticulous inspection of what it means to be geographically diverse, this paper does not make this assumption and instead allows for each subregion to contribute differently towards a measurement of a bank’s geographic diversification. This can be accomplished first by examining geography at a county level. Magnifying my measurement of geographic diversification by the 3,143 counties in the non-territory United States and the District of Columbia as opposed to its 384 MSAs grants larger sample sizes and enables proper analysis of rural banking. Further, the marginal contribution of each county to a bank’s measure of geographic diversification is, unlike previous studies, nonlinear and a function of the county’s risk profile as it differs from the rest of the counties where the bank has a presence.

Following the analysis of Hughes et al. (1999), which posits that macroeconomic diversification can be assessed as the standard deviation of the deposit-weighted average of unemployment rates across states, my measurement for geographic diversification is derived from the unique employment compositions of each county.1 In specific, the HHI is adapted to index all industries in a county as defined by the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 2-digit code stratification. The contribution of each industry to the HHI is

8 Deng, S., Elyasiani, E., & Mao, C. X. (2007). Diversification and the cost of debt of bank holding companies. Journal of Banking &

Finance, 31(8), 2453-2473.

weighted by its share of total employment in the county as reported by the United States Census Bureau. As a result, this HHI not only describes the concentration of branches within geographical units, but also their concentration within subregional industries, hereafter referred to as “local industry exposures.”

This is an advantageous distinction when modeling deposit stability if assuming that the frequency and magnitude of client deposits and withdrawals are highly correlated with the frequency and magnitude of the client’s employment. That is, the more stable that employment is within a county, the more stable that the deposits in that county’s branches will be. Moreover, if diversification is to be interpreted as a mitigation of microeconomic shocks that affect particular locations or industries, then a county with a low concentration of employment by industry could be said to be diversified from potential microeconomic shocks to any one of them. By accounting for a county’s concentration of local industry exposures, my measurement of geographic diversification is closer linked to the fundamental roots by which deposit stability is inherited. Additionally, this methodology is applicable both to an analysis by branch and by bank, such that at either scope an appropriate measurement of geographic diversity is calculable. By this approach, a branch is geographically diverse if its respective county has a low concentration of employment by industry, and a bank is geographically diverse if its total deposits are dispersed among branches who are thusly diversified, both independently and as an aggregate.

1.2 Assessing Diversification in the Context of an Economic Shock

As previously mentioned, the inspection of geographic diversification in the context of economic shocks closer resembles the true dynamic by which diversity interacts with volatility. While simple measures of distance and quantity can approximate the risk mitigation of local industry exposures, the geography of banking is clustered, human-dependent, and ever-changing. Because deposit stability is a product of time, it can be thought of in terms of temporal changes in deposit bases as a result of economic growth and decline. The distinction of a stable deposit base is therefore most pronounced in the face of a transitional economic shock. Yet strictly financial analysis of economic shocks in banking typically either restricts implications of causality (due to endogeneity of the shock) or requires an instrument that limits predictive accuracy.9

Fortunately, the study of geography is uniquely disposed to present us with an abundance of natural experiments in which the resulting shocks can be understood as exogenous. Interpreting a shift in geographic diversification as an exogenous product of a natural, geographical event allows for its predicted effect on deposit stability to be causally attributed. This paper introduces insights from natural geography to the discussion of diversification in banking by examining the emergence of hydraulic fracturing or “fracking” in the early 2010s. During this period, banks were unable to proactively account for the rapid growth of the fracking industry, given the discovery of new technology, natural gas shale plays, and estimates suggesting unforeseen volumes of productivity.10 As such, the disruption to regional employment caused by the fracking industry can be translated into shifts in geographic diversity for proximate branches. Likewise, the degree to which our diversification measure was affected by fracking can be causally linked to patterns observed in these branches’ deposit stability.

2 A Case Study in Fracking

While the technique of hydraulic fracturing as a method of extracting shale gas has been known since first experimented with in 1947, high-volume horizontal fracking was not considered commercially viable until the late 1980s when an operation in the Austin Chalk formation of southeastern Texas began employing slickwater to increase fluid flow rates.11

Applying this slickwater treatment to natural gas shales proved highly effective and became exponentially adopted by energy firms in Texas leading up to the turn of the 21st century. Industrial-scale fracking spread within a matter of years from the

When a series of studies released in 2008 proposed that the Appalachian Basin held far more potential for natural gas production than previously thought, with some estimates of the Marcellus shale rising over 250 times the volumes proposed by the U.S. Geological Survey, economic interest in the industry skyrocketed.10 An Environment Protection Agency (EPA) study on the proximity of fracking sites to drinking water resources found that 14,560 new wells commenced fracking operations in 2012 as compared to just 1,809 in 2005,12 a majority of the new locations targeting the Marcellus and Utica shales of the upper Appalachians and the Niobrara-Mowry shales of the Rocky Mountains.

2.1 Stratifying Counties by the Presence of Fracking

To identify the effects that these new wells had on their regional economies in the context of geographic diversity, I transform the data collected by the EPA into a collection of counties which saw at least one new well begin fracking operations within their borders during 2012. This group of counties includes both those which had fracking activities take place within their borders prior to 2012 and those for which the observed wells were the county’s first instance of fracking. Because our analysis isolates the consequences of the operations in 2012 in particular, this distinction is negligible. Counties included within this group are hereafter referred to as “fracking counties” to simply denote their classification.

In obtaining a control group against which the fracking counties can be compared, I employ a geographically discontinuous treatment methodology in which I sample counties which did not have any fracking operations begin within their borders in 2012, but share a border of any length or coordinate with one or more fracking counties. These counties are hereafter referred to as “bordering counties” to indicate their relationship to the fracking counties. The use of these bordering counties as a control for the fracking counties takes advantage of the core insight behind the geographic regression discontinuity framework and benefits from its weak assumptions. Keele and Titiunik (2015) describe these as a natural spatial correlation between attributes of bordering locations, where the absence of their respective border would not significantly alter their aggregate demographics, markets, and other fixed effects.13 Fracking counties and bordering counties are assumed to be geographically similar where proximate, and therefore exhibit analogous trends in banking before the treatment of fracking.

13 Keele, L. J., & Titiunik, R. (2015). Geographic boundaries as regression discontinuities. Political Analysis, 23(1), 127-155.

While the number of wells in each county is not uniformly distributed across regions, this disparity is reflected instead in the varying increases in fracking employment and their corresponding effects on our measurements of geographic diversity following the year 2012. Of notable mention, there appear to be five defining formations that constitute a majority of the counties depicted. These clusters, from west to east, coincide with the Bakken, Woodford, Barnett, Eagle Ford, and Marcellus shales, respectively. Counties in the center of these clusters, despite having wells begin fracking in 2012, are dropped from the following analysis because they do not share a border with any non-fracking county and thus cannot be evaluated within the outlined geographically discontinuous treatment methodology.

As mentioned earlier, pursuing a county-level scope greatly standardizes the size of each observation in contrast to MSAs, whose erratic sizes are difficult to compare spatially. Apart from the more expansive observed counties of the Rocky Mountains, which are still generally comparable between neighbors, the 250 fracking counties and 393 bordering counties are consistent in size and representative of both urban and rural environments. Therefore, my modeling of these counties can account for the natural differences between urban and rural economies and prove applicable in either case.

3 Hypothesis Development

Given the literature on geographic diversification as it pertains to lending risk and the mechanisms by which industry diversity may be tied to deposit stability, it would intuitively follow that there is some relationship between the geographic diversification of a bank’s branches and the stability of their deposits. Namely, a low concentration of industries in a county is likely to mitigate the effect of any industry-dependent microeconomic shock on the deposits in proximate banks. This dynamic necessitates that deposit stability be at least partially derived from its geography, and therefore I expect to observe spatial autocorrelation in

Figure 2. Map of fracking counties and bordering counties as defined by the presence of hydraulic fracturing wells that began operating in 2012.

deposit stability across all counties. As such, I will test the following hypothesis:

H1: Deposit stability is positively spatially autocorrelated between branches.

If, in fact, spatial autocorrelation is observed in the deposit stability between counties, then it would be appropriate to regress deposit stability on a geographically-based index such as my modified HHI. More specifically, in the context of fracking, I expect the emergence of fracking to have variable effects on the measured diversity of fracking counties, depending on whether a county was previously concentrated in the energy sector. The dynamic effects on deposit stability of the treatment of fracking can then be translated into bank-level insights. Based on the arguments given above, I expect this relationship to be positive and causal. In other words:

H2: Geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stabilization.

Not only this, but by taking the economic shock of fracking as exogenous, this relationship can be inferred as causal, proposing geographic diversification as a tool by which banks can intentionally mitigate variability and potentially increase their leverage of deposits.

4 Data and Methodology

Industry and employment data by county are obtained from the United States Census Bureau’s County Business Patterns (CBP) series across the 7-year period of 2009 to 2015.14 The CBP provides information on total employment by county as well as the employment of each NAICS 2-digit industry present in the county. Information on the location of fracking operations commencing in 2012 is given by the EPA’s 2016 report on Hydraulic Fracturing for Oil and Gas,12 and this data is consolidated with the CBP series to categorize fracking counties and bordering counties by the dummy variable fracking. Deposit data by branch is acquired from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Summary of Deposits (SOD) for all

14 United States Census Bureau County Business Patterns (CBP).

(2021, February 9). Retrieved from https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/cbp.html.

FDIC-insured banking institutions.15 The SOD database is used to segment banks by organizational structure using the categorical variable bhc, which denotes the type of holding company associated with each branch (a one bank holding company, a multi-bank holding company, or neither). I also use the SOD annual deposit balance variable deposits to calculate a three-year moving coefficient of variation as an inverse measure of the stability of deposits in each branch, deposits_cv. Because the coefficient of variation, unlike a standard deviation, is normalized for all branches irrespective of the magnitude of deposits, the estimated effect of the diversification variable on deposit stability will not be directly influenced by branch size.

My sample procedure draws only FDIC-insured branches belonging to a non-unit bank and therefore being a member of a branch portfolio. These branches are then sorted by the FDIC’s branch service type classification (brsertyp), from which I only select those which accept on-site client deposits as a brick and mortar, retail, or drive-through office (codes 11, 12, and 23). I obtain 21,542 branches meeting this criteria belonging to 1,590 distinct banking institutions. The panel format of the data is balanced by year with each year’s observations representing between 13.40% and 14.84% of the total observations. Lastly, the SOD data is matched with the CBP industry and employment data to assign county-level statistics to each branch’s observations.

4.3 Identifying Geographic Diversification Effects on Deposit Stability

To empirically test H2, I construct a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences model which estimates the causal effect of a change in geographic diversity on deposit stability. The temporal trend in deposit stability among the bordering counties which did not receive the treatment of new fracking operations in 2012 serves as a counterfactual to the fracking counties which did experience this exogenous shock. Subject to the validity of the parallel trend assumption, which in this case would necessitate that annual changes in deposit stability pre-2012 were symmetric in both fracking counties and bordering counties, this model will identify the causal treatment effect of being located within a fracking county in 2012 on a branch’s subsequent change in deposit stability. Using the natural log of deposits_cv to interpret percentage changes in deposit stability as a log-linear function of the treatment and its covariates, I estimate the following model:

𝑙𝑛_𝑑𝑒𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑠_𝑐𝑣𝑖𝑡= β0 + β1 * 𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑡+ β2 * 𝑓𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑖𝑡+ β3 * 𝑏𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑐ℎ_𝑑𝑖𝑣𝑖𝑡+ where αi is the branch fixed effect and μt is the year fixed effect. Of most importance are the coefficients of β4 and β7, which can be interpreted as the treatment effect of fracking in 2012 on a branch’s deposit stability and the degree to which this effect differed by the geographic diversity of that branch’s county, respectively. In particular, the coefficient of the triple interaction term postit*frackingit*branch_divit will indicate the directionality in which geographic diversity impacts deposit stability for branches and, by proxy, for their parent banks.

5.2 Difference-in-Differences Model

Annualized trends in deposit stability by geography can be visualized in Figure 5, which plots the median deposit variance for both fracking counties and bordering counties by year. The parallel trend assumption is assessed for the years 2010 to 2015, as banking diagnostics in 2009 were exogenously impacted by the global financial crisis of that year. As illustrated in the line plot, deposit stability in both fracking counties and bordering counties experienced parallel shifts across all years except 2012, in which fracking counties became more stable while bordering counties became less stable. This inequality was sustained for all years following 2012, as the median deposits_cv in fracking counties remained roughly 3% less than that of bordering counties.

Figure 5. Line plot of annual median deposit variance by county type (fracking or bordering).

The estimation results of my difference-in-differences model are outlined in Table 2, including robust standard errors and coefficient indicators of statistical significance. Consistent with Figure 5, these estimation results imply a negative effect on deposits_cv for all counties post-2012, and an additionally negative effect for fracking counties in particular. The coefficient estimate for the treatment effect post*fracking is positive and statistically significant at the 0.1% level, suggesting that the emergence of fracking in 2012 caused deposit instability for branches in counties with little to no geographic diversity.

However, much if not all of this instability is mitigated by the effect of geographic diversity on the treatment. The coefficient estimate for post*fracking*branch_div is negative and also statistically significant 0.1% level.

This indicates that branches in more geographically diverse counties saw less deposit instability as a result of fracking, and in some cases even became more stable as a result. Whereas a macroeconomic, observational model would seek to identify the coefficient estimate for branch_div, a measure of diversification effects outside of the context of economic shocks, the focus on its triple interaction with the treatment effect yields much more explanatory results. At a glance, the magnitude of diversification effects in the context of the economic shock of fracking is estimated to be roughly eight times greater (and far more statistically discernible) than its magnitude as estimable without considering the shock.

To assess the robustness of the model, I first test the null hypotheses that the covariates bhc and brsertyp are equal to 0 and calculate the two leftmost results of Table 3. Likewise, I test the null hypothesis that the year fixed effects are jointly equal to 0 and calculate the rightmost result of Table 3. The covariates bhc and brsertyp are determined to be different than 0 and statistically significant at the 5% and 0.1% levels, respectively. The year fixed effects are determined to be different than 0 and statistically significant at the 0.1% level. Thus, the model is justified in including these covariates and fixed effects.

Noteworthy is the strongly positive coefficient corresponding to branches with the FDIC branch service type of 23, representing drive-through offices. The estimate suggests that, as compared to typical brick and mortar offices, branches offering drive-through depositing services are much more prone to deposit instability, especially in the face of an economic shock such as fracking. This makes intuitive sense given the relatively low opportunity costs to clients of making drive-through deposits and withdrawals without having to physically enter the branch.
