As an additional robustness assessment, a second model is estimated with random effects in place of branch fixed effects and compared against the original model in accordance with the Hausman (1978) econometric model specification test.17 The results of the specification test are given in Table 4, which rejects the null hypothesis that there is no systematic difference in the estimated coefficients given either fixed or random effects. Therefore, the inclusion of branch fixed effects in my model is justified. An important intuition as to why branch fixed effects are key covariates in modeling geographic diversity lies in their derivation. Since a branch will be located within the same county for all years observed in the dataset, the fixed effects of its county are inherited within the branch fixed effects when absorbed. By including branch fixed effects, the model not only controls for static characteristics of each branch such as locational advantages and management style, but also controls for static characteristics of each branch’s county such as demographics and, to an extent, its competitive landscape of banking.

Together, the treatment effect and its triple interaction with geographic diversity are substantiated by the above statistical robustness analysis. More importantly, it tells a story consistent with both the proposed underlying mechanisms of diversification and the existing literature on branch banking, exogenous economic shocks, and the industry of fracking. As hypothesized, the introduction of fracking as an exogenous economic shock was an industry-specific destabilizing event whose effect on deposit stability was augmented by geographic

17 Hausman, J. A. (1978). Specification tests in econometrics.

Econometrica, 46(6), 1251.

diversity, where a greater level of diversity generally lead to more overall stability.

While the magnitude of the coefficient estimates are ambiguous in their relation to a bank’s total deposit stability as a product of geographic diversification, their statistical significance and directionality in the context of this model are transferable. That is, since changes in branch geographic diversity and deposit stability are positively proportional to their corresponding effects on bank geographic diversification and deposit stability, the insights of this model can be applied at a bank level as well. The estimated values infer that the effect of geographic diversification on a bank’s total deposit stability is positive and significant. Therefore, H2 is affirmed: geographic diversification is positively associated with deposit stabilization.

6 Conclusions

Since every county poses a unique risk profile to the branches located within it, it is crucial to account for the differences in their economic profiles when measuring geographic diversity. Further, as the geographic diversification of a bank relies on a portfolio of branches with low concentrations of local industry exposures, analyzing trends within individual branches as opposed to entire banks is a valuable tool. This insight can likely be transferred to other individually subtle but aggregately potent banking dynamics. By taking this approach in the context of an economic shock, we arrive at several interesting results that would be unobtainable from a macro-level, non-panel analysis.

The extent to which we observe positive spatial autocorrelation in deposit stability between branches is predominantly among neighbors less than 25 arc distance miles apart. An alternative interpretation of this statistic is that past 25 arc distance miles, branches share no discernable spatial autocorrelation in deposit stability. Given that the smallest state in the United States, Rhode Island, stretches 37 miles in width, the notion of taking each state to represent a single risk profile is misguided since, in each, there are at least two uncorrelated spatial clusters of deposit stability. Adapting the previous literature on geographic diversification in branch banking to index counties rather than states, and to represent both rural and urban regions, is an important development that the results of this paper corroborate.

Contrary to their connotation, economic shocks can often provide a source of stability for the regions which they affect. The emergence of fracking in the early 2010s and its effects on deposit stability is an excellent case study in substantiating this thought. Branches in fracking counties with a low industry concentration of energy employment could be said to have benefited in terms of stability by the introduction of fracking, since the employment it spurred increased the county’s industry diversity. However, it may be more advantageous to think of the treatment effect of fracking as quadratic, with an inflection point at which its energy industry employment equals the mean level of employment among all present industries. If fracking employment were to surpass this inflection point, the county’s measured diversity would actually decrease along with its branches’ predicted deposit stability. Therefore, it should be prefaced in further discussion of economic shocks in banking that shocks are not necessarily destabilizing events, but rather their effects on stability are augmented in either direction by the shock’s corresponding impact on each affected region’s risk profile. While the case study in fracking does not prove any universal relationship—perhaps shocks to other industries impact deposit stability differently—its study does aid us in our comprehension of the microeconomic mechanisms by which geographic diversification may be an important consideration for growing banks.

Altogether, these understandings form a compelling story for the types of diversification advantages proposed by Demsetz and Strahan (1997).3 For banks seeking to improve predictability and leverage of their deposit bases, opportunities to expand towards geographically diverse and dissimilar regions may prove an effective means to do so. In particular, mergers and acquisitions of smaller, regional banks may principally provide economies of experience and localized knowledge of markets that mitigates risk in lending, but may also serve to diversify the deposit base of the parent bank as a whole. The mass consolidation of banking institutions following the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994 was predominantly fueled by an interest in the former advantage, but future consolidation may likely be encouraged from further discovery of diversification effects and their potential benefits to leverage and subsequently profitability.

Diversification advantages may also belong in the macroeconomic discussion of the United States banking sector in its entirety, especially when compared with the banking sectors of more geographically homogenous countries. In the first major global recession since the passage of the Riegle-Neal Act in 1994, the United States economy and banking sector in particular was able to recover far quicker in the years following 2009 than were European countries like Italy, Spain, and Greece.18 Much of this disparity was due to debt-related policies governing bankruptcy and credit, however the results of this paper propose another reason embedded in differences in geographic diversity. Given the vast geographic heterogeneity of the United States and its numerosity of distinctive regional economies, its interstate banks had more opportunity to mitigate the deposit instability caused by the financial crisis through diversification than did banks in the smaller and more homogenous countries of Europe.

Finally, a discussion of diversification in banking, even when rooted in physical geography, cannot overlook the contemporary migration toward online banking as a primary deposit servicing medium. The rapid growth stories of fintechs over the past decade have challenged the predominant trends in branch banking on which most research is founded, largely by minimizing overhead costs and maximizing client access in an unprecedented fashion. Despite not conforming to any physical plane of geography, the digital presence of online banking is actually quite relevant to the analysis of geographic diversification. Because online banking extends access to populations across the country regardless of their proximity to physical branches, its potential for geographic diversification is elevated to a ceiling beyond that of any physical branch banking portfolio. The identification of diversification effects in facilitating deposit stability may even premise that fintechs can be leveraged to a point beyond that of traditional branch banks without any greater risk of insolvency. Considering geographic diversification is therefore a vital piece to understanding why fintechs are optimally positioned to disrupt the modern banking sector.

18 Schildbach, J., & Wenzel, C. (2013). Bank performance in the US and Europe. Current Issues, Global financial markets, B. Speyer, Ed.,

Frankfurt am Main, Germany: Deutsche Bank Research.

In learning from the dynamics of the more than 146,000 FDIC-insured branch banks across the United States, further research on the topic of geographic diversification will serve as a foundation on which innovation in branch banking, both digital and physical, can continue at the remarkable rate that it has. By taking advantage of diversification effects, fintechs especially may continue to triumph in growth and profitability over traditional banking while maintaining both stability and solvency. If preparedness for an uncertain future of economic shocks and disruptions is a key to success in the speculative business of banking, then knowledge of the underlying mechanics through which uncertainty interacts with risk is the toolkit by which the banks of the future will reign most lucrative.

When Women Teach:

Female Pedagogues on the Early Modern Stage

Sam Lien Nguyen

Advisor: Professor Kasey Evans

Honors Coordinator: Professor Vivasvan Soni

April 30, 2021

English Department

Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences

Northwestern University

A thesis submitted in partial fulfillment of the requirements for graduation with honors from the

Department of English

To younger Sam, who fell asleep thinking about radicalizing education

Table of Contents

Acknowledgments i

Introduction 1

Chapter 1: The Case of Male Pupil and Female Pedagogue in Love’s Cure 10

Chapter 2: Doctor Rosalind Dismantles Patriarchal Authority in As You Like It 20

Coda 33

Bibliography 35

Acknowledgments

A little bird once quoted E.L. Doctorow: “Writing is like driving at night in the fog. You can only see as far as your headlights, but you can make the whole trip that way.” Actually—it wasn’t a little bird. An angel in the shape of my supervisor, Professor Kasey Evans, said that to me when I was having doubts about my ability to complete this thesis, and I cannot communicate how much those words helped tide me over during moments of intense uncertainty. From sage advice to language exchange to funny robot arm emoji, Professor Evans, your wisdom, endless compassion, and warming sincerity make this process (and in general my experience as an

English student) so much more fulfilling. From the bottom of my heart, thank you.

To the incredibly talented, supportive, and empowering group of women who make up the 2021 cohort: YAS QUEENS! I am so proud to be a part of this team and witness every single one of us persevere through and grow from difficult moments. Thank you, Professor Viv Soni, for keeping us on track with your *generative* comments and accompanying us throughout this journey as our Honors Coordinator.

My sincere appreciation to all the exceptional professors in the English Department, whether or not I have had the honor of working with you. Professor Jules Law’s evident passion for literature inspired freshman me to declare the major two weeks into college. Professor Nick

Davis feels more like a friend who always welcomes more nerdy conversations. Special thanks to Professor Jeffrey Masten, Professor Wendy Wall, and Professor Whitney Taylor, for teaching the classes that helped me realize how much I love Renaissance literature. You make me want to read and write like I’m running out of time: voraciously and unapologetically.

Shout out to the Northwestern Library for all the chapter scans! COVID might keep me

(literally) thousands of miles away from you, but it definitely cannot keep me from knowledge.

Thank you to Josh Honn especially, for your valuable assistance in the purchase of books and other research materials.

Cảm ơn bốmẹfor being excited even though you know close to nothing about this thesis.

I regret that my subpar Vietnamese means a significant portion of my college career is kept away from you. And my loving little sister, thank you for your deadpan humor and midnight hot chocolate. What would I do without you?

Selin, Van Anh, and Lin. My best friends, my anchor, my muse. My let’s-go-on-a-coffee-work-date-because-I-don’t-want-to-work-alone-but-also-let’s-not-talk-becau se-I-have-so-much-to-do buddies. My

I’m-sorry-I’m-calling-you-at-2AM-but-I’m-so-stressed-about-this-thesis-thing hype women.

Merci d’être l’épaule sur laquelle je peux toujours compter.

Femi, thank you for putting up with all my rants and random thoughts over the past three years. Sorry I kept interrupting your work with weird (early modern) words. You are the best roommate I could ever ask for.

Last but not least, I thank 3712 Vietnamese coffee shops for sponsoring this FLAMIN’

HOT ® thesis. The days might be long and the nights even longer, but coffee makes everything possible.

Introduction

Growing up in Vietnam, I was haunted by a proverb, Nhất nam viết hữu thập nữviết vô, which roughly translates: “Having one son means having a child, having ten daughters means not having any child.” I learned it from the textbooks; I heard it in conversations; I saw manifestations of it in the way parents relentlessly tried to have more babies in order to beget a son, regardless of their preparedness. The implicit lesson, both inside and outside of the schoolroom: being a girl meant I was deficient compared to boys.

Several years later, in a college Renaissance Literature class, I noticed with both amusement and chagrin that the notion of the defective female not only spans hemispheres, cultures, and eras, but also bleeds into scientific pursuits. According to Galen, the ancient Greek anatomical structures, but “[women’s] lack of vital heat—of perfection—…result[s] in the retention, inside, of structures that in the male are visible without” (Laqueur 4). This means, among other things, that women’s genitalia and men’s are structurally homologous—with the vagina and ovaries corresponding to the penis and scrotum—except that women’s organs fail to extrude. In other words, women are men turned outside in. This model, later termed the “one-sex model” by Thomas Laqueur, makes it clear that maleness is the default, the product of successful gestation, while femaleness is incomplete, defective, faulty.

While this model consolidates male superiority, it also introduces a prominent issue of the early modern period: if men and women are anatomically parallel, how can gender differences be enforced? Jean E. Howard explains, “Because by this [Galenic] account male-female difference was less grounded in ideas of absolute bodily difference than is typical today, much emphasis was placed on behavioral differences and on distinctions of dress” (1619). More specifically, early modern England relied on education to generate these behavioral differences that would distinguish boys from girls: “Renaissance humanists… sought to gender young children through pedagogy” (Wall 61). As Caroline Bowden puts it, “the provision of education in the family was 1 gendered, with girls receiving less tuition than boys, and in some cases it is clear that girls gained only very basic skill” (90). The location and content of their education also differed: while boys left home at the age of seven to receive formal training in Latin, rhetoric, grammar, logic, and mathematics at grammar school, girls remained at home for domestic and religious lessons. As 2 education aimed to condition learners into virtuous citizens, Danielle Clark argues, it “inculcated social values, acculturated the individual, and provided the learning deemed appropriate to the social status held by the pupil,” directing boys toward a vocation and girls toward a “discourse of containment” (19). In other words, the early modern educational model served to produce and reinforce social and gender roles: men trained to become powerful and eloquent state leaders while women prepared to become chaste, silent, and obedient wives, mothers, and mistresses of the house. There was also an emphasis on women’s education not as an opportunity for 3 self-edification but rather as a preparation for fulfilling their matrimonial and household duties.4

Walter Ong specifically examines Latin language training as an enforcement of a gendered education. In his influential paper “Latin Language Study as a Renaissance Puberty

Rite,” Ong considers the early modern teaching of Latin as a “puberty rite” through which young

4 See Vives; Bowden 88-90; Moncrief and McPherson, Chapter 1.

3 This is not to discredit the significant content of the female education “track.” As Wendy Wall’s work on domesticity reveals, the “mistress of the house” needed expertise in multiple fields, including cooking, medicine, pharmacology, nursing, food preservation, and home budgeting and economics.

2 For further discussion, see Moncrief and McPherson, Chapter 1.

1 Interestingly, Elizabeth Hutcheon is the only scholar I have encountered who argues that humanist education is inherently non-gendered. See Hutcheon.

boys were inducted into a male tribe—an “extra-familial life which involve[s] a sense of break with the past … together with segregation from the family and from those of the other sex, and chastisement under the direction of elders for didactic purposes” (106). In essence, the cleavage between Latin and vernacular English mirrors the division between an exclusively male world and a domestic world with (and of) women. To become full members of the learned society, boys must leave the company of women for the social milieu of powerful preceptors.

Implied in Ong’s argument is the notion that masculinity requires socialization in the right environment, while femininity is the state that can be informally taught within the domestic setting. This claim offers another model for understanding maleness and femaleness that may, at 5 first, appear to be in conflict with Galen’s, but Galen’s is a model for sexual, gestational difference while Ong’s emphasizes differences that result from separate gender training. Early modern sex and gender, then, undergo divergent (yet interconnected) processes of construction.

This important distinction between early modern sex and gender resonates with the modern understanding of the sex/gender distinction proposed by Judith Butler, building on Simone de

Beauvoir’s generative argument in The Second Sex. In her analysis of de Beauvoir, Butler contends that de Beauvoir’s powerful formulation, “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” (de Beauvoir 301), suggests that gender and sex are separated, and that gender is an aspect of identity acquired over time. Butler expounds, “sex is understood to be the invariant, anatomically distinct, and factic aspects of the female body, whereas gender is the cultural meaning and form that that body acquires, the variable modes of that body’s acculturation”

(Butler, “Sex” 35). Being “female” and being a “woman” are distinct modes: one is born into a

5 For further discussion of this argument, see Hartstock 133-52.

sexed body but grows into one’s gender during the process of socialization and cultural acclimatization. However, neither Butler nor the early modern is strictly binary: Butler addresses the instability of the binary distinction between sex and gender as well as the instability of the male/female distinction even in biological sex; early modern philosophers made sense of 6 anatomy through the lens of social expectations (gender) even as they were performing dissections. Vesalius’s illustration of the vaginal canal, reproduced below, reflects Galen’s erroneous belief and makes a powerful statement about how much our beliefs and expectations regulate our perception. Although it was produced after Vesalius operated on real human cadavers, the illustration looks more like a penis (without testicles) than a vaginal canal.

6 For example, Butler writes, “If the immutable character of sex is contested, perhaps this construct called ‘sex’ is as culturally constructed as gender; indeed, perhaps it was always already gender, with the consequence that the distinction between sex and gender turns out to be no distinction at all.” See Butler, Gender Trouble, 10-11.

Image 1. Vesalius’s illustration of the vaginal canal

Due to the significance of education in the imposition of gender, the “relative democratization of learning” for groups that had previously enjoyed little access to education, and the wealth of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century printed texts on pedagogical methodologies and the value of education for both boys and girls, among other reasons, early modern education 7 blossomed “on both the stage and page” (Moncrief and McPherson 1-2). Several playtexts display explicit concern with education, as suggested by Rosaline’s question, “Shall I teach you to know?” (Love’s Labor’s Lost IV.1.103) and Bianca’s statement, “I’ll not be tied to hours nor

‘pointed times/ But learn my lessons as I please myself” (The Taming of the Shrew III.1.19-20).

7 For a few examples, see Vives; Elyot; Ascham; Salter; Mulcaster; Batt; Pritchard; Kempe.

Interestingly, Renaissance playwrights sought to challenge the very education that shaped them and to destabilize the deep-rooted framework of gender through their dramas. It is not difficult to find examples of female characters from this period who “suggest both an awareness of the constructed and performed nature of gender roles, and a desire to problematise and complicate the classifications typically available as ways of seeing women” (Kamaralli 1123). In her investigation of names in The Taming of the Shrew, Laurie Maguire points out that even when

Katherine sanctions Petruchio’s right to name everything, she still finds the space to slyly reassert the full form of her own name, which Maguire interprets as an act of resistance.

Similarly, Patricia Parker contends, Bianca establishes herself as an independent scholar who masters her own masters by flaunting fluency in Latin and demanding to study “as [she] pleases

[herself].” Anna Kamaralli offers an excellent reading of the four female characters in John

Webster’s The White Devil and Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale and their performance of traditionally masculine traits, thereby calling into question the definability of womanhood. Janet

Adelman identifies in the characterization of Cleopatra in Shakespeare’s Antony and Cleopatra a tension with the phallogocentric parameters according to which women are faulty men. These characters also invite us to upend the teacher-pupil roles and imagine women not as passive students but powerful instructors, an invitation that I will later take up in this thesis.

These plays, along with copious early modern instructional texts—such as Juan Luis

Vives’s Instruction of a Christen Woman (1529), Roger Ascham’s The Scholemaster (1570), and

William Kempe’s The Education of Children in Learning (1588)—also testify to the inextricability of education, the construction of gendered and hierarchical social configuration, and the (re)production and performance of both masculinity and femininity. The early modern stage was, according to Moncrief and McPherson, a “key pedagogical site” to examine how educational practices disciplined students as representatives of their social station and gender (4).

Nevertheless, scholarly discussions of early modern education until the first decade of the twenty-first century gave only minimal attention to the matter of gender and almost none to the ways in which pedagogy and performance intersect: Rebecca Bushnell’s The Culture of

Teaching: Early Modern Humanism in Theory and Practice offers a thorough discussion of the advent and development of humanism throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries but neglects its interplay with gender; Jeff Dolven’s Scenes of Instruction in Renaissance Romance attempts to formulate a “poetics of pedagogy” by studying instructional scenes in prose romances rather than the drama of the age; and a variety of texts concentrate on women’s literacies in the early modern with little to no consideration of gender and performance. Moncrief and McPherson’s edited collection goes furthest in exploring the rich intersection of gender, pedagogy, and performance. The essays in this collection examine a variety of Renaissance instructional and literary texts to illustrate that early modern pedagogy, especially the teaching of gender, is explicitly performative. Moncrief and McPherson also examine the inseparability of performance on stage and performance of gender in everyday life. As aforementioned, distinctions of dress were meant to signify male-female differences, and crossdressing, “however playfully undertaken, always threatened to expose the artifice of gender distinctions by showing how easily one sex could assume the clothes and ape the behavior of the other” (Howard 1619).

As we know, early modern stage performances licensed crossdressing in plays that do and do not thematize gender, since female parts were played exclusively by young boys during this time.

Nevertheless, not enough attention has been paid to scenes of (sexual and gender)

pedagogy in which women rise to the role of educators and men are relegated to studenthood.

What occasions women to teach? What conditions must be satisfied for women to safely transition into an instructional role? What does it take to educate a man into manhood? In the first part of my thesis, Love’s Cure offers an excellent platform to entertain these questions, especially in its portrayal of budding romantic relationships. The play’s attempt to realign the gender performance of its two protagonists, who are both transvestites, with their biological sex 8 sparks a complex series of educational imperatives that simultaneously deconstruct and reconstruct its understanding of sex and gender. For the purpose of this thesis, I will focus only on Lucio and his relationship with Genevora, for two reasons. First, Lucio regards himself as a woman at the beginning of the play and maintains his femininity almost until the end. As my research aims to examine gender presentation not as equivalent to biological sex but rather as the product of social acculturation partially distinct from sex, I view Lucio as gender-fluid and fruitful for the scope of my study. Second, this relationship features a female pedagogue. In my 9 analysis, I read Genevora as simultaneously a mother, a lover, and a teacher, and thus as a challenge to Walter Ong’s proposition that early modern masculinity was only learned in the closed male schoolroom. Lucio’s character arc illustrates a masculinity taught in the domestic setting by a woman to a male-born student originally alienated from male society. More importantly, I contend that while Genevora adopts a similar pedagogy to other male characters who attempt to transform Lucio, her successful tutelage results from her acknowledgment and encouragement of Lucio’s gender fluidity and performativity. Instead of viewing his femininity

9 That said, I will follow the playtext in using he/him/his pronouns for Lucio and she/her/hers for Clara throughout this thesis for ease of reference.

8 And arguably transgender, though I am aware of my anachronism in using both terms here.

as an ignominious property to be cast off, Genevora is interested in the various gender expressions that Lucio occupies and commands him to assume different gender roles as they suit her needs.

The second part of my thesis shifts into a discussion of Shakespeare’s As You Like It.

Although this is a canonical text, there are surprisingly few materials written on Rosalind’s role as an educator in the play. A large body of scholarship on As You Like It comments on her crossdressing and the effect that it has on surrounding characters and the dramatic plot. My thesis briefly explores her transvestism, but only in the service of a larger investigation into the opportunities that playing a man opens up for Rosalind in her education of Orlando. More specifically, I argue that under the guise of the young man Ganymede, Rosalind performs the dual roles of a teacher and a physician, both versions of the “doctor.” Throughout the play, she assumes these two “doctor” roles in parallel to bolster her authority and to exact a “transgressive reinscription,” to borrow a term from Jonathan Dollimore: using irony or parody as “a mode of transgression which finds expression through the inversion and perversion of just those preexisting categories and structures …; a mode of transgression which seeks not an escape from existing structures, but rather a subversive reinscription within them—and in the process a dis-location of them” (Dollimore 57). In other words, instead of striving for transcendence, this 10 version of transgression takes the form of upending or destabilizing ideological, “natural” categories. For Rosalind, this transgressive reinscription means establishing her position in traditionally male-dominated fields so as to effectively infiltrates the patriarchal order and destabilizes the extant epistemological paradigm.

10 I mention this notion in passing in my examination of Love’s Cure, but will employ it more substantially in my chapter on As You Like It.

As a whole, this project endeavors to disrupt the narrative of uninterrupted early modern patriarchy. Love’s Cure and As You Like It tells the stories of women who upset the power differential between the sexes and claim authority they could not ordinarily assume. These plays explore and interrogate the theater and the classroom as sites where gender performance can vitiate entrenched power structures. By examining the gendered pedagogical dynamics in these plays, I hope to reveal how every instance of teaching and learning offers opportunities for shifting the grounds of power and authority. They always allow for the possibility of resistance, transgression, and subversion—incrementally, perhaps, but no less powerful for that.

Chapter 1: The Case of Male Pupil and Female Pedagogue in Love’s Cure

Who is the average schoolteacher in the United States? A 43-year-old white woman with over a decade of teaching experience, according to data published in April 2020 by the U.S.

Department of Education (Tai and Westat). While it is true that the demographic of schoolteachers (excluding higher education) is now predominantly female, this has not always been the case. Up until the common school movement of the late 1830s, men dominated the teaching profession (Provenzo). During the early modern period, it was at best bizarre and at worst transgressive to imagine women as pedagogues. More often than not, early modern literary works, especially playtexts, position women as students who need instructions from male masters. Highly canonical examples include Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, which features two sisters as students and three male suitors acting as teachers, and The Tempest, in which Prospero teaches Miranda about the male species for the first time.11

However, the multiplicity of female student figures in literature does not imply that there was no attempt to question the standard male-tutor-with-female-pupil dynamic. Just as modern society questions the pay gap between men and women undertaking the same work, or the tendency for women to end up in lower-ranking and untenured positions in higher education, several early modern dramatists interrogate the gender dynamics and politics in their scenes of instruction through educational, social, and ontological lenses. One salient example appears in

Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher’s Love’s Cure, or The Martial Maid. The main plot deals with the gender transformation of two siblings—Clara and Lucio—who have been brought up separately as members of the opposite sex—Lucio raised by their mother Eugenia and Clara by

11 As I will briefly mention later, ballads and pornography more often portray women as the dominant and experienced participant, in keeping with their exploration and inversion of social norms. Dramas are the opposite: women in early modern drama tend to be delicate tabulae rasae.

their father Alvarez. Twenty years later, the family is reunited, and the siblings are commanded to conform to their expected gender behaviors. This play offers a divergent narrative in its construction of the relationship between its male lead Lucio and his love interest Genevora, a noblewoman. The pedagogical dynamic between the lovers skews toward the woman: Genevora appears to be simultaneously an experienced woman showing a naïve man the “sexual ABCs” and a mother teaching her child the tenets of (wo)manhood (Traub 295).

These two possibilities interweave closely, as is evident from the ambiguous diction in

Genevora’s speech at the double duel. In this final scene, Vitelli and his second Lamorall prepare to duel against Alvarez and his son Lucio to resolve their long-running feud. When the time for combat comes, the intended duelists are interrupted by Clara (Alvarez’s daughter and Vitelli’s lover), Genevora (Vitelli’s sister and Lucio’s lover), and Eugenia (Alvarez’s wife), who plead with them not to fight. Genevora declaims:

Oh Lucio! Be thou more mercifull: thou bear’st fewer yeers, Art lately wean’d from soft effeminacy, A maidens manners, and a maidens heart Are neighbours still to thee: be then more milde, Proceed not to this combat; bee’s thou desperate Of thine own life? yet (deerest) pitty mine: Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee, These eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up, This breast would lodge it: doe not use my gifts To mine own ruine: I have made these rich, Be not so thanklesse, to undoe me for’t. (V.3.110-121, emphasis mine)

The Oxford English Dictionary defines “wean” as the act of “accustom[ing] (a child or young animal) to the loss of its mother’s milk” (OED, “wean” v., 1). This word immediately recalls a mother-and-child dynamic in the interactions between the lovers. In fact, Genevora’s speech is littered with language of parenting, italicized in the quotation above: “to beget” means to bring (a child) into existence (OED, “beget” v., 2.a), while “to breed” not only implies the environment in which one grows up but also connotes the education of young persons (OED, “breed” v., I.10.b).

By employing these verbs, Genevora firmly establishes her position as a mother without whom there will be no masculine Lucio. In other words, she imagines Lucio as the feminized infant who comes to be through her parturition and requires her parenting.

Genevora is not the first theatrical character to acknowledge the necessity of women in the formation of masculinity, however. In fact, her speech harks back to a moment in

Shakespeare’s Love’s Labor’s Lost, when Lord Biron (or Berowne) declares:

[For] women’s sake—by whom we men are men— Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves, Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths. (IV.3.334-6)

Here, Biron relinquishes the definition of masculinity as an exclusive single-sex academy and acknowledges that “masculinity is expressed only in relationship” (Moncrief 123). That is, men 12 do not gain masculine honor and self-enhancement through isolated study but through interactions with and positioning relative to women, for whose sake (and by whose maternal offices) “men are men.” Of course, Biron might just be referring to the fact that we are all born of women—an interpretation that Love’s Cure certainly takes advantage of. But Biron does not claim that “people are people” or “babies are babies” or “boys are boys,” but specifically “men are men,” insisting that women play a role in boys’ maturation into men, not just their existence as human beings. Love’s Cure is essentially making the same claim, but the play takes its

“transgressive reinscription” a step further by having Genevora proclaim her own significance.

As opposed to Love’s Labor’s Lost, what we witness in Love’s Cure is not a reflection by the man

12 For an excellent analysis of this speech, see Moncrief, “‘Teach Us, Sweet Madam’.

but an explicit assertion of authority by the woman: Genevora knows herself to be the master and claims her role: “Thy valour’s not thine owne, I gave it thee.”

Interestingly, Love’s Cure proposes more than one way “we men are men” by women.

The first, as we have identified in the use of “wean,” is through the narrative of motherhood, which signals that Lucio’s manhood results from the entire process of Genevora’s gestation, parturition, and parenting. Another route interprets “to breed” not as parenting but as copulation and reproduction: not only has Genevora birthed and raised Lucio, but she also breeds with him, thus conflating the parental and erotic dynamics between the two. This word, along with previous scenes in the play, explicitly spells out sexual education as the catalyst for Lucio’s gender transformation. For the first half of the play, Lucio presents as a young, innocent boy/girl so ignorant of the “sexual ABC’s” that he expresses surprise at the prospect of desire beyond a kiss. He is not exceptional in his cluelessness. Valerie Traub makes a case that “Renaissance texts are populated with women and men who simply do not know what other people seem to know; and more often than not, this lack of knowledge consistently evokes a pedagogical imperative that is elided or refused or fails” (295). In the case of Love’s Cure, the “pedagogical imperative” that springs from Lucio’s lack of knowledge, his initiation into the arts of love, officially begins with Genevora’s erotic instructions. Their kiss in Act 4, Scene 4 communicates new sexual knowledge that leads to “strange new motions” and “alteration,” which serve as a turning point for Lucio’s gender formation (IV.4.12-14). Shortly after this kiss, in response to

Genevora’s chiding for not protecting her love token, Lucio exclaims:

My womanish soul, which hitherto hath govern’d This coward flesh, I feel departing from me; And in me by her beauty is inspir’d A new, and masculine one: instructing me What’s fit to do or suffer; powerful love

That hast with loud, and yet a pleasing thunder Rous’d sleeping manhood in me, thy new creature, Perfect thy work so that I may make known Nature (though long kept back) will have her own. (IV.4.54-62, emphasis mine)

This monologue details Lucio’s most conscious utterance of his gender transformation from a

“womanish soul” into a “masculine one.” Crucially, this transformation relies heavily on

Genevora’s beauty, which Lucio claims to have “inspir’d” a new soul into him. Etymologically derived from the Latin prefix “in–” and the verb “spīrāre,” which means to breathe, “inspire” imagines the couple’s kiss as the literal act of Genevora breathing out and Lucio breathing in.13

This literalization signifies that Lucio’s soul, be it “womanish” or “masculine,” is not an inherent element within his natural body but rather a property obtained through and gendered by his participation in an erotic act. Intriguingly, Lucio’s sexual socialization, particularly his description of the kiss as Genevora “instructing [him]/ What’s fit to do or suffer,” bears a striking resemblance to that of the hapless male lover, Tomalin, in Thomas Nashe’s narrative poem “The

Choise of Valentines.” Tomalin, just like Lucio, is “clueless about the mechanics of sex, specifically about how to pleasure a woman” (Traub 114-15). On the whole, their experiences fit into the larger sexual narrative, which employs the compelling trope of naiveté that invites tutelage from the more experienced woman who performs the role of instructor. In Love’s Cure,

Lucio and Genevora’s sexual encounter inaugurates a pedagogical process, or at least a pedagogical dynamic, that Lucio identifies in this soliloquy and that conforms to Genevora’s speech in the dueling scene cited above. In this fashion, Lucio’s gender transformation is

“revealed to be the result of a particular social production, a process of knowledge construction,”

13 Interestingly, the image of Genevora breathing into Lucio harks back to the biblical account of the creation of men: “And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7 identify which translation you’re using here). This parallelism solidifies Genevora’s position of power, possibly at the expense of the erotic dimension of the relationship.

one that relies heavily on education through participation in sexual acts (Traub 117-18).

What these two scenes illuminate is that whether she plays the role of a mother or a romantic partner, Genevora undeniably activates Lucio’s integration into masculinity through her

(sexual) tutelage. This proposition stands in contrast with Walter Ong’s influential observation that the departure from domestic life into Latin training was a kind of male “puberty rite” (Ong

103). In fact, Lucio has never fully entered the exclusively male society and remains entirely foreign to it, until Genevora’s interposition. We see this in Alvarez and Bobadilla’s futile attempt to redeem Lucio’s manliness:

Alvarez. Thou hast made me mad: and I will beat thee dead Then bray the in a morter, and new mold thee But I wil alter thee. Bobadilla. ‘Twill never be: He has bin three days practicing to drink, Yet still he sips, like to a waiting woman, And looks as he were murdering of a fart Among wild Irish swaggerers. (IV.3.25-31)

Bobadilla highlights Lucio’s status as an outcast who fails to enter the male world by comparing him to “a waiting woman,” a sneer at not only Lucio’s womanly behavior, but also the accompanying threat of downward social mobility. Furthermore, while the play is set in Spain, it is performed to an English audience well aware of English colonialism in Ireland. Ireland, like many others colonized countries, was often feminized, “increasingly imaged in wifely terms” in direct contrast with England, her masculine imperial master (Valente 190). In positioning Lucio 14

“among wild Irish swaggerers,” Bobadilla relegates him to the world of uncultured, unlearned

(wild) women (Irish) who lack proper, courtly behaviors (swaggerers). All three layers of otherness—in terms of gender, class, and race and ethnicity—simultaneously pronounce the

14 For further discussion of the English colonial discourse about Ireland, see also Stevens et al.

danger of Lucio’s wanting manliness and confirm the men’s desperation and inability to transform him. When all their efforts prove to no avail, they resort to rage, carnality, and violence:

Ther’s only one course left, that may redeem thee, Which is, to strike the next man that you meet, And if we chance to light upon a woman, Take her away, and use her like a man, Or I wil cut thy hamstrings. (IV.3.37-41, emphasis mine)

While Anne Duncan cites this passage as an example of “the connection between rage and the performance of masculinity,” I am more concerned with the implication that sexual knowledge is an agent or catalyst of manly honor (399). We have seen in Lucio’s soliloquy above that it is not rage that “rous’d sleeping manhood” in him; it is his kiss with Genevora. In other words, sexual experience, rather than violence, triggers this process of masculinization. However, as Valerie

Traub makes clear, “eroticism isn’t just something that people do (…); it is something that people learn; it requires initiation, experimentation, education, [and] practice” (119). In that case,

Alvarez’s appeal to a final “course,” a term with forceful pedagogical connotations, does not terminate where he imagines it would: at a single lewd act of “[using] her like a man.” Instead, it

(unintentionally) marks the beginning of Lucio’s courtship with Genevora and thus occasions an erotic educational process. Ironically, this educational process at once echoes and fundamentally differs from the one implemented by the men themselves. As a pedagogue, Genevora chides as the men have chided: “Nay you are rude; pray you forbeare; you offer now/ More then the breeding of a Gentleman/ Can give you warrant for.” (IV.4.1-3). She instructs as the men have instructed: both parties adopt the learning-by-doing approach, Genevora with desire and kissing and Alverez with fighting and violence. Finally, when Lucio’s indecisiveness causes him to lose her “favour”—that is, her gloves, which were given as a love token—to another suitor, she resorts to “torment” in the same manner as Alvarez has threatened to “bray [Lucio] in the morter”:

For thy torment, If my poore beauty be of any power, Mayst thou doat on it desperately: but never Presume to hope for grace, till thou recover And weare the favour that was ravish’d from thee. (IV.4.45-52, emphasis mine)

In other words, Genevora employs similar pedagogical techniques as Alvarez and Bobadilla.

And yet, she yields the desired outcome as the men could not. Lucio’s successful education in masculinity, then, results not from the method of instruction but the instructor and the content.

Instead of drinking and “strik[ing]” with men, Lucio thrives under the sexual tutelage of a woman. More broadly speaking, he moves from one domestic scene—where he finds in his mother Eugenia a model for imitation—into another—where he learns from his mother-like fiancée. Contrary to Walter Ong’s argument, what the men fail miserably to do can be achieved rather seamlessly by two women: Eugenia teaches him to be a woman, and Genevora allegedly turns him into a man.

What exactly renders Genevora a more proficient educator than Alvarez and Bobadilla? I contend that Genevora’s success is attributable to her disinterest in the binary caricature of masculinity; on the contrary, she acknowledges that Lucio has the wisdom of all the different gender roles that he has played and employs her various roles to capitalize on this fluidity and capaciousness. A salient manifestation of this practice is in her speech at the double duel where

Genevora at once establishes her position as the mother and reasserts her power as the instructor.

“[B]e then more milde,” she commands her lover, asking him to temporarily reassume his “soft effeminacy,” which Lucio has practiced in his feminized infancy. Her directive encourages us to read “effeminacy” and by extension “masculinity” as a performance that one dials up and down rather than something that can be wholly eradicated and superseded. Her use of “soft effeminacy” in conjunction with “wean’d” also reinforces this idea of gender performativity, for the definition of “wean” as the act of “accustoming to” anticipates Butler’s language of acculturation and a “contingent construction of meaning” (Butler, Gender Trouble 139). In other words, gender in Love’s Cure is neither innate nor constant, but a series of possibilities to be performed as convenience and/or ethics dictate. To Genevora, Lucio’s earlier childhood femininity is not something shameful; instead, it contains useful information for him to draw on to become more expansive, more compassionate, and an altogether better partner for her. Thus, what makes Genevora stand out from Lucio’s other instructors is her cognizance of what we might now call the performativity of gender, her appreciation of Lucio’s various qualities of different genders, and her awareness of the significance of her presence. As a result, Lucio’s change of gender depends not on his will but hers: when she is upset that he cannot protect her love, he assumes masculinity; when she is upset that he is about to harm her family, he is compelled to revert to softness. Ultimately, Lucio’s gender is not only a performance; it is a series of performances cultivated and authorized by a female director and pedagogue.

In looking at Lucio’s gender transformation, which results from his accumulation of sexual knowledge, I have illustrated not only that, and how, a woman can occupy the role of an educator, but also the efficacy of her tutelage. Throughout Love’s Cure, Genevora weaves together motherhood and professorship, and in so doing, successfully trains Lucio to become a man—a considerable feat that other male figures in the play fail to do. What is remarkable is that

Genevora adopts a similar approach to teaching as Alvarez and Bobadilla do, with an emphasis on instruction, punishment, and practice, but yields vastly different results. Her favorable outcome, then, must be attributable to her ability to perceive Lucio as both the feminized, helpless infant and the masculine partner who has adult sexuality and can relate to her with desire. By understanding this simultaneity and by imagining her authority as both motherly and teacherly, Genevora asserts her claim to the result—Lucio’s honorable manliness/ manly honor—in both familial and academic terms: she simultaneously begets his outstanding qualities and trains him to develop a full consciousness of and mastery over those qualities. Consequently, she also reserves the right to revoke those characteristics and skillfully manipulates Lucio’s gender performance, calling on him to privilege his masculinity or femininity as she sees fit.

Read this way, the play is as invested in recording Genevora’s growth as a pedagogue as it is keen on the notion of gender as a performance, or the actual erotic content and training that contributes to Lucio’s increasing masculinity. Whatever the case, Love’s Cure undeniably compels its audience to interrogate and dismiss patriarchal assumptions about who can be a teacher, and what it means to be, become, or perform a gender.

Chapter 2: Doctor Rosalind Dismantles Patriarchal Authority in As You Like It

In December 2020, Joseph Epstein wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal, calling for

First Lady Jill Biden to drop her honorific. “‘Dr. Jill Biden’ sounds and feels fraudulent, not to say a touch comic,” writes Epstein, suggesting that only physicians with M.D. are entitled to, well, the title. Dr. Biden only earned an Ed.D., a Doctor of Education, “through a dissertation with [an] unpromising title,” so she should think again and “forthwith drop the doc.” Never mind that it reeks of misogyny and sarcastic condescension; the piece leaves me questioning whether

Epstein fully comprehends what the doctorate signifies. The term “doctor” was originally a linguistic derivative of the Latin verb docēre, meaning “to teach.” Over time, it gained use as an academic title when the first doctorates were conferred in Europe, for those who have obtained a doctorate were qualified to teach or express an authoritative opinion. A physician, who had gone through a long university education, would therefore also be referred to as a “Doctour of 15

Phisyk” (documented in Chaucer, Canterbury Tales Prol. l. 413) or “doctour of deth”

(documented in Langland, Piers Plowman B. xviii. 362), to distinguish from their colleagues in church (Doctor of the Church) and law (Doctor of Law). Throughout its history, the term

“doctor” has accumulated nuances, each becoming more or less salient depending on the context in which the term appears. These nuances are not mutually exclusive—on the contrary, they are closely connected, and the activation of one does not inhibit or negate the (linguistic) validity of others. So, Mr. Epstein, the answer to your question is yes, not only is there a doctor in the White

House, but women have also presumed upon the title and role of doctor for centuries.

15 Not every medical practitioner in early modern England earned the title of doctor. In fact, only physicians, who had received extensive training and schooling in universities, were singled out for the appellation. This was because university education not only transmitted knowledge about healing but also trained students in cultivating and exercising their good judgment and advice, two crucial concepts in establishing professional authority. For further discussion, see Cook.

The inquiry into these varying resonances of the term “doctor” and their interplay is not merely a twenty-first century phenomenon: we can also see manifestations of it in early modern literature. The present chapter concentrates, in particular, on the maneuvering of the role and its various forms of authority in Shakespeare’s pastoral comedy As You Like It. In this play, the main character Rosalind is a witty woman with a delightful tongue-in-cheek sense of humor. When she meets her love interest, Orlando, in the forest, she pointedly performs—literally so, for she remains in disguise as the young, male Ganymede during the majority of her interactions with

Orlando—as both a teacher and a physician to shape him into the lover she desires. Throughout the play, she uses the two most prevalent resonances of “doctor”—physician and teacher—in parallel as roles to mutually bolster her authority and to infiltrate the patriarchal order. By doing so, Rosalind effectively ridicules and destabilizes the existing epistemological paradigm.

One salient moment in this pattern appears as soon as Rosalind sees Orlando in the forest, when she asks about the time and then demands to “tell” him about how time functions

(III.2.314). Rosalind unapologetically rejects the Renaissance trope of “the swift foot of time,” which is often cited in early modern literature, especially in Shakespeare’s sonnets, and 16 proceeds to explain that time moves at different speeds for different people. Her seemingly trivial question becomes highly productive when considered in conjunction with Jaques’s earlier musings on time and the different stages of maturation:

All the world’s a stage, And all the men and women merely players. They have their exits and entrances, And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages. At first the infant, …

16 Two examples: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 19: “Make glad and sorry seasons as thou fleet,/ And do whate’er thou wilt, swift-footed Time”; and Sonnet 65: “O fearful meditation! where, alack,/ Shall time’s best jewel from time’s chest lie hid?/ Or what strong hand can hold his swift foot back?” (emphasis mine).

Then the whining schoolboy …

And then the lover, Sighing like furnace, with a woeful ballad Made to his mistress’ eyebrow. (II.7.146-156, emphasis mine)

In this passage, “time” refers to one’s lifetime, which can be divided into seven stages: infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (or foolish old man in pantaloons), and finally,

“second childishness and mere oblivion” (II.7.172). Thus, the concept of time in Jaques’s model refers to not only a point of existence measured in hours or minutes, but also to the broad idea of time as the continued progression of existence and events. This progression is not linear but circular; humans ultimately return to a second iteration of “childishness” and then finally quietus.

Subsequently, Rosalind’s question can be understood as partially a query about where Orlando is in the stages of men: it is not just “what is ’t o’clock?” but “what is ’t o’clock with him?” The phrase “o’clock” is also apt to evoke the cyclicity of time: etymologically an abbreviated form of

“of the clock,” both the letter “o” and the image of the physical clock suggest a circular contour and movement. Read this way, Rosalind is feeling out what her role is going to be in making the clock move forward, essentially giving Orlando a placement test before writing a curriculum.

This curriculum, it is hinted, is not going to be straightforward, for time itself is not linear, nor will Orlando’s progress be. Furthermore, if we use Jaques’s multi-stage model of time to assess

Orlando’s level and progress, then Rosalind’s proposition to “give him some good counsel” is appropriate. Jaques’s description of a lover here aligns with what Rosalind later cites as cues to

“know a man in love” (III.2.376-377). By dismissing Orlando’s claim to “loverness”—I offer my detailed analysis of this dismissal below—she positions him as a “whining schoolboy,” the stage immediately preceding lover (for it is clear he is no longer an infant “mewling and puking in the nurse’s arms” [II.7.151]). If this is so, Orlando’s earlier poetic declarations of love can be regarded as “whining,” and he the schoolboy “unwillingly to school.” This taxonomy provides the pedagogical imperative for Rosalind to rise to the role of the doctor (teacher) who can mentor

Orlando to the next stage: lover.

At the same time, this opening motif of time initiates Rosalind’s process of “transgressive reinscription,” the term Jonathan Dollimore coined to the subversive inversion or reversal of ideological categories. In rejecting the conventional understanding of time as swift-footed and 17 constant, and in providing humorously realistic evidence for her argument, Rosalind inaugurates her own system of knowledge independent of masculine poetics and courtly parameters. In this system, the foundation of Renaissance humanist education—that is, Latin language learning—is not the “puberty rite,” the required condition for young boys to be inducted into an exclusive male tribe, as Ong would have it. Instead, Latin training is degraded into “the burden of lean and wasteful learning”—something that offers little reward for abundant effort (III.2.329). This trivialization of Latin also serves as a vicarious critique of institutionalized masculine learning 18 and its various pedagogical methods as impractical and ineffectual in imparting transferable knowledge and skills.

In Rosalind’s system of understanding, the “natural” categories of male and female are also problematized, curiously, through the establishment of the categories of “lover” vs.

non-lover (or “loving yourself”). As I explained in the introduction, the Galenic model of anatomy proposes that men and women share the same anatomical structures, the only difference

18 Isn’t it ironic that I’m using this Latinate word to describe Rosalind’s disapproving attitude toward Latin? Perhaps the more profound point lurking in this playful question is that although Rosalind can play with and partially subvert the patriarchal structures in which Latin reigns supreme, there is no way to entirely get around it. In fact, as I have repeatedly demonstrated, it is not her goal to escape or transcend the system; she is more concerned with revealing the loopholes that can pervert it.

“one-sex model” contends that maleness is the telos of gestation, while femaleness is a form of incompletion. A sloppy or lay interpretation of this model, which disregards anything invisible or intangible as irrelevant, is the (in)famous use of “nothing,” such as in Much Ado About Nothing, as a slang for a woman’s private part, for she has “no thing” or lacks a penis. This phallocentric discourse perpetually confines women within a negative space: always lacking, always 19 needing. In her conversation with Orlando, Rosalind sets out to invert this use of the negative: 20

ROSALIND, as Ganymede There is none of my uncle’s marks upon you. He taught me how to know a man in love, in which cage of rushes I am sure you are not prisoner.

ORLANDO What were his marks?

ROSALIND, as Ganymede A lean cheek, which you have not; a blue eye and sunken, which you have not; an unquestionable spirit, which you have not; a beard neglected, which you have not … Then your hose should be ungartered, your bonnet unbanded, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you demonstrating a careless desolation. But you are no such man. You are rather point-device in your accouterments, as loving yourself than seeming the lover of any other. (III.2.380-391, emphasis mine)

Here, instead of repudiating this patriarchal theory of women, Rosalind delegates the negative space to Orlando. In describing his not-a-lover mien, she reiterates the phrase “which you have not” four times and attaches the negative prefix un- to almost every adjective, emphasizing the lack that is, ironically, glaringly present in his accouterments. In the same way that Galen and other prominent early modern anatomists define the female body strictly in relation to its male
