nurj_title: From Farm to Fork: Exploring the Phenomenon of Organic Food Purchasing Behavior in Individualist and Collectivist Societies
text:
From Farm to Fork: Exploring the Phenomenon of Organic Food Purchasing Behavior in Individualist and Collectivist Societies

Emily Chow

Introduction

The saying, “you are what you eat,” is an undeniable truth that highlights the profound connection between an individual’s diet and overall health. The nutrients we consume energize our bodies, and the types of nourishment we choose in broader terms impact the chemistry in our brains and emotions. The brain requires a constant supply of fuel, and what this fuel is can make all the difference to the individual.[0]1 The relationship between food and mood affects the way we think about our health through habitual eating patterns. Whether it’s a fresh kale salad or a rich sugary donut, the healthy or unhealthy food choices we make are a direct translation of our motivations and well-being.[1]2 Consumers recognize organic foods as more healthy, nutritional, and environmentally friendly than everyday processed and junk foods. Purchasing and ingesting nutrient-rich foods has also become increasingly popular in communities, giving rise to better-for-you grocery stores such as Whole Foods and Erewhon, and even trends like “green juices” and “acai bowls.”[2]3

In a survey conducted by Grimmelt et al. (2022), of 8,000 consumers in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, at least 70% of the respondents across the markets surveyed desired to become healthier; 50% of consumers, across age groups, say healthy eating is a top priority for them, while only 33% say sustainable eating is too.[3]4 It is claimed that organic products possess better taste and flavors that conventional brands seem to lack and customers have the willingness to spend a little extra on goods they believe are better for them.[4]5  The demand for nutritional groceries continues to rise, driven by a growing desire for transparency, authenticity, and sustainability in the food system. However, do customers participate in these practices to promote humanitarian attitudes or merely for their own health benefit? In recent years, the trend towards organic food purchasing behavior has surged, reflecting a growing consumer awareness of the impact of food choices for various gains. Grasping the attention of research inquiry and analysis in the psychological realm, this phenomenon remains a source of continued interest.[5]6 It is the theory that assesses the intentions and motivations behind purchasing and consuming healthier food options, and especially why we participate in this action.[6]7 A consumer’s purpose to shop for organic foods and engage in these behaviors can be influenced by numerous factors such as value, quality, social norms, health benefits, convenience, availability, taste, price, the environment, etc. By understanding the dynamics and internal influences of this trend, this paper aims to better navigate the complex reasoning behind these conscious food choices.

Problem/Motivation & Thesis

The existing issue is that a general psychological perspective simply does not suffice. There is current research using general psychology that inadequately explains the need to jump on the bandwagon of the organic food lifestyle. According to Canova, Bobbio, & Manganelli (2020), they propose that these purchasing behaviors adopt the theory of planned behavior (TPB) as a theoretical framework that postulates “that a given behavior is determined by the intention to execute it.” [7]7 This is ultimately driven by attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. It suggests that consumers buy organic foods because they plan to do it, which is very individually driven. This also goes hand-in-hand with the heuristic of trust in the organic brands and companies, which acts as a shortcut to reduce the large amount of information that consumers take into account when making these health and wellness decisions.7 Apart from this logical theory, another psychological framework that interprets organic food purchasing behavior is through subjective factors such as emotion and internal feelings. Ayaviri-Nina et al. (2022) write that “consumers express emotions when they interact with a product which directly influences their purchasing attitude.”6 Emotions affect the cognitive state of individuals, which can impact the positive impulses they feel towards certain commercial products. The researchers suggest that “when making a purchase, motivation can be divided into categories, such as altruism (including environmental protection, animal welfare, and productive development) and selfishness (which consists of nutritional values and negative opinion on organic food).”6

However, cultural psychology should also be significantly considered in the phenomenon of organic food purchasing behavior. This is because aside from a general psychology lens, there remains a gap in understanding that could be attributed to patterns from culture that also heavily affect these attitudes toward choosing healthier food options. If one retains the traditional approach, one will lack the ability to compare patterns of learned and shared behavior that are cumulative and transmitted across generations, as general psychology merely assumes a “psychic universal.” The motivations for organic food purchasing whether for altruistic or egotistical intentions can be further developed through a cultural lens. These varying motivations, emotions, attitudes, and levels of selfishness, can all be experienced differently. Cultural interpretation adds value to choosing healthier alternatives and how humans extract meaning from their food choices. One can discover if these purchasing behaviors are cultural products of the practice. A cultural reanalysis would uniquely add to the meaning-making behind certain societies that contribute to these eating patterns, specifically in individualist and collectivist societies. The cultural dimension of individualist and collectivist communities will allow one to also particularly magnify the effects of their independent and interdependent self-construals, without assuming a universal.

It is argued that individuals from collectivist cultures will tend to choose healthier food options due to altruistic motivations; these motivations foster interdependence as these individuals self-inconvenience themselves in group efforts to improve the environment and better their community. On the other hand, those from individualistic cultures will intend to choose healthier food options because of selfish motivations in which they lead more with independence and follow the pursuit of personal health benefits, the satisfaction of themselves, and the push for national financial success. This claim will be supported by arguments on how organic food purchasing behavior is influenced by responses to environmental concerns versus social norms related to fitness. Additional support will come from research on the role of self-conscious emotions like shame and guilt in shaping self-construal, as well as the greater emphasis on innovation and economic growth typically found in individualist societies.

Arguments

Going Green or Getting Fit?

Responses to organic food purchasing behavior affect environmental concerns in collectivist societies compared to social norms of desiring to stay fit and obtain health benefits in individualistic societies.[8]8 Collectivist societies will resort to environmentally friendly attitudes through horizontal collectivism as an effort to genuinely support sustainability for the improvement of their community.

Horizontal collectivism underscores the interdependence in a group that strives for a common goal with cooperation and equality.[9]9 In collectivist societies where there’s an emphasis on group harmony and collaboration, individuals are more inclined to support environmental initiatives that benefit their communities as a whole rather than focusing on personal interests. This is because a healthy diet leads to a healthier planet, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving animal welfare, supporting sustainable agriculture, conserving natural resources, and more.[10]10 Collectivist individuals are more likely to engage in organic food purchasing behavior for these pro-environmental actions because they desire to cooperate in advancing greater shared goals.[11]11

For example, a survey was conducted in New Zealand by Semenova (2015) which inferred that individualism and collectivism are significant predictors of pro-environmental behavior.[12]12 It was found that the more environmentally active groups from sustainable communities were more collectivist in their value orientation and were more likely to endorse self-transcendent values.11 Collectivist worldviews were positively related to concerns about climate change, willingness to behave in climate-friendly ways, and acceptance of environmental policies.12 Therefore, these types of societies will regard the action of purchasing organic foods as a collective mission, where small individual contributions still matter.11 They are more willing to believe their support towards the environment is a force that is able to be controlled and managed if everyone devotes their part to the cause. If citizens band together through the action of individually choosing healthier food options, they self-inconvenience themselves and put their personal interests aside to reach an overall goal of better sustainability and environmentalism for true altruistic motivations.8

On the other hand, individualist societies are more likely to view these environmental outcomes as intractable.11 These individuals desire nutrient-rich diets for their personal interest and gain, such as obtaining an ideal body shape and conforming to societal beauty standards. Body image is a multidimensional construct that reflects attitudes and perceptions of one’s physical appearance, especially body weight and shape.[13]13 This can also contribute to body dissatisfaction or feeling negatively about one’s appearance. Researchers have found that body dissatisfaction is more pronounced in affluent countries where people are driven by lifestyles more characterized by high levels of individualism and consumption.13 As a result, these individuals may “experience greater pressure to conform to the ‘ideal body’ due to having greater access to body-centered information and images through the media.”13

In addition, the influence of individualistic Western cultures,  and its emphasis on thin bodies for women and buff bodies for men, is on the rise. According to Ekern (2023), women from Eastern collectivist cultures such as China and Croatia reported greater body dissatisfaction when primed with Western “thin-ideal” images.[14]14 People in Western communities struggle with low self-esteem to fit the ideal body shape and size one may observe in consumerist media. Thus, these external factors in individualistic societies motivate selfish individuals to eat more healthily and exercise more for their personal benefit. Overall, this results in buying products from grocery stores that allow them to conform to societal beauty standards, reduce body dissatisfaction, gain higher self-esteem, and simply “feel good” about themselves. Whether it’s going green or getting fit, individualist and collectivist societies differ greatly on the internal motivations of interdependence and independence that they project out into the world through organic food purchasing behavior. As this is based on group efforts for an improved environment or personal gain to stay slim, the incentive behind this phenomenon remains in separate selfless and egotistical categories of reasoning.

The Presence of Shame and Guilt

Emotions contribute a major role in consumption behavior. The presence and experience of self-conscious emotions impact how one construes the self, especially in the forms of shame in collectivist societies and guilt in individualist societies.[15]15 Guilt is a complex feeling one can feel alone however, shame requires other people. Shame appears to be more effective for those who support other-focused ideals and feel as though one is disappointing an entity of in-group people. However, guilt seems to be more effective for those who care about self-image and feeling inferior to others who do purchase organic foods.[16]16

Shame can be characterized as an intense form of embarrassment involved with condemnation of others for breaking a social standard.[17]17 In collectivist cultures, when shoppers buy processed junk foods instead of organic foods, there is accompanying shame especially when faced with the choice to purchase environmentally friendly products. In addition, shame is persuasive for those that care about social norms. Group identification has been theorized as an important factor for people to endorse similar tendencies and strongly relate with their group.[18]18 Therefore, shame is a key motivator for citizens to follow a certain behavior of shared orientation and when there is a threat to a social bond. They are often provoked by perceptions of what other people think they ought to do.[19]19 For example, especially on the topic of environmental concern (EC), a study was conducted by Nielsen et al. (2024), which observed that eco-shame led Danish participants in a medium EC group “wanting to be more sustainable or reflecting desires to pro-environmental behaviors in order to avoid being below average in terms of sustainable conduct.”19 Despite the Danish participants identifying from an individualistic culture, being primed with ecological shame has promoted these individuals to adopt more ecological concerns. This is due to being judged by other members and not following social norms for the greater benefit of the group itself. Therefore, when individuals from collectivist cultures don’t participate in organic food purchasing behavior — and purchase junk foods instead — they are afraid of feeling shame and judged by others as a moral failure. They are not seen as interdependent through personal inconvenience in group efforts to support environmental initiatives, which may be viewed as damaging to the ingroup’s reputation. Individuals are more concerned with fitting in with the rest of the group and charitably working towards a common goal to avoid this negative feeling.

On the contrary, guilt is an alternative negative emotion associated with not participating in organic food purchasing behavior, particularly in individualistic societies. Guilt is a feeling that one has done a wrong deed, and in a sense has committed a moral transgression.17 Individualistic customers feel a sense of guilt when choosing processed foods because they feel they are engaging in wrongdoing solely for themselves. Citizens place an emphasis on personal responsibility for their health and well-being;when they perceive they may have failed to meet their own expectations, they may experience guilt as a result of not living up to these standards. For example, when independent people expect to eat healthier, but purchase potato chips instead of a fruit cup they feel they are not taking adequate care of themselves by consuming these unhealthy foods. Furthermore, these cultures focus primarily on personal achievement and success, including maintaining a healthy lifestyle. As a result, individuals may internalize societal expectations to excel in various aspects of their lives such as staying fit and conforming to natural beauty standards. When they believe they have fallen short of their own greatest potential in having an ideal body shape, they are more willing to participate in behaviors of healthy eating that overcome these negative feelings.15 Individualistic cultures foster comparison in each other to strive for personal improvement. This may lead to feelings of wrongdoing if individuals perceive that they are not measuring up to the health and wellness levels of their peers or societal ideals. This forces them to want to engage in selfish organic purchasing food behavior and empower themselves to the standards of others.

According to Eom et al. (2016), individualist cultures such as the United States respond more to environmental concern overall compared to collectivist cultures such as Japan which respond more to social norms about the environment.8 This sheds light on how there is a greater value on self-expression of internal attributes for U.S. citizens, whereas there is a greater value in “fitting in” for Japanese citizens. Thus, individualistic societies follow more strongly with their own egotistical beliefs and attitudes. For this reason, failing to fulfill this sense of self-worth leads to guilt, compared to letting down others leading to shame.8

Priority of Economic Growth

Contrasting priorities of innovation and economic growth are placed on these different societies. Individualist societies are primed for higher productivity and long-run growth which is linked to esteemed social status. This fuels the need for financial incentives on an individual level from the profit of organic foods and high-end pricey grocery stores.[20]20

Due to individualist culture’s prized values of personal control, autonomy, and individual success, these societies “will promote economic development by sharpening distinctive incentives to invest, innovate, and accumulate wealth.”20 This is contrary to collectivism’s altruistic emphasis on loyalty and cohesion for mutual and shared gain. By attaching achievement to self-reliance on a personal level, individualism is able to put entrepreneurship and productivity at the forefront of consumerism. Encouraging citizens to stand out and maintain ingenuity not only allows monetary reward to reign supreme, but also rewards social status as well[21]21

From Gorodnichenko & Roland’s study (2011), they surveyed IBM employees from 30 different countries of varying corporate cultures around the world.21 They used a baseline measure of individualistic culture as a set of scores developed by Dutch sociologist Geert Hofstede (known as Hofstede’s index of individualism) compared to variables such as income per worker and the innovation performance index. They found that there was a strong positive correlation between individualism and measures of long-run growth and innovation due to a causal effect. It also can be observed that when countries become wealthier, their cultures seem to become more individualistic.21 Thus, independent societies are linked to greater economic growth in explanation of their selfish motivations and less likelihood of self-inconveniencing themselves when it comes to organic food purchasing behavior.

Individualist cultures also tend to harness an entrepreneurial mindset that encourages people to take risks and maintain wealth. Economic growth provides opportunities for starting businesses and achieving financial success which is why organic food price tags are set very high.[22]22 Despite this, individuals are more willing to buy these products to preserve their health and well-being for a few extra dollars. Consequently, high-end grocery stores such as Whole Foods and Erewhon are on the rise where organic foods are absurdly overpriced. Furthermore, economic advancement is also associated with lifestyle well-being. This includes higher incomes, better living standards, and access to upgraded goods and services. Individuals will place higher priority on material success and the pursuit of a comfortable livelihood. In addition, purchasing high-priced organic foods contribute to national financial growth which provides a competitive advantage in the global economy.[23]23 It allows individualist countries to uphold and enhance their position in the world marketplace to maintain economic superiority. Through Western culture’s massive efforts in hiked-up prices, expensive grocery stores, more job opportunities, and fixation on consumer success, organic food purchasing behavior is further due to egotistical motivations in individualist societies than collectivist societies.

Conclusion

Summary

Humans need food to survive, but more importantly, the type of food matters. Eating is one of our primary motives in life, yet there are many intricate layers of cultural influence to it. With factors such as taste, value, quality, health benefits, sustainability, economic growth, and more, organic food purchases are seemingly sweeping the nation. It also depends on the type of cultural environment that surrounds these choices we make for ourselves. Organic food purchasing behavior is a reflection of our societies and the motivations we hold internally.

The problem with viewing this purchasing epidemic through a general psychological lens is that it lacks the ability to compare patterns of learned and shared behavior that are cumulative and transmitted across generations while assuming a “psychic universal” and not recognizing that cultural analysis adds personal meaning to our food choices. The main thesis was that individuals from collectivist cultures intend to choose healthier food options due to altruistic motivations in which they foster interdependence and will self-inconvenience themselves in group efforts to improve the environment and better their community. On the other hand, individuals from individualist cultures intend to choose healthier food options because of egotistical motivations in which they lead with independence more and will follow the pursuit of personal health benefits, conforming to beauty standards, and push for national financial success. This is addressed by the arguments of responses to environmental concerns vs. social norms of staying fit, the presence and experience of self-conscious emotions of shame and guilt impacting how one construes the self, and differences in innovation and economic growth that are placed with higher priority in individualist societies.

Cultural Limitations

Despite these compelling arguments, it may have fallen flat due to remaining sources of cultural limitations. For example, in the home field disadvantage, researchers have the capability to essentialize, or portray someone in terms of stereotypes or supposedly intrinsic traits, and to pathologize, or treat someone as psychologically abnormal.[24]24 Without the acknowledgement of other cultural positions, one is highly at risk of shortchanging others and misattributing them, regardless of good intentions. One category of the home field disadvantage that may have been violated is the concept of homogeneity vs. heterogeneity, as these individualistic and collectivist cultures are grouped together and essentialized into being characterized as humans of identical views of altruism and selfishness, but this may not be the case.[25]25 There could be many individual differences and not everyone may fall into the logic of the assumed organic food purchasing behavior based on these basic societal norms. For instance, societies could be influenced by factors of personal income or individual eating habits and diets, which pokes holes in the argument on how individuals can have similar patterns when it comes to organic food purchasing behavior. Another category violated was the theory of regression towards the mean. Observing buying patterns in individualistic societies, especially with the presence of more trendy grocery stores with higher pricing, unfairly highlights individual behaviors in which purchasing is biased in the West. Organic foods could be geared more towards WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations while leaving others out that don’t fit this description.[26]26 Therefore, measures that are geared towards these WEIRD people that influence purchasing behavior could be higher income (and better education to obtain this) to buy the pricey foods, closer to grocery stores in location, enhanced agriculture for fresher ingredients, etc.

Furthermore, another limitation is the idea of the cultural attribution fallacy.[27]27 This is due to making cultural interpretations regarding a phenomenon of differences between groups without the proper empirical evidence. For instance, this exploration could be done by conducting satisfaction surveys to factually observe customers’ contentment with purchasing organic foods or even measuring behaviors on how many minutes one spends reading the packaging of organic foods. The aforementioned arguments may fail to possess concrete evidence that is measurable to specifically compare these purchasing patterns in different societies. There may also be challenges of confounding variables that could have an effect on organic food purchasing behavior as well that could correlate with the cultural dimension of individualism and collectivism, such as age, location, organic food accessibility, dieting habits, social media influence, and more, that may also influence these overall internal altruistic and egotistical motivations.

Future Directions

For future directions,  to prevent these cultural limitations and strengthen the argument at hand, necessary changes would need to be made. Specific empirical evidence or measurements would aid my argument and combat the cultural attribution fallacy, such as calculating how much money people spend on organic foods at the grocery store compared to other cultures, surveying if buyers agree more with statements of sustainability or health, or interviewing shoppers about their motivations to purchase these foods, for instance, in addition to satisfaction surveys and package observation timing.

Avoiding stereotypes and automatic grouping would be necessary to resist the home-field disadvantage. One could also expand their scope of understanding various collectivistic and individualistic cultures as they are not all the same from the homogeneity vs. heterogeneity of the home-field disadvantage. For example, in individualist societies, not all of them have the means necessary to access organic foods such as high-end grocery stores specifically found in the United States or possess ways to always incorporate healthy eating into their daily lives.[28]28 Additionally, it may be compelling to also observe the opposing purchasing behaviors of processed and junk foods and compare these findings with the organic food purchasing behaviors, to see if this type of consumption decreases and matches the motivations of various attitudes, norms, and values in the arguments made. It is within these reasons that food is a reflection of who we are and the saying proves to be right that we truly are what we eat.

nurj_title: Time to BeReal!: The Effects of BeReal Usage and Gender on Self-Esteem
text:
Time to BeReal!: The Effects of BeReal Usage and Gender on Self-Esteem

Emily E. Chow

Department of Psychology, Northwestern University

PSYCH 205: Research Methods in Psychology

Dr. Ben Gorvine

November 3, 2022

Introduction

The widespread emergence of social media has been known to have a significant effect on the well-being of adolescent users. While there are many positives to the use of such platforms including staying connected with friends and family members, convenient communication, networking, publicizing businesses, and promoting worthwhile causes, there are also many downfalls to the use of social media.

On platforms such as Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, Twitter, VSCO, TikTok, and more, teenagers and young adults nowadays are susceptible to certain detrimental impacts on one’s own self-esteem as this can lead to results of depression and anxiety. The root cause of such poor mental health is due to the natural tendency to compare ourselves to others, whether intentionally or not. With the implementation of photo-sharing in a larger social realm, it is no surprise that adolescents often compare the number of likes, comments, and followers and even body image to other users. This comparison may make one feel inferior or inadequate to others. In addition, it’s important to observe other factors in which social media may affect one’s self-esteem including gender and how males and females are differently impacted by these effects. Females are observed to place a higher value on social comparison and evaluation than men do.

As technology and social media are ever-evolving, there are new platforms on the rise. One specific app gaining rapid popularity is called BeReal. BeReal is an attempt to combat the artificialness of social media by allowing users to post unfiltered photos of themselves once per day to show what they’re doing in real-time in a two-minute window after receiving a notification from the app. Once a user posts, they are able to see other people’s “BeReals.” It encourages people to be their more authentic selves and decreases the tendency to compare themselves on an unrealistic scale.

Literature Review

Social Media Usage and Self-Esteem

Previous research has shown that social media runs the risk of a decline in one’s mental health. While self-esteem increases from adolescence into young adulthood, it can be influenced by environmental-stimuli that they surround themselves with.[0] On these social media platforms, there is an ongoing battle between a teenager’s outlook on success and failure.1 Furthermore, excessive worry about other people’s opinions concerning oneself is associated with clinical symptoms such as depression.[1]

It is this social comparison and care for what others think that allows one to note the flaws in themselves and what they don’t have. The use of social media has become a growing addiction that acts as a plug into the outside world. For example, general Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram use have been linked to lower self-esteem among college students.1

All in all, a social media user enters this ongoing cycle of social comparison, social feedback, and reflection. Whether online or offline, there is a constant decrease in self-esteem and self-image. While undergoing major life changes, the sensitivity to social evaluation creates a negative outlook even during the time of significant self-concept development.2 With the newest platform of BeReal, it is skeptical to believe this app can combat the dilemma of social comparison hiding behind an empty promise of an “unfiltered” experience as a disguise. If one spends more time on BeReal, one will have lower levels of self-esteem due to social comparison of real-time events and feedback.

Gender and Self-Esteem

The lens of gender is a significant perspective to observe when evaluating social media usage and self-esteem. Low self-esteem drives behavior that craves social feedback and previous studies have demonstrated that this motivation for using social media is different among genders, specifically male and female.[2]

Significantly, it was found that women consider their activities on social media more important and have greater value on social media feedback than men do.3 Women are also more likely to engage in social feedback and social comparison on these platforms in areas such as attractiveness which lowers self-esteem. On the contrary, social media was shown to have a more positive outlook for men. Men place less value on social feedback from online and rather seek other ways to increase social belonging when they have low self-esteem than women.3 This disparity of outlook on social comparison addresses compelling interpretations of gender and self-esteem. The relationship between social media usage and low self-esteem may be more prevalent in women than men.3 If men and women use social media, then women would be more likely to socially compare themselves and have lower self-esteem than men.

Methods

Participants

The participants of this study were chosen by convenience sampling in which a survey was sent out by college students of a ‘Research Methods in Psychology’ course to people that they knew and were the easiest to obtain while close to hand. This also led to snowball sampling in which the participants chosen by the researchers then recruited other people they knew. There were 110 participants (83 women and 25 men) that took the questionnaire. The participants were predominantly college students between ages 18 and 22 who use the app BeReal. They were not compensated and they had the free will to cooperate if they would like as they also had to fill out a consent form before accessing the survey questions.

Materials

The survey was conducted on Qualtrics, which the participants had access to with electronic devices such as a tablet, computer, or phone. With a survey, researchers present questions with a relatively narrow focus to the participants, which they can complete on their own. The questionnaire for data collection allows them to respond freely or choose from a preselected set of options. While surveys are advantageous for being efficient, economical, anonymous, flexible, and effective for large sample sizes, there are also disadvantages like bias, response fatigue, and social desirability. The link to the Qualtrics survey regarding BeReal usage and self-esteem was shared via text, group chats, or social media platforms with the participants.

Procedure

The design of the study was an experimental method in which an experimental group and a control group were used. The experimental group includes the participants who received the experimental treatment which were the people who spend a lot of time on BeReal. The control group includes the participants who do not receive the experimental treatment which is the people who do not spend a lot of time on BeReal. There were also independent and dependent variables. An independent variable is a factor that is manipulated or varied in an experiment and a dependent variable is the response of interest that the researcher thinks is influenced by the independent variable. For the hypothesis examining social media usage and self-esteem, the independent variable was participants' frequency of using and posting on BeReal, while the dependent variable was their resulting levels of self-esteem. For the hypothesis of gender and self-esteem, the independent variable was whether the participant was a male or female and the dependent variable was levels of self-esteem of using social media.

Therefore, a survey was imperative to collect this type of data in an anonymous and efficient way with a large sample size. Various survey questions on social media usage and self-esteem were evaluated on different types of likert scales. Some examples of sample items in the survey was “I post my BeReal daily” on a scale of 1 = Never, 2 = Rarely, 3 = Sometimes, 4 = Often, 5 = Always, or “I often feel insecure about who I really am” on a scale of 6=Strongly Agree, 5=Agree, 4=Slightly Agree, 3=Slightly Disagree, 2=Disagree, 1=Strongly Disagree (See Appendix). In addition, some sample items were reverse scores to avoid participants carelessly selecting the same response for each question.

Results

In regards to the relationship between general social media usage and self-esteem, there are significant results to note. Out of 110 participants (n = 110), the average score out of 5 (lower scores meaning lower levels of BeReal use and higher scores meaning higher levels of BeReal use) was 3.2432 (SD = 0.60598) (See Table 1 in References) with a minimum of 1.50 and a maximum of 4.63. For general self-esteem, the average score out of 6 (lower scores meaning lower levels of general self-esteem and higher scores meaning higher levels of general self-esteem) was 4.5714 (SD = 0.71860) (See Table 1 in References) with a minimum of 2.57 and a maximum of 6.00. In addition, according to the correlation table, there was a Pearson correlation between the frequency of BeReal use and general self-esteem of 0.126 which was not statistically significant. Similarly, there were no statistically significant correlations to social self-esteem and physical appearance self-esteem being 0.112 and 0.006 respectively. The Pearson correlations being close to 0 indicate that there is no strong or meaningful relationship between frequency of BeReal usage and general self-esteem. Although the association is weak, the statistics are still positive which could reveal that there could be a direct relationship between the two variables in which as frequency/usage increases, self-esteem increases, however, this information is only slightly compelling.

Concerning the factor of gender with BeReal usage and self-esteem, there are also further essential results to emphasize. Out of 110 participants, there were 83 females and 25 males. It is important to note that there were not enough individuals who identified as non-binary to do a group comparison. For general self-esteem, the average within the women (n = 83) was 4.5215 (SD = 0.71513) and the average score within the men (n = 25) was 4.7771 (SD = 0.65476) (See Table 2 in References). Significantly to note, the means and standard deviations were also higher for men than women in similar scales of general self-esteem including social self-esteem and physical appearance self-esteem. T-tests between gender and BeReal frequency and general self-esteem were also performed to determine its inferential statistics. An independent samples t-test was conducted to compare the frequency of BeReal use between men (n = 25) and women (n = 83). The t-value was 0.256, indicating a difference in usage frequency between the two groups (t(106) = 0.256, p = 0.798). For general self-esteem, the t-value was also not equal to 0 which exemplified a difference in general self-esteem between men and women (t(106) = -1.596, p = 0.113). The p-value was marginally significant as it had an effect size of 0.36. This indicates a notable relationship between gender and levels of self-esteem as there were found to be differences between means of the sample groups that were greater than 0 which goes against the null hypothesis that there isn’t a difference (See Table 3 in References).

Discussion

The relationship between BeReal frequency usage and general self-esteem and the relationship between gender and general self-esteem were tested in this study. There are critical interpretations to be discussed for both correlations.

For BeReal frequency usage and general self-esteem, it was found to be surprising that the mean frequency was moderate (M = 3.2432) compared to the mean of general self-esteem which was also moderately high (M = 4.5714). In addition, it is even more compelling to note that the Pearson correlation was indicated to be 0.126 which is a weak, nonlinear, and positive relationship that was not statistically significant. This demonstrates that there isn’t a strong relationship between the two variables, although there is a slight positive correlation that if BeReal frequency usage increases, self-esteem increases as well, which is unexpected. This, this goes against my original hypothesis that when frequency increases, self-esteem would decrease. This concludes that social media use potentially has a smaller effect on self-esteem than one would’ve thought. It suggests that the relationship between social media use and self-esteem may be due more to person-specific factors such as individual susceptibilities, uses, personality, etc.1 Adolescents may differ in their susceptibility and interpretation to social comparison because of individual sensitivity and bias. The way in which an adolescent receives this social feedback can be subjective. For example, while one may view social comparison as envy which can decrease self-esteem, another may see it as inspiration which can increase self-esteem.[3] It depends on the way the user visualizes their social feedback and analyzes it. One cannot ignore person-specific effects as positive or negative observations of social comparison on social media can lead to positive or negative reactions to one’s self-esteem.4 Contrary to my hypothesis, there is reason to believe that BeReal frequency of use and self-esteem are not as related as initially predicted.

Regarding the relationship between gender and self-esteem, these results were especially crucial in analyzing. It was compelling to see that the average score of general self-esteem for women (M = 4.5215) is lower than the average score for men (M = 4.7771). According to the findings, this indicates that women would generally have lower levels of self-esteem compared to men by a small margin. Furthermore, with the independent samples t-test examination, it was crucial to discover that the t-value did not equal 0 (t(106) = -1.596) meaning it goes against the null hypothesis that there is no difference between the two groups of men and women. Alternatively, because there was a non-zero value, and with marginal significance, there is evidence that there is a difference between these two groups and their self-esteem levels. Although the effect size is not an immensely strong finding due to it only being marginally significant (p = 0.11), it is still guiding information that there is a relationship between the two. Thus, the results from this study support my initial hypothesis that women will be more likely to socially compare themselves on social media and have lower self-esteem. Such gender differences can be due to how social media is used between men and women. For example, men were found to usually use social media for “real-life” social interactions which facilitates more communication-driven motivation for opening these apps, while women use social media to rely more on social feedback from others which promotes social comparison and analyzing attractiveness.3 This can also lead to poor mental health and lower self-esteem by perceiving constructs of self-image, body dysmorphia, mental distress, depression, anxiety, etc.3 Even as a result, women with low self-esteem will turn to social media to boost their self-concept which can potentially make matters worse.3 As discussed in my prior finding, it is also still important to note that self-esteem is subjective and feedback can be perceived in individual ways. Other factors such as culture, age, and how self-esteem is assessed can also play into these gender differences.1 Nonetheless, there is compelling evidence that women are more linked to lower self-esteem than men due to their susceptibility to social comparison on social media.

There are some limitations to the study that are essential to indicate as well. One limitation is a potentially small sample size (n = 110). Although this isn’t a poor number, there is always a preference towards more participants which will make generalizability better for a large target population. Another limitation is the uneven distribution of men and women when comparing gender and self-esteem. Since the sample size of men (n = 25) and women (n = 83) had an important disparity, it is difficult to generalize these numbers to greater populations of each gender. This significant difference may make the data not as representative as it could be, however, this could be because it may be tougher to get men to participate in research than women. Furthermore, a limitation of sampling is also an issue. The methods of convenience sampling and snowball sampling used may not be the best for being representative or generalizable. This can lead to biases and not being reflective of true effects among a population of interest. In order to make the study better for future research, one would recommend obtaining a larger population with an evenly distributed gender pool of participants. This would also be effective with random sampling or stratified sampling to get the most representative groups for generalizability.

All in all, there were many meaningful findings from this study. BeReal is more likely “real” and “unfiltered” than one would’ve thought. Due to the frequency of BeReal use and general self-esteem not having a significant relationship, it may not just be another social media app in which social comparison is continuously fostered. Instead, it could be an app that allows one’s own authentic and genuine self to be seen. On the other hand, gender differences in self-esteem still seem to be prevalent as women are found to have lower levels of self-esteem due to social comparison and feedback. While one has to be aware of the subjectivity of self-esteem and the perception of it, the issue of women having poorer well-being still runs its risks.

When conducting this study, the process of making our research question and finalizing a process ourselves was truly engaging and effective. It allowed me to take control of what I wanted to learn more about and have a say in the types of factors in an experimental design. One thing I learned was how specific the questions need to be in the survey to obtain a certain focus for our study. For example, being in the social media usage group for creating survey questions, we were constantly editing and revising our questions so they would produce responses that we intended to analyze. We finally came to the two scales of frequency of BeReal use and approach to using BeReal. I also found it interesting how there needed to be reversed scored Likert scales which I did not know before as I never really thought about how effective this actually is to prevent skews and outliers in the data.

nurj_title: Predicting Employees' Remote Work Policy Recommendations: Disruption, Organizational Support, and Positive Transformation During the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Predicting Employees’ Remote Work Policy Recommendations: Disruption, Organizational Support, and Positive Transformation During the COVID-19 Pandemic

Ainsley Lauer

Introduction

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, national health organizations across the globe mandated lockdowns and stay-at-home orders, forcing millions of employees to shift to remote work almost overnight. In the United States alone, the number of employees who worked remotely tripled from 2019 to 2021, an increase of almost 19 million people.[0] Often, the remote work necessitated by the pandemic disrupted employees’ lives and work, upending their established routines. This disruption in routine was associated with worse adjustment to remote work[1] and feelings of depletion.[2] Over time, however, employees adjusted to this “new normal”; they learned to balance well-being and home demands while productively working from home.[3]

Today, rates of COVID-19 remain on a steady decline from their peak in 2022. Lockdowns have ended and organizations must now decide whether to bring their employees back to the office, stay remote, or employ a hybrid option. Overwhelmingly, employers favor in-person policies, with most organizations planning to require a return to the office by the end of 2024.[4] At the same time, almost all U.S. employees — up to 98% — say they want to work remotely at least part of the time,[5] likely because they perceive the benefits of remote work, which include improved performance, greater organizational commitment, and increased job satisfaction,[6] to outweigh any drawbacks. Thus, when companies implement return-to-office mandates, employees threaten to leave, a tension that three quarters of human resources managers believe has caused conflict in their organizations.[7] This also presents a problem for recruitment; since employees prioritize remote options when looking for jobs, requiring in-office work may cause significant talent loss.[8]

This conflict is further complicated by evidence showing that working from home may come with significant disadvantages. Research findings on the utility of remote work are equivocal, noting that it can boost productivity but also increase stress, burnout, and loneliness[9] and decrease well-being and engagement.[10] Likewise, research finds that remote work increases job satisfaction and performance for some employees but decreases these factors for others.[11]

The current literature does not explain these conflicting findings, nor does it clarify why most employees seem to prefer remote work while others prefer to work in-person. Van Zoonen and colleagues offer one clue to why preferences may differ, reporting that the more disruption remote employees experienced, the worse they adjusted to this new work style.[12] Employees' experiences with remote work also seem to vary as a function of perceived organizational support. For example, professionals were less likely to leave their jobs during pandemic-related remote work if they perceived a higher degree of support from their organizations.[13] Finally, to understand remote work outcomes, it is necessary to consider evidence that experiencing adverse circumstances often causes positive transformational growth.[14] As a whole, it is likely that employees’ experiences with disruption, organizational support, and positive transformation would impact the remote work preferences they have today, but these relationships have not yet been examined. This represents a significant theoretical and practical gap. For organizational scholars, examining these relationships may help disentangle conflicting findings relating to remote work preferences and outcomes. For organizational leaders, understanding employees’ work preferences is critical for making important policy decisions.

The purpose of this study is to address this gap. Specifically, we examine how employees’ experiences over the pandemic shape the recommendations they have for remote work policy. From a sample of more than 200 employees who worked remotely over the pandemic, we first evaluate the relationship between disruption and positive transformational growth, and whether this relationship was moderated by perceived organizational support. We also evaluate the relationship between positive transformation and remote work policy choices, hypothesizing that the more employees were positively transformed by the disruption to remote work, the more likely they will be to advocate for remote work policies. These relationships are illustrated in Figure 1. Understanding how employees’ unique experiences during the pandemic shape their preferences today can help organizations make decisions about the remote work policies that are best for their workforces.

Literature Review

Disruption

The events of the COVID-19 pandemic constituted a massive disruption to many employees’ work practices and routines. Drawing on work by van Zoonen and colleagues, we define disruptions in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic as changes in routine necessitated by the shift to remote work.[15] Routines, or stable patterns of everyday behaviors,[16] are associated with several important aspects of well-being, such as positive mood,[17] job satisfaction and work concentration,[18] and reduced depression, anxiety, stress, and negative affect.[19] Therefore, routines may have been essential for supporting remote workers during the stress of the pandemic.

Unfortunately, many employees’ routines were significantly disrupted by the shift to remote work. Increased stress, changing work locations, and reduced in-person interactions all presented disruptions.[20] Work hours increased; at the beginning of the pandemic, remote workers worked significantly more than those who worked in-person.[21] Communication with coworkers became entirely virtual, becoming more siloed and less synchronized.[22] The home office also proved to be a distracting environment, with family members often unintentionally interrupting remote workspaces,[23] and even those without family at home often had new distractions from housework and leisure activities.[24] These interruptions to remote employees’ work routines increased work-family conflict and emotional exhaustion while hampering performance.[25]

Even employees who had previous experience working remotely may have been subject to significant disruption to their routines and work practices. The type of remote work that employees engaged in during the pandemic was different from previous remote work in that it was less flexible, unexpected, and fraught with the stress of a global health crisis.[26] The freedom which many enjoyed while working remotely before the pandemic turned into greater intensity and poorer work-life balance when the pandemic began because of demands that employees be “always on.”[27] Therefore, nearly every remote worker — from remote work novices to practiced teleworkers — had to adjust to an altered work environment and shifting routines.

While disruption to routine had a significant impact on employees’ experiences with remote work, this impact was not the same for every employee. Rather, a variety of risk and protective factors may have affected this relationship, making the effects of disruption more severe for some and less so for others. One particularly salient factor is perceived organizational support, or employees’ perceptions that their employers value their contributions, care about their well-being, and provide sufficient technical, managerial, and emotional aid.[28]

Perceived Organizational Support

Perceived organizational support (POS) is defined as employees’ “global beliefs concerning the extent to which the organization values their contributions and cares about their well-being.”[29] POS has been found to reduce absenteeism,[30] improve employees’ attitudes towards their organization,[31] and increase job satisfaction, positive mood, and performance.[32] Perceptions of a fair work culture, support from one’s supervisor, and favorable working conditions are necessary conditions for employees to feel supported by their organizations.[33]

Organizational support served a protective role against the stressors of remote work over the pandemic,[34] which ranged from work-family conflict, problems with technology, inadequate workspaces, and isolation,[35] as well as various mental health problems.[36] Fortunately, many organizations provided sufficient support for their employees. Most remote workers felt listened to by their supervisors[37] and believed that their organizations prioritized their health, well-being, and safety.[38] In fact, remote workers perceived greater organizational support, on average, than those who worked in-person.[39] This support boosted remote workers’ well-being, delivering a wide range of benefits from increased feelings of engagement[40] to a more successful transition to remote work.[41] This evidence suggests that POS was a principal factor in shaping remote workers’ pandemic experiences.

Positive Transformation

Counterintuitively, it may be that the challenges created by disruption and buffered by POS led to positive outcomes. Supporting this hypothesis is the fact that many employees viewed the shift to remote work in a positive light: in fact, 56% of remote workers believed that working at home was positively transformative and 61% reported that they would continue to work from home even if remote work was no longer required.[42] These findings may be explained by literature suggesting that people often grow after facing adversity. A wide variety of challenging circumstances, from injury and illness to bereavement, can trigger this “adversarial growth”[43] because they encourage people to try to derive meaning from their circumstances and thus grow in a positive direction.[44] The challenges presented by remote work were no exception. Conceptualizing one’s shift as a positive transformation may have also served an adaptive purpose, as positively appraising events protects against stress, plays a key role in resilience, and is associated with effective emotion regulation.[45] Thus, employees may have used the benefits of positive appraisal to counter the many challenges presented by the shift to remote work.

Whether the transition to remote work was a negative experience reappraised as positive or simply a positive experience, many employees viewed this shift as a positive transformation. People who viewed the shift to remote work as positively transformative are likely to want to continue working remotely, so variation in positive transformation may help explain some of the differences in employees’ remote work preferences.

Hypotheses

Disruption and Positive Transformation

The negative effects of disruption in routine became particularly salient after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. From changing employees’ work locations to reducing face-to-face communication, pandemic restrictions forced employees to alter their established routines on an unprecedented scale.[46] This disruption may have had significant negative consequences; for example, the more disruption remote workers experienced, the worse they adjusted to this work style.[47] This is not surprising when considering that disruption to routine has been linked to increased depletion, decreased work engagement, and reduced goal progress,[48] as well as greater stress, depression, and anxiety.[49] Disruption also affected physical health by reducing the amount that people exercised[50] and was associated with greater overall distress.[51] Therefore, disruption to routine likely explains some of the variation in the quality of employees’ remote work experiences.

While many studies highlight the adverse outcomes of pandemic-related disruption to routine, a parallel set of findings reveals that some fared positively after the shift to remote work. The latter findings align with research demonstrating that people often overcome challenging circumstances and even benefit from them. Adversarial growth is a common response to challenging or traumatic events, ranging from illness to witnessing violence.[52] It may reflect a positive reappraisal of adverse events, which can help buffer against the effects of stress.[53]

Since the disruption to routine that resulted from the shift to remote work greatly challenged employees, and people who experience challenging circumstances often reappraise these challenges as positively transformative, we predict:

Hypothesis 1: Employees who experienced greater disruption will have experienced greater positive transformation than those who experienced less disruption.

The Interactive Effects of Routine Disruptions and Perceived Organizational Support

The disruption presented by the shift to remote work was challenging for most employees, but the effects of this disruption differed between individuals. As noted earlier, studies have found that the shift to remote work is associated with both increased and decreased job satisfaction,[54] and that the shift increased performance for some but reduced performance for others.[55] We posit that the relationship between disruptions and positive transformation may vary as a function of organizational support.

Specifically, POS likely buffered the negative effects of disruption and enhanced the positive effects of the shift. Feeling supported by one’s organization causes employees to feel more favorably about their work,[56] be more satisfied, and perform better.[57] Therefore, employees who experienced greater organizational support may have better coped with the challenges of remote work and appraised the challenges as opportunities for growth rather than hindrances. For this reason, we predict:

Hypothesis 2: The positive relationship between disruption and positive transformation will be stronger for people who perceived greater organizational support.

Positive Transformation and Policy Recommendation

In today’s post-lockdown world, organizations must now decide whether to bring their employees back to the office or stay remote. Critical to making these decisions is understanding how employees’ experiences with remote work shape their preferences today. It seems that employees who had a better experience working remotely — who experienced the shift to remote work as a positive transformation — would be more likely to advocate for policies that allow partial or fully remote work than those who had a more negative remote working experience. Therefore, we predict:

Hypothesis 3: Employees who experienced greater positive transformation will be more likely to recommend a policy that requires more remote work.

Methods

Sample

Our sample consisted of 261 employees who worked remotely during the pandemic. Just over half (55%) of our sample were women and 45% were men. Participants also represented a variety of age groups. Most participants (89%) identified as White or Caucasian, 4% as Black or African American, 4% as Asian or Pacific Islander, and 2% as belonging to other or multiple racial or ethnic groups. Finally, about 39% of participants had at least one child under 18 in the house during the pandemic, 12% lived with at least one child above the age of 18, and 82% lived with at least one other adult. In total, 88% of participants lived with at least one other person during the pandemic.

Procedure

We used Prolific, an online research platform, to recruit 300 participants who worked remotely during the pandemic. Participants completed a two-wave survey on the online platform SurveyMonkey. The first questionnaire included demographic questions and measured disruption to routine, perceived organizational support, and several control variables. The second questionnaire evaluated positive transformational growth and remote work policy choices.

Following the recommendations of DeSimone and Harms[58] and Ward and Meade,[59] we used multiple procedures to clean the data. Specifically, we eliminated responses from individuals who answered attention-check questions incorrectly, those who completed a survey in an unusually short amount of time, or those who provided the same responses for more than 15 questions in a row. This review yielded responses from 283 of the 300 initial survey participants. Of these, 264 (93%) responded to the second survey. After we cleaned the data from the second survey and combined responses from both surveys, our final dataset contained 261 matched pairs of high-quality responses.

Finally, we conducted a thematic analysis of the qualitative data, drawing inspiration from (though not exactly replicating) Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework.[60] First, after reading the qualitative responses several times, we identified recurring themes which we used for the initial codes. Then, we aggregated any initial codes that had significant overlap, refining them until all codes were distinct and clearly defined. The themes identified in this qualitative analysis were used to support and explain the quantitative findings.

Measures

To measure disruption in routine, we used a nine-item scale developed by van Zoonen and colleagues.[61] Cronbach’s alpha for this scale was 0.90. We measured perceived organizational support with six items adapted from Armeli et al..[62] This scale was also reliable with a Cronbach’s alpha value of 0.92. We evaluated positive transformation by adapting an eight-item scale from George and colleagues.[63] This scale was not designed to measure one latent construct but rather to evaluate several distinct areas of positive transformational change. However, it was also reliable, with a Cronbach’s alpha value of 0.91. The high internal consistency suggests that each area of positive transformation may be part of a larger construct.

We also measured policy recommendations by asking participants to imagine that they were the CEO of an organization, deciding whether to require in-person attendance from their employees or provide a remote or hybrid option. Participants could choose between seven options, ranging from most remote to least remote. For example, the most remote option required employees to work remotely 100% of the time, and the least remote option required employees to work almost always in the office, with remote work only on a case-by-case basis. Participants could also select “Other” and write a different remote work policy.

Finally, we measured six control variables: age, gender, race, number of other individuals in the home, segmentation preference, and job security. We asked people to report the number of other individuals living in their home during the pandemic because living with others increased distractions for remote workers, which impaired productivity and increased stress (Bergefurt et al., 2022). Therefore, this variable may have markedly shaped their work experiences. We also included a single-item measure of perceived job security because fear of losing one’s job may have amplified the negative effects of the switch to remote work.[64] Finally, we evaluated segmentation preference, or the extent to which individuals prefer to keep their home and work lives separate, with a four-item scale adapted from Kreiner.[65] We chose to measure segmentation preference because those who preferred high segmentation may have experienced greater emotional exhaustion and reduced work-life balance when remote work granted them greater job control, as compared to their colleagues who preferred less segmentation.[66] Thus, segmentation preference may have been linked to remote work adjustment and perceptions of disruption.

Results

Means, standard deviations, bivariate correlations, and reliability statistics for the dataset are summarized in Table 1.

There was a significant negative correlation between disruption and organizational support (r = -0.15, p < 0.05), such that those who perceived greater organizational support experienced the shift to remote work as less disruptive. Disruption (r = 0.15, p < 0.05) was also positively correlated with policy choice. Finally, positive transformation and policy choice were strongly and negatively correlated (r = -0.43, p < 0.01): the more positive an employees’ shift to remote work, the more likely they were to recommend a policy that allowed more remote work.

We computed simple linear regressions to test each hypothesis. Hypothesis 1 predicted that disruption and positive transformation would be positively related. This relationship was not supported (t = 1.28, p = 0.20).

Hypothesis 2, which predicted that organizational support would moderate the relationship between disruption and positive transformation, was not supported (t = 0.33, p = 0.74). However, post-hoc analyses (Table 2) showed that organizational support was directly associated with greater positive transformation (t = 3.26, p < 0.01).

Hypothesis 3, which predicted that greater positive transformation would be associated with a more remote policy choice, was supported (t = -7.45, p < 0.001). Table 3 shows the results of this regression analysis.

Finally, to interpret these results, we examined participants’ responses to an open-ended question asking them to provide a rationale for their policy choice. This analysis revealed 10 themes which are described in Table 4.

Analyses revealed that flexibility (r = -0.183, p < 0.01), in-person meetings (r = -0.139, p < 0.05), and cost (r = -0.163, p < 0.01) were significantly and negatively correlated with policy choice, such that those who advocated for a more remote policy were more likely to give these explanations. On the other hand, productivity (r = 0.151, p < 0.05) and teamwork (r = 0.147, p < 0.05) were positively correlated with policy choice. We also found that people often gave the same explanations for vastly different policy choices; for example, flexibility was the most common reason for choosing options 1 (completely remote) through 4 (in-person most of the week with up to two days remote).

Discussion

In this study, we examined how employees’ experiences with remote work over the pandemic shaped their policy choices today. We predicted that disruption and organizational support would affect whether the shift to remote work was positively transformative, which in turn would predict whether employees chose policies that required remote, in-person, or hybrid work. Understanding why employees prefer certain work styles is important for organizational leaders who must balance employee preferences with the needs of their businesses.

We found that perceived organizational support, but not disruption, predicted positive transformation, which in turn predicted employees’ policy choices. Those who perceived greater support experienced more positive transformation, and those who experienced more positive transformation chose more remote policies. POS did not moderate the relationship between disruption and positive transformation.

Our findings on POS add to a growing body of literature that links this factor with a wide range of positive outcomes. For example, studies have found POS to increase engagement,[67] decrease stress and turnover intentions,[68] and improve performance, well-being, and positive feelings towards one’s organization and work.[69] Feeling positively may predict growth after challenging circumstances,[70] which may explain why employees who perceived organizational support experienced more growth after the shift to remote work than those who did not. Taken together, our findings and the literature on POS suggest that feeling supported by one’s organization is a critical factor in how employees manage challenging circumstances such as the shift to remote work.

We also found that employees who experienced greater positive transformation were more likely to advocate for remote policies. It is unsurprising that people who were positively transformed by remote work were more likely to want to work remotely; what is more interesting is the rationale behind these policy choices. To examine this question, we analyzed participants’ qualitative explanations for their policy recommendations. We found 10 themes: Flexibility, Productivity, Well-Being, In-Person Meetings, Socialization, Balance, Teamwork, Cost, Experience, and Retention. Interestingly, some of these were associated with a specific policy choice, while others were popular regardless of one’s choice. For example, well-being was the most cited explanation for options 1 (completely remote), 5 (almost completely in-person with one day remote), and 7 (other). This suggests that a variety of work styles can be positive for well-being depending on the employee, which may explain why flexibility was the most common explanation for policy choices. As one respondent explains, “In my team I have one person who works in the office every day because it suits him, another that goes in a couple of days a week … that level of choice allows them to get on with their work.”

These findings are consistent with existing literature that describes the benefits of flexible work arrangements. For example, remote work-related flexibility has been associated with improved performance,[71] productivity and creativity,[72] and trust.[73] Taken together, this implies that employees value freedom at work so that they can make the decisions that best support their performance and well-being.

One surprising finding was that disruption did not predict positive transformational growth. The simplest explanation is that employees adjusted well to disruption, preventing any negative effects and eliminating the challenge required for adversarial growth. Another explanation is that disruption had paradoxical effects: it contributed to a markedly negative experience, but challenging circumstances often trigger positive transformational growth.[74] Therefore, a simultaneous increase and decrease in positive transformation resulted in a neutral overall effect. Future research may clarify the mechanisms behind disruptions’ lack of effect.

Limitations and Future Research Suggestions

One limitation of this study is that we did not distinguish between participants who held a managerial role and those who did not. Managers (more than non-managers) often did not feel supported by their administrators during the shift to remote work,[75] which may explain the recent increase in managers’ feelings of burnout.[76] Future research should consider the distinction in POS between managers and non-managers and examine whether this has implications for employees’ remote work experiences. A second limitation of our study is that our sample was largely not diverse and thus not representative of the U.S. or global population. Specifically, participants tended to be younger than the average employee and were overwhelmingly White. This is likely a result of our decision not to screen participants by their demographics. Further research should aim to study a more representative sample and clarify the population being studied.

Implications for Practice

As employers decide whether to bring their employees back into the office, continue remote work, or adopt a hybrid work model, several findings from our study can help guide these important decisions. First, employers should recognize that employees tend to prefer remote work to in-office work. They enjoy the flexibility it brings, the opportunity for greater productivity, and the practical advantages, such as a reduced commute and cost savings. Though employers’ policy decisions need not be driven by employees’ preferences alone, it is important to consider these preferences; such “organizational listening” has been linked to improved employee morale, loyalty, retention, and productivity.[77]

Our findings also suggest that perceived organizational support, rather than disruption, predicts whether major shifts will be positively transformative for employees. Thus, employers should provide technical and emotional support to their employees and convey that the organization values their contributions when implementing any kind of shift, whether that is a shift to remote work or a shift to working in the office again. This will facilitate the transition and help employees experience it as positively transformational.

Finally, if organizational policy makers decide to mandate in-person work, they should consider the reasons employees prefer remote work to reduce talent loss. In-person work options that offer flexibility, work-life balance, or opportunities for growth may be valued as much as remote work. By understanding the reasons for employees’ work preferences, employers can retain a satisfied and productive workforce, whether in-person or remote.

Synthesis and relaxivity of gadolinium-based DOTAGA conjugated 3-phosphoglycerate†

Andrew R. Brotherton, Shifa Noor Mohamed and Thomas J. Meade

*

The synthesis and characterization of a gadolinium-based contrast agent conjugated to 3-phosphoglycerate (Gd-3PG) are reported.

The synthetic steps are optimized to incorporate a selective deprotection strategy for a primary tert-butyl dimethyl silyl (TBS) hydroxyl over a secondary one. The relaxivity of Gd-3PG shows characteristic improvement, likely due to secondary sphere effects and/or an increase in molecular weight (5.39 ± 0.14 mM−1 s−1 at 1.4 T and 37 °C). Michaelis–Menten enzymatic kinetics was measured on the modified 3PG-arm and it showed similar activity to the native 3PG metabolite, Km = 240 ± 30 µM. This agent and future versions of this type of GBCA, which are conjugated to glycolytic metabolites, were designed to monitor in vivo allosteric regulatory events in glycolytic processes.

Introduction

Gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are routinely used in the clinic for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and for molecular imaging in important discovery experiments.1–4

Conjugation or binding of GBCAs to a protein enhances the relaxivity (r1) by slowing down the rotational correlation time (τr), commonly known as a τr boost.5 The GBCAs are likewise investigated using electron nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) as alternatives for measuring the amino acid distances of proteins in situ,6 where typical crystallization techniques have difficulties elucidating the dynamic conformations.

Biomolecular chemistry is challenging to visualize in vivo, especially with its unique allosteric regulatory effects. For example, highly energetic metabolites like 1,3-bisphosphogly- cerate (1,3-BPG) have been shown to non-enzymatically and co- valently tag exposed lysine residues on nearby proteins in a metabolic regulatory process.7 Our work focuses on the synthesis and characterization of such an agent by conjugating 3-phosphoglycerate (3PG) to a GBCA. Gd-3PG shows an enhanced r1, most likely attributed to secondary sphere effects or an increase in molecular weight from the 3PG-arm.8 The 3PG-arm had a similar Michaelis–Menten constant (Km) to that of reported 3PG in the phosphorylation to 1,3-BPG by phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK).9

Experimental

General methods

Unless otherwise noted, all synthetic manipulations were performed under a dry nitrogen atmosphere using standard Schlenk techniques. Solvents were still dried using Glass Contour columns or over-activated molecular sieves (4 ang- stroms). Reactions were monitored by TLC using precoated plastic plates (0.20 mm silica gel 60, UV254, Macherey-Nagel GmbH & Co., Duren Germany). Spots were visualized using potassium permanganate stain, Dragendorffstain, CAM stain, or UV active methods. 1H NMR and proton-decoupled 13C NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker Avance III spectro- meter (499.37 MHz for 1H, 125.58 MHz for 13C, and 150 MHz for 31P) and were processed using Bruker TOPSPIN 2.1 soft- ware. 1H, 13C, and 31P chemical shifts are reported as δ values in parts per million downfield from tetramethylsilane (TMS) or external triethyl phosphate. High-resolution mass spec- trometry (HRMS) was performed using an Agilent 6210 time- of-flight (TOF) LC/MS instrument using electrospray ionization (ESI). Deuterated solvents were purchased from Cambridge Isotope Labs or Sigma-Aldrich. For high-performance liquid chromatography, an Agilent 1160/1260 DAD was used for traces, with ESI for ionization and 6120 Quadrupole LC/MS for detection. The analytical column was a Synergi 4 µm Polar-RP 80 Å, 4.6 × 150 mm column, and the semipreparative column was a Synergi 4 µm Polar-RP 80 Å 21.2 × 150 mm column. †Electronic supplementary information (ESI) available.
