Nazi Critique: A Post War Political Tool

Margaret Sprigg-Dudley

Introduction

Nazis are bad. This sentiment was shared by both Western superpowers and anti-colonial writers following the end of World War II. However, when analyzing the individual components of Nazism – colonial conquests, racial brutality, discriminatory laws – the story becomes more complicated. In actions if not in words, these individual components were not universally condemned. Despite this, during WWII we see an ideological shift where global superpowers started to critique colonialism because it was associated with Nazism. These critiques also served to give the allied powers – especially the United States and Britain – the moral high ground in the war. They released statements recognizing the right to self-determination and the dangers of fascism. They used Nazis are bad as evidence for we are good.

They were not the only ones who used critiques of Nazism for other intentions. Anti-colonial writers also critiqued Nazism, not to condemn Nazis but to condemn the West. Two intellects in particular stand out: W. E. B. Du Bois and Aimé Césaire. Du Bois was a well-established Black sociologist from the US. Along with many other accomplishments, he was the head of the sociology department at Atlanta University and was known for his critiques of the racial system in the US. Césaire was a poet and politician in Martinique and helped found the concept of negritude – an anti-colonial political and cultural movement that spot lit the value of Blackness.[0] Both of these writers used Nazism to criticize Western imperialism. They used Nazis are bad as evidence for and so is the West. Both anti-colonial writers like Du Bois and Césaire and world powers like the US used critiques of Nazism to advance their preexisting arguments. Du Bois used Nazis to criticize US racial systems, Césaire to highlight European barbarianism, and the US to give itself a moral high ground. In doing so, Césaire and Du Bois provide an antithesis to US documents such as the Atlantic Charter, the UN Charter, and the Casablanca Conference, highlighting the hypocrisy of the US’s moral high ground stance.

Anti-Colonial Writers

Before Du Bois started drawing comparisons between Nazi Germany and other imperial powers, his analysis of Germany was not scathing. This harsher criticism came later as he used the critique of Nazism to advance other arguments. In 1936 Du Bois travelled to Germany for six months to study their industrial education system. He hoped to gain knowledge that could advance the education of Black people in the US.[1] His entire reason for being there was to emulate Germany. Later, in 1936 and 1937, he wrote a series of opinion pieces in The Pittsburgh Courier about his time overseas. He shared several positive attributes about Germany: he stated that he experienced no racial prejudice while being there and that the changes in the German economy had decreased unemployment and provided new buildings, roads, and houses.[2] Before the war, his analysis of the Nazi bureaucracy was not overly critical. That came later.

Du Bois did, however, recognize German crimes against Jewish people. He stated that “[t]here has been no tragedy in modern times equal in its awful effects to the fight on the Jew in Germany.”[3] Despite this recognition, he was tentative at this point in his life to draw connections between the Jewish and Black experience. He stated that the discrimination in Germany was done lawfully, whereas anti-Black discrimination in the US subverted the law (he later clarified that he was referring to illegal lynching in the US. This argument is still odd because of the long history of legal anti-Black discrimination in the US).[4] He went on to say that Germans have hated Jewish people for centuries, "[b]ut the reasons have varied and are not at all analogous to white dislike of blacks in America."[5] Though he recognized German atrocities as an attack on civilization – attacks that were similar to other imperial actions – he did not equate the two yet. Later, when he used Nazi brutality to critique imperial brutality, he more readily connected the Jewish and Black experience.

After the war, Du Bois became more critical of fascism as an institution and in doing so used it to condemn imperialism. In January 1945, he published Color and Democracy: Colonies and Peace, outlining the ways in which democracy was in danger. He argued that imperialism was more dangerous to democracy than fascism because it disenfranchised masses of people.[6] He was not criticizing fascism but instead using fascism to criticize colonialism. He went on to argue that Hitler used techniques of the West. He said that "Hitler seized on ‘negroid’ characteristics to accuse the French of inferiority."[7] Here, he also explicitly connected the Black experience to the Jewish experience: “[The US] gives rein and legal recognition to race hate, which the Nazis copied in their campaign against the Jews, establishing it on American lines of caste conditions, disfranchisement, mob murder, ridicule, and public disparagement."[8] Once again, his thesis was not that Nazis were brutal towards Jewish people. His evidence was that Nazis were brutal towards Jewish people, copying the US system. He was more critical of Nazism in this publication than he was nine years prior in The Courier because he was using Nazi brutality to condemn US actions.

The timing in which this piece was published also gives more power to this use of Nazi critique. Color and Democracy was written towards the end of WWII whereas his Courier pieces were written pre-war. When he published Color and Democracy, the Nazis were established – and soon to be defeated – enemies. The comparisons he drew between the US and Germany held more weight because Nazis were widely considered enemies of civilization. Back in 1936, though anxieties about Nazism were growing, their status as an enemy was not as defined. Du Bois was one of the early academics to recognize the anti-Jewish brutality that was occurring.[9] Even if he had used Nazi critique to criticize the US, it would not have held the same weight. Post-war, Du Bois did not need to argue that Nazis were brutal – the world had already accepted that. He instead connected Nazism to imperialism to argue that imperialism was a threat to democracy and civilization. This, the global powers had not yet accepted.

Césaire similarly used Nazi critique to support his argument against colonialism. Again, he was not critiquing Nazism but instead Western brutality. He outlined this stance in Discourse on Colonialism, published in 1950. Like Du Bois’s Color and Democracy, this was published after the Nazis were established as an enemy of the West. He argued that colonization decivilizes and brutalizes the colonizer.[10] He argued that Europeans used Nazism to excuse Western crime as if this brutality was a momentary lapse in civilization instead of a product of their own history.[11] He argued that there is a Hitler inside every Western leader.[12] This argument recognized that Nazis were brutal and uncivilized, but Césaire did not provide any evidence to back up this claim. That was not the point of the essay. Instead, Nazi brutality was the evidence he used to argue that the West is brutal. He used Nazi brutality to support his existing argument.

Though Du Bois and Césaire both used Nazism critique to condemn the West, their arguments were slightly different.They both argued that Nazi techniques already existed in the West’s treatment of People of Color. Césaire said that Europeans put up with brutality before WWII because it had only been directed at non-European people. [13] Du Bois argued that there was no Nazi atrocity that Europe had not already inflicted on People of Color.[14] However, the focus of their arguments was slightly different, something that can be attributed to their backgrounds. Du Bois focused more on the downfall of democracy and US racial systems. This is because he was a US scholar studying the sociology of race. Césaire talked less about the downfall of democracy. He instead promoted Black civilization while condemning Western. We can see the components of negritude in this argument. As previously mentioned, negritude is an anti-colonial idea that celebrates Blackness and Black civilization. His writing used Nazism to condemn the West to uplift Black civilization. Ultimately, Du Bois and Césaire had similar ideas, with different focuses.

The United States

Anti-colonial writers were not the only ones who used critiques of Nazism to advance their argument: the US criticized Nazism to give themselves the moral high ground. Instead of using Nazism as evidence of the West’s brutality, the US condemned Nazism as a political tool. We can see this most clearly at the Casablanca Conference and in the Atlantic Charter. The Casablanca Conference was a meeting between ally leaders in 1943 where they decided that they would only accept unconditional surrender from the Axis powers. This, they decided, was the only way to ensure the end of fascism.[15] In their declarations, they promoted the idea that they were morally superior to the Germans. In his radio address following the conference, Franklin D. Roosevelt stated: “In the years of the American and French revolutions the fundamental principle guiding our democracies was established. The cornerstone of our whole democratic edifice was the principle that from the people and the people alone flows the authority of government."[16] He was using this critique of Nazi totalitarianism to promote US and French ideals. In another document following the conference, he stated that they were dedicated to the destruction of Nazi philosophies.[17] Roosevelt sought to replace Nazi philosophies with US ideologies: he used Nazi critique to give the US the moral high ground. Though his thesis was completely different from Du Bois and Césaire’s, Roosevelt too used Nazi critique to advance an argument.

This approach also appears in the Atlantic Charter. The Atlantic Charter was published by both the US and the UK in 1941. It recognized the right to self-determination and laid the groundwork for the foundation of the UN. However, it also invoked Nazi criticism to give these powers the moral high ground. The sixth point says: “after the final destruction of the Nazi tyranny, they hope to see established a peace which will afford to all nations the means of dwelling in safety within their own boundaries."[18] Here, they were explicitly criticizing Nazi totalitarianism and imperialism. This shifted the focus away from the imperialism of the West and onto the Nazis. Again, it gives the US the moral high ground by – at least in writing – taking the side of oppressed people. Once again, the US used Nazi critique to advance their political position.

Some may argue that these documents were not political tools but instead that the US’s only agenda was the destruction of fascism. Though there is some truth in that – the US was fighting to end fascism – we can see that there was a lack of follow-through on the ideals presented in these charters. In 1946, Ho Chi Minh wrote to President Harry Truman asking for support in ending French rule in Vietnam. He asked him to intervene to stop French aggression “in keeping with the principles of the Atlantic and San Francisco charters.”[19] Truman never responded. This suggests that these documents were political tools, tools to promote US political standing. This lack of follow-through highlights US hypocrisy. This hypocrisy was also pointed out by Césaire and Du Bois. According to Césaire’s argument, the US cannot critique Nazis without being a hypocrite because the West helped breed Nazism. Both anti-colonial writers and Western superpowers invoked Nazi criticisms to advance their arguments. As a result, anti-colonial writers provided an antithesis to each of these US documents.

Antitheses

Césaire’s argument counters the Atlantic Charter and the Casablanca conference by arguing that Nazism was embedded in Western powers. Roosevelt stated that the unconditional surrender of Axis powers would bring about “the destruction of the philosophies in those countries which are based on conquest and the subjugation of other people.”[20] However, Césaire argued that Hitler and his ideologies existed within every Western leader; according to that argument, the destruction of Axis powers would not end the conquest and subjugation of other people. Césaire cites the French emphasis on blood purity that increased post-WWII.[21] This also counters Roosevelt’s emphasis on French ideals of democracy. Césaire argued that the West bred Hitler and continued to emulate him post war. This directly opposed US claims of moral superiority. Césaire also believed that US domination was just as or more dangerous than European imperialism. He argued that Truman’s declaration of the end of old colonialism “means that American high finance considers that the time has come to raid every colony in the world.”[22] This counters the Atlantic Charter. Both the US and Césaire use critiques of Nazism but came to opposite conclusions about US domination and morals.

Du Bois also disagreed with this notion of US moral superiority, but his book Color and Democracy most closely provided an antithesis for the UN Charter. The UN Charter was the founding document of the UN, signed in June 1945. Chapter XI of the charter defined the legal status for non-self-governing territories – former colonies that had not yet gained full independence. Compare the opening statement of Color and Democracy to the opening statement of the UN’s Chapter XI. Du Bois wrote:

The present war has made it clear that we can no longer regard Western Europe and North America as the world for which civilization exists; nor can we look upon European culture as the norm for all peoples. Henceforth the majority of the inhabitants of earth, who happen for the most part to be colored, must be regarded as having the right and the capacity to share in human progress and to become copartners in that democracy which alone can ensure peace among men, by the abolition of poverty, the education of the masses, protection from disease, and the scientific treatment of crime[23]

Whereas the UN Charter Chapter XI begins with:

Members of the United Nations which have or assume responsibilities for the administration of territories whose peoples have not yet attained a full measure of self-government recognize the principle that the interests of the inhabitants of these territories are paramount, and accept as a sacred trust the obligation to promote to the utmost, within the system of international peace and security established by the present Charter, the well-being of the inhabitants of these territories[24]

Both of these documents were published in the same year. Both were concerned with global peace and highlighted the importance of global stability following the brutality of WWII. Both recognized the importance of democracy. However, where Du Bois argued that the West was not civilized, the UN placed the West as the protector of civilization. Where Du Bois pointed out the atrocities that the West had committed against People of Color in their colonies, the UN charter entrusted these colonies to the West. Where Du Bois saw Nazism as proof of Western barbarianism, the UN saw Nazi defeat as proof of Western heroism. The two documents have the same goals yet opposing approaches. Though an antagonism towards Nazis was shared between anti-colonial writers and Western powers, what to do with that antagonism was not.

Finally, it is important to recognize that Césaire and Du Bois’s arguments were not the only approach to anti-colonial Nazi critique. Some anti-colonialists invoked Nazi critique to appeal to, not just criticize, Western powers. Though Césaire and Du Bois were both involved in politics and tried to create change through their writing, many of their pieces still existed within the academic space.These writings were philosophical, literary, and had space to flesh out critical arguments against Western powers.

Another approach condemned Nazis to advance a political agenda. This is what the US did during WWII, but it is also what anti-colonial politicians did post-war. Léopold Sédar Senghor – a poet and politician who founded the concept of Negritude with Césaire – condemned Nazis to advance Senegal’s political agenda. In 1946 he said, "We are ready, if need be as a last resort, to conquer freedom by all means, not excluding violence. I do not believe that France, which has just eliminated Hitlerian racism, can blame us for this decision."[25] Again, this statement carried power because Nazis had been established as enemies such as France. Similarly, in 1945, People of Color in South Africa wrote to the UN, stating: “if it was a crime in Nazi Germany for an ‘Aryan’ to mix with or marry a non-Aryan, it is equally a criminal offence in South Africa for a member of the Herrenvolk to mix with or marry with the slave race."[26] The conclusion of these politicians was the same as Césaire and Du Bois – Western powers enacted the same brutality that the Nazis did. However, the politician’s strategy was slightly different. They were condemning Nazis to both criticize Western powers and to appeal to them. They were condemning Nazis to gain rights and independence.

Conclusion

Following WWII, we see opposing sides of the political spectrum invoke Nazi criticism. None of these figures were trying to convince their audience that Nazis were bad or brutal or uncivilized – that was generally accepted. Instead, they were using Nazi critique to advance their own arguments and politics. Nazis are bad was not their thesis. Nazis are bad was their evidence. For Du Bois and Césaire, that meant highlighting the similarities between Nazi and Western ideologies to show the long history of Western racial systems and colonial violence. This use of Nazi critique gave their arguments more weight because Nazis were the accepted enemy. For the US, using Nazi critique meant highlighting the differences between Nazi and US ideologies to promote themselves as a moral leader. Though they both used this tool of Nazi critique, the two groups created opposing documents. Nazis were condemned. Political agendas dictated what this condemnation meant for the future.

nurj_title: VAI O LE OLA: SĀMOAN WOMEN'S WATER ECOLOGIES
text:
VAI O LE OLA:

SĀMOAN WOMEN’S WATER ECOLOGIES

Lula Blas Fox

Northwestern University

SIT Sāmoa: Social and Environmental Change in Oceania

Fall 2024

ADVISOR

Anita Latai-Niusulu

ACADEMIC DIRECTOR

Fetaomi Tapu-Qiliho

INTRODUCTION

Sāmoan identity is intimately tied to Indigenous relationships with water, as water sources, such as natural springs, are rich in ancient legends, myths, meanings, and practices.[0] In the ancient Sāmoan belief system, water is genealogically connected to man, as well as lands, the cosmos, and the gods. This shared genealogy is considered sacred, and establishes a, “legacy of responsibility on all living things (trees, clouds, volcanoes, water, animals, people) to respect through reciprocity, the divine balance or harmony they share.”[1] The relational space that binds responsibility between creator, created, and all of creation is known as the vā––the foundation of most Polynesian societies––as it “governs all things and holds all things together.”[2] The vā thus represents a crucial ethical and religious orientation for Sāmoan interactions with the environment. In the context of water sources, natural springs are particularly important within Sāmoan relations, as it was often believed that the gods inhabited these spaces. The presence of natural springs became the defining characteristic of many communities, as they named themselves, “after the aitu who created, and often inhabited, springs or acted as guardians of springs in pre-Christian times.”[3] The village was thus defined by those who shared the springs and communally cared for them.

Water sources eventually became the foundation of the village-wide fa’amatai (chiefly) structure, where chiefly titles became directly tied to land and water sources. Sites such as mangroves and natural springs were placed under the pule (authority) of a matai (chief), and the stewardship of the water sites by the matai therefore verified and validated their honorifics as village leaders.[4] The fono a matai (village council), for example, “met regularly to manage all activities in the village and, in this process, enacted regulations to maintain springs and their surroundings and to control human conduct around the pools.”[5]  In the present day, over 80% of the land in Sāmoa is considered customary, collectively owned by matai that represent each ‘āiga (family) (Macpherson & Macpherson, 2009). Thus, stewardship of local water sources remains a village-wide endeavor, as the matai, village women, and elders contribute towards sustaining Sāmoan water stewardship.

The deep, millenia-maintained connections to water have cultivated a system of reciprocity amongst all Sāmoans, where they care for and honor the water systems that nourish them.[6] Stewardship of the springs was institutionalized in ancient Sāmoan spiritual and religious beliefs; many Sāmoan villages described the presence of aitu (human spirits), who would punish any individual that did not treat the springs with respect. In order to maintain the va fealoa’i, or the relational space between humans, the spirits, and the environment, Sāmoan villagers strived to “ensure quietness and respect for the spirit,” by managing human conduct around the springs.[7] The introduction of Christianity to the Sāmoan archipelago in the mid-19th century initiated rapid change amongst Sāmoan religious practices, challenging and reshaping the ancestral values that influenced human interaction with the environment.

Throughout these various periods of change, natural springs sustained the cultural and historical significance they held in Sāmoan communities, especially amongst Sāmoan women. For women of the villages in particular, collecting water was an, “...established part of daily routines for young women because, ‘Sāmoans refuse to drink river water, which they called suamalō.’”[8] The pools of the springs were often divided into specific areas for women’s daily tasks, such as collecting drinking water, bathing, and cleaning laundry. As everyday frequenters of these pools, Sāmoan women have always played a crucial role in stewarding local water sources, however, little academic work focuses on documenting their participation in the management of village ecosystems. This research seeks to add to existing scholarship on the implicit feminisms of Sāmoan women, where they are the, “backbones of families and villages.”[9] By emphasizing core Sāmoan values, such as community care, good relations, and collective self-determination, Sāmoan women play a crucial role in perpetuating cultural systems of reciprocity and environmental stewardship.[10]

This research project sought to understand the role of Sāmoan women in village-wide environmental management systems by examining women’s participation in protecting the natural springs of Faleapuna, a village located on the northeast coast of Upolu. Utilizing a Pacific Research Framework that emphasized Sāmoan conceptions of feminism, semi-structured interviews were conducted with multiple Sāmoan women of different age groups, as well as one elder male matai. All interviewees were from the village of Faleapuna, and held a significant stake in protecting the natural environment as community members. Lengthy conversations with women in the village revealed the deeply entrenched desire to care for the environment, in order to protect and preserve the land for future generations. This research seeks to position the case-study of Faleapuna in the broader context of Indigenous governance, feminism, environmental health, and climate resilience, examining the socio-cultural and spiritual beliefs that drive Indigenous stewardship––an essential institution amidst the current climate crisis.

FALEAPUNA: HOUSE OF SPRINGS

Organization of the village

Faleapuna is a Sāmoan village on the north coast of Upolu. The name of the village stems from the words fale (house) and puna (to boil, swell, as in a natural spring/pool), indicating the presence of natural springs.[11] Adjacent to the sea, the village is separated into four pitonu’u (districts) that are demarcated by their proximity to the main natural pools. The village economy is largely subsistence based; family-operated plantations abundant in taro, bananas, and breadfruit are found throughout the village. Less than a mile from shore, there is also a coral reef where men, women, and children alike fish. Day-to-day life in the village therefore consists of fishing, farming, household feau (chores), and swimming in the natural springs, while a majority of children attend school in Faleapuna, other nearby villages, or in Apia (Personal Interview #1, 2024). Food is often shared communally throughout the village, and once the seafood or agricultural products are distributed, a member of the family may sell any surplus goods at the nearby market in Apia for additional income.

The village is organized around the fa’amatai (Sāmoan chiefly system), where each ‘āiga (family) has a matai (family chief) representing them in the village fono (council). Both men and women can become matai in the village, and there are currently, as of November 2024, at least two women matai in the village.[12] Women matai are not allowed to join the women’s committee, another crucial institution towards running the village. Women’s committees, or komiti tuamama, were first formed in the 1920s, during New Zealand’s military occupation of Western Sāmoa. Women in the committee are responsible for cultivating respectful relations amongst villagers and the environment, increasing public health awareness, and keeping the village clean––all of which are crucial aspects of environmental and community health.[13] Elder non-matai women in the ‘āiga, including those that are not genealogically from Faleapuna but rather married into the village, often participate in village decision-making through the women’s committee. Faith is an equally important institution in Faleapuna, in addition to fa’amatai and the women’s committee; the village has multiple churches in the village, each catering to different denominations, such as the Catholic Church, the Congregational Christian Church (LMS), and the Church of Jesus Christ and the Latter-Day Saints (LDS). These institutions all play a significant role in the stewardship of the natural pools.

Rules of the Puna

There are four main springs in Faleapuna: Vai levi, Vai alae, Vai apo’a, and Vai punaleilei. The pools are divided into four main districts, with each district defining its respective boundaries around a centrally-located pool. Since they are located on village land, the pools are largely open to all people, including tourists. They are primarily cared for by the women’s committee, who organize monthly village-wide beautification initiatives of the pools, invest tourist money into infrastructure upgrades, and cultivate respectful behavior that protects the pools from disturbances, such as pollution. Women are additionally responsible for passing down the stories of the pools, and ensuring the village youth learn about the importance of taking care of them.

The leadership of the women’s committee in maintaining the natural pools is linked to women’s everyday presence at the pools throughout village history. In the past, the other four main pools were used for bathing, laundry, and swimming, with stones, “laid around the springs to form small pools one yard across that are used for drinking water.”[14] Women in the village spent a significant portion of their day at the pools, completing household feau (chores) such as fetching water for the family, cleaning laundry, and bathing the children. The women always made sure to clean the pool before they left, washing out any remnants of their daily activities: “We always cleaned the pools. In the olden days, our ancestors always cleaned them after using them. We never left them dirty. We take care of them.”[15] In this regard, the pools were central towards women’s everyday life in Faleapuna.

Over the last decade, the use of the pools has shifted as Faleapuna adopted different amenities associated with Sāmoa’s integration into the capitalist market, resulting in changes to the village lifestyle. Now, villagers have increased access to alternate water sources, such as tap water and bottled plastic water from Apia and other surrounding villages, so most of Faleapuna no longer requires drinking water from the pools.[16] The exception is during times of storm, when water is collected from the pools and boiled to be used for cooking and drinking.[17] Around a decade ago, the women’s committee helped upgrade the pools for tourists, so village members no longer wash laundry or bathe in them to ensure they remain clean.[18] Community members continue to use the springs for recreational purposes, however, with many families going to the pools after finishing their daily feau, swimming between the hours of 12:00 p.m. and 6:00 p.m.[19] The responsibilities of the women’s committee includes managing money given from tourists to swim in the pools (however, there is no set charge to use the pools), ensuring people are not polluting the pools with rubbish or other materials, and enforcing behavioral rules/norms that are considered respectful ways of acting in the presence of the pools.

The rules, which both tourists and locals alike are suggested to follow, comprise of: no fishing in the pools (except for ceremonial purposes); no swimming in the pool after 6:00 p.m. or sunset (most villagers seem to obey); no yelling or loud voices used in the pools; no jumping in the pools; and no disorderly behavior, such as consuming alcohol.[20] The rules were created to, “protect the springs and have people respect them.”[21] Since these rules are partially rooted in pre-colonial notions of tapu and maintaining the vā between humans and aitu, the women told me that most people in the village follow the rules, but some villagers do not truly believe in them because of Faleapuna’s conversion into a Christian village.

Sacred Ecologies: Legends of Aitu

Derived from the ancestral Sāmoan religion, etiquette codes that guided human behavior and tapu (sacredness) were established at the natural springs due to the presence of certain aitu (human spirits/Gods). Remaining quiet and respectful while in the space of an aitu was crucial so as not to anger them; thus, the rules instituted at the springs were created in consideration of the vā between humans and ancient spirits.[22] The primary goal of the pool rules was to prevent any sort of human-caused disruptions at the springs, as ancient Sāmoan proverbs, “...warned Sāmoans to leave springs as their spirit guardians had created them and not attempt to alter them.”[23] In Faleapuna, one of the stories that was shared with me concerned an aitu that was an old male ghost, said to lurk at one of the pools. He was easily angered, so in order to respect the aitu, ancient villagers remained quiet when at the pools, ensuring they did not disrupt the spirit.[24] Villagers also did not swim at the pool after dark, as they believed the aitu came out while the sun set––hence why some women still do not enter the pools after 6:00 p.m.

Another story consisted of a tele sā, or a ‘spirit woman’ that guards specific forests, pools, villages, and falls in Sāmoa. Tele sā are considered protectors of the earth that get easily intrigued or angered by beautiful women.[25] Sāmoan women and girls are often told to cover their mirrors at night, and to have their hair up so as not to attract or provoke the tele sā. Tay,[26] one of my interlocutors, a younger mother who was not a member of the women's committee, told me about a tele sā that lived in Saleimoa, a nearby village on the northwest coast of Upolu. In the old days, despite the distance between her and Faleapuna, the tele sā was acutely aware when a girl was being “naughty” at one of the pools by wearing a sei (flower worn in the ear) with her hair hung down. She also got angry when people disrupted the pools or left rubbish in them. In response, she would “transform into an animal and tell the person to stop what they are doing.”[27] If one did not comply with the words of the tele sā, there would be severe consequences, ranging from the person’s hair falling out to the tele sā even creating storms or flooding; “When she gets angry, the water rushes and the wind gets rough.”[28] In the old days, one would apologize to her before they left the pools, pick up any rubbish they left, and go straight home. If their actions angered the tele sā to a severe extent, the villager would have to formally apologize to the fono.

When discussing the rules of the pools with my interlocutors, all of them emphasized the importance of the rules in protecting the pools, but some explained to me that the rules did not matter as much to them since they no longer believed in aitu.[29] Despite all of my interlocutors following the rules with great caution, even teaching them to their kids, many of them had complex emotions regarding the fact that the rules stemmed from aitu. One of my interlocutors said to me about the aitu, “Samoa is Christian now. The [ancient] ancestors are gone, and so are their rules.”[30] Tay, however, who notably did not subscribe to either of the dominant churches in the village (Congregational and Catholic), said to me, “You must respect the tele sā and the ancestors in the olden days. Now Sāmoa is Christian, but still you must respect the rules and what came before.”[31] Tay told me a story about her experience of seeing a woman from her husband’s village disrespect tapu, wearing a sei and singing at one of the village pools. The tele sā warned the woman to stop, but she did not listen. “She disrespected the tele sā and she got sick. Her hair even fell out, and her ears bled. You have to learn about the tele sā and respect her.”[32] Most Sāmoans I spoke with have heard of similar experiences between humans and aitu, and many can describe the aitu located in other villages. Despite holding Christian beliefs, most Sāmoan women I spoke to still chose to respect the stories of the aitu, regardless of whether or not they personally believed in them.

The connection between aitu and environmental protection can be located within a greater body of academic literature that has described the linkage between faith and Indigenous stewardship as a form of ‘sacred ecology.’ Within the concept of sacred ecology, Indigenous ecological knowledge includes “spiritual or religious dimensions” that fall outside the realm of western science, as the use of resources is regarded as, “an exchange and a privilege that comes with stewardship responsibilities, and the knowledge that to waste has direct consequences on the web of interactions that sustain life.”[33] These spiritual beliefs are largely responsible for the regulation of human interactions with the environment––known as tapu in the Sāmoan context.[34] Within a sacredness ethic, Tapu, or rules restricting human behavior in sacred spaces, became essential in the island context, where resources were understandably finite and islanders learned to follow the seasons and migrations in earthly and aquatic harvest so as to allow regrowth and regeneration amongst non-human life. Tapu thus ensured that all forms of life were not overexploited, polluted, or desecrated by human activity. In this regard, tapu represented the marriage between spirituality and sustainability ethics, consecrating balance and harmony into the Indigenous human-environment relationship.

Due to the large-scale, village-wide conversion of Sāmoans into Christians, however, the dynamic between ancestral sacred ecology and contemporary Christian faith has resulted in complex socio-cultural beliefs where elements of both spiritual systems are present.[35] The introduction of Christianity in the Pacific Islands did not wholly result in the demise of belief in spirits, but rather it, “altered the beliefs in certain kinds of spirits and their powers.”[36] Spirits that regulate human-environment relationships have, “diminished in the eyes of Christians,” but the underlying ideologies and practices related to environmental management have persisted, albeit, “challenged and reshaped.”[37] Thus, while Sāmoans abandoned many aspects of the ancestral religion, stories of the aitu and notions of tapu remained present within Sāmoan society, although they were communicated in continuously evolving forms that coexist with Christianity. The sacred nature of the pools is reaffirmed in church practices, for instance, since the water from Faleapuna’s springs is often used to baptize babies.[38] The continued utilization of spring water into Christian practice reflects how sacred entities have taken on new meaning as they are adapted into Christianity; within the Christian belief system, water is purifying agent that cleanses of sin.

Christian institutions in the village are essential towards fostering environmental stewardship. Since all village matters are discussed in church, church pastors play a significant role in informing Faleapuna’s residents on the importance of conservation. The pastor in the Catholic church, for example, regularly reminds the village youth to refrain from polluting the pools or acting disrespectfully. “The pastor tells them not to leave rubbish and to act good, and the youth listen because that is their pastor.”[39] Churches are central to contemporary Sāmoan society, and by wielding their influence to inform their congregations on the value of preserving the environment, they are able to positively contribute to local Indigenous stewardship in ways that may have been overlooked by previous researchers (Wildermuth, 2012).

Transcending Generations: Women as Environmental Storytellers

As primary caretakers of the children in the village, Sāmoan women in Faleapuna rely on spiritual and historical stories to describe the importance of the pools to the younger generations. While not all of the women I interviewed necessarily believed in the continued existence of the aitu, they all shared stories of the spirits with their children in order to scare them into acting properly at the pools.[40] When telling their children about the rules of the pool, such as no jumping or screaming, the kids, “mostly listen, but some don’t,” however, “they listen more when they are told the old stories about the aitu in the pool. They get scared, so they follow the rules.”[41] The women in the committee emphasized to me that they were responsible for teaching their kids about respecting the environment, and that their own mothers first taught them about the history of the pools, and how to treat them with respect.[42]

For the women in the village, caring for the pools therefore represented the continuation of ancestral practice, as women were raised by their mothers, grandmothers, and other elders to become stewards and maintain the generational commitment of protecting the pools. In this respect, the passing of knowledge was linked to the processes of relationality through the vā; “The giving and receiving of information is closely dictated by observance of the vā.”[43] The vā is relationship, stewardship, affiliation, and in this application, the transcending of environmental stories across time is a practice associated with sustaining the vā between humans generationally; respect is taught, passed down, learned, and subsequently perpetuated. The women I spoke to all went on to raise their own children and ensure they understood the significance of protecting the pools as well. When asking my women interlocutors about how they taught their own children about the pools, they explained that passing on the knowledge imparted to them by their own mothers was extremely important to them:

I teach my kids about the pools just like my mom taught me. I don’t let them go in the pools until they’re older. They go with me to the pools when they are six or seven. I tell them they will get punished if they act naughty or leave rubbish at the pools. They learn from me how to respect the pools and the tele sā.[44]

Stories of a religious nature were also critical towards the environmental education imparted on children, as my women interlocutors emphasized to me the importance of having children understand they had a responsibility to protect God’s creation; “The water is sacred to us and we have to remind the kids that.”[45]

The women in the village considered it their responsibility to not only educate the village children, but also share the stories of the pools with tourists: “We have to tell tourists about the rules to make sure they respect them, and so that they know the story of the pools. Then they know about the village.”[46] Since women largely act as custodians of the pools, they have also taken on the crucial role as storytellers and historians of the pools, sharing with both future generations, as well as visiting tourists, the rules, stories, and legends of the natural springs. In this regard, women play a pivotal role in sustaining the local, everyday ecologies of the springs by ensuring that Indigenous knowledge systems are sustained amongst all people who use them; “...As people retell village histories embedded in tala le vavau (ancient stories of myths, legends, and customs), their sense of place is affirmed, and the meanings they give to their connections to fanua persist.”[47] By combining contemporary Christian narratives with tala le vavau, the women of Faleapuna engage in oral storytelling that effectively furthers the importance of Sāmoan ecological conservation.

DISCUSSION: SĀMOAN WOMEN’S WATER ECOLOGIES

As this research has revealed, the women of Faleapuna comprise an essential role in the management of the village’s natural springs. By regularly maintaining the springs, preserving and passing down the springs’ histories and legends, and affirming the spiritual and socio-cultural beliefs of the springs, the women of Faleapuna embody a successful Indigenous stewardship system that has transcended generations.

The case study of Faleapuna’s natural springs ecologies fits well into the growing body of literature that emphasizes Indigenous eco-spiritual relationships as a necessary element of land management. Eco-spiritual relationships are instrumental in localizing Western sustainability science, which have already largely invested in dispossessing Indigenous peoples of their lands, cultural autonomy, and sovereignty for the sake of conservation.[48] Sāmoan theologian Reverend Dr. Upolu Lumā Vaai, for example, has written extensively on the need to address the spiritual and religious components in community-based environmental knowledge and relationality systems: “relationality sees the world as an eco-relational multidimensional whole that sustains itself only through a healthy flow of connections and deep relationships.”[49] The notion of eco-relational spirituality is akin to the Indigenous Pasifik vā, or the relational space in between the creator and the created, the visible and the invisible.[50] The principles of the vā reveal that all aspects of life are, “multi-dimensional, distinct and different yet mutually and inextricably related,” and thus, there must be balance and harmony between them.[51] According to Rev. Dr. Vaai, Pasifik multi-dimensionality can be seen within the dual meanings of terms such as fanua/vanua/fenua, which indicate both land and placenta, showing how the life of humans and the land are therefore intertwined.[52] This eco-relational understanding is experienced within the village of Faleapuna, where the protection of the natural springs is a labor of respect––for the springs, God, the elders, and the ancestors who have passed––a labor of faith, and a labor that extends past the despiritualized Western perception of ‘preserving resources’ and thinking of land only as a commodity, rather than a living, breathing extension of the people themselves.

The commodification of nature, ingrained in capitalism and stemming from Western colonial ideologies that view the land as both separate and below humans––thus rendering it subject to human expansion and exploitation––continue to pervade Western climate and sustainability science. Western climate science often ignores the spirituality of Indigenous environmental knowledge, deeming it superstition and instead advancing secular notions of rationality that originated in the Enlightenment period.[53] Instead, western sustainability science is largely dedicated toward infrastructural and economic development to maintain access to resources.[54] The disregard for Indigenous spirituality in the Western sustainability ethic has removed ecosystems from their human context and rendered Indigenous management systems inferior to Western conservation. Pasifik academics and climate activists, however, emphasize the importance of “embracing the sacred”:

When we reclaim and embrace the sacred in everyone and all around us, when we act in ways that maintain spirit-focused relationships with family, with community as an extension of our family, and with environment as an extension of our community, we grow out capacity to love and attain a soulful state––joyful, fulfilled, connected, and undeniably sustainable.[55]

Indigenous frameworks of “embracing the sacred” are already embodied in the village of Faleapuna, where the management of the natural springs is just as much about Sāmoan relationality as it is about protecting a ‘resource.’ The springs were and continue to be considered sacred by Faleapuna visitors, who have protected them from human-related disturbance even after no longer requiring them for daily activities.[56] The entire village works together to maintain the springs, with every individual playing a role; whether this means collecting the rubbish, building cement fixtures around the springs, educating tourists about the springs’ histories, or enforcing the pool rules, the women, the youth, the taule’ale’a (untitled men), and the matai all aid in sustaining the local water ecologies.

Within Sāmoan and other Indigenous Pasifik communities, “beliefs about the sacred are tightly coupled to place-based knowledge systems and culturally driven management practices.”[57] These knowledge systems take effect within a set of, “shared responsibilities that bind communities… and are transferred across generations through regular community practice.”[58] Through Kealiikanakaaoleohaililani and Giardina’s description of sacred ecologies, it is evident that the village of Faleapuna demonstrates a form of place-based management with knowledge systems and practices intimately connected to the land that villagers reside on. The naming of the village itself reinforces the notion that the ecology and place are central; Faleapuna translates to house of springs, representing how the springs are integral towards village identity and everyday life.

In Indigenous communities across the globe, it is widely held that the land is not only a provider, but it is an extension of us. The land holds our ancestors, our histories, our practices, and our genealogies. This sentiment is echoed in Sāmoa where Indigenous connection toward the earth can be explained by the phrase: “‘O le faavae o le mau nei, o le sootaga ma le ‘ele’ele,’” or, “our cultural claim to any land or earthly inheritance is premised on a genealogical connection with the earth.”[59] As this statement articulates, humans are not separate from their environment, but rather genealogically connected. In this regard, Indigenous kinship and stewardship are integral in the status quo, as they challenge the hegemony of colonial logic entrenched in the Western capitalist worldview, which emphasizes the exploitation of land––an entity subject to relentless domination––for profit.[60]

Ultimately, this case-study of Faleapuna serves to demonstrate a form of community-based sacred ecologies, where faith-based and religious orientations are crucial towards local land management systems. Uplifting these forms of Indigenous ecologies are integral at a time when conservation zones across the globe are being established on Indigenous lands, but excluded from Indigenous peoples.[61] This form of ecocolonialism, however, predicated on the forcible transfer of, “resource rights from their traditional owners and managers to a relatively new ‘nation state,’” displaces Indigenous peoples from their ancestral lands, interrupting the continuation of ecological knowledge.[62] As Cox and Elmqvist reveal, Western conservation systems alienate Indigenous forms of collective land management, where land is not owned by an individual but rather genealogically connected to a family title. The commodification of land into private property that can be sold or usurped by a dominating political entity, such as a nation-state government, therefore disrupts communal land practices and Indigenous genealogies. Rather than continuously violate Indigenous stewardship and its associated worldviews, global and local environmental policy must reorient itself similar to the model of Sāmoa and emphasize community-based initiatives that reaffirm Indigenous land rights, sovereignty, and self-determination.

CONCLUSION

This case-study of Faleapuna reaffirms the necessity of women in building climate resilience and sustainable land management systems. As stewards, educators, culture keepers, and protectors, Sāmoan women’s participation in environmental initiatives is critical towards fostering a healthy ecosystem. Through the cultivation of generational knowledge and practice and stewardship rooted in ethics of care, faith, and reciprocity for their people and their land, the women of Faleapuna exhibit how Indigenous stewardship is central toward building a sustainable Indigenous future. Environmental, cultural, and spiritual health are intertwined, as the women of Faleapuna reveal. By not only cleaning the springs regularly, but by telling the stories and legends of the springs, and caring for the springs to sustain ancestral practice––while simultaneously teaching future generations––the women villagers of Faleapuna depict how protecting their environment is also an act of community care that nurtures Indigenous understandings of eco-spiritual relationality. In an era where Indigenous peoples across Oceania continue to face land dispossession, environmental racism, and the denial of sovereignty and self-determination from colonial powers, the success of Faleapuna in maintaining traditional land tenure and empowering community-led environmental management is an essential model for Indigenous-led climate resilience.
