Focusing on bivariate relations between traits and narrative themes, the first hypothesis— that higher levels Conscientiousness and Agreeableness will predict a greater tendency to emphasize the deliberate nature spiritual phenomena—did receive some support from the data.

Significant correlations were obtained for both Conscientiousness and SA scores, and

Agreeableness and SA scores. This finding is consistent with previous studies that show a relationship between higher levels of Conscientiousness and Agreeableness and spirituality

(Beitel et al., 2004; Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). Scores on the

SA scale were also significantly correlated with Extraversion, but inversely with Neuroticism and Openness to Experience. The findings about Neuroticism are also consistent with previous research that shows the usefulness of religiously grounded coping mechanisms for managing life stressors (Labbé & Fobes 2009; MacDonald, 2000; Womble et al., 2013). The tendency of people higher in Openness to deemphasize any possible intentionality behind spiritual phenomena may be reflective of the finding that Openness is negatively associated with more fundamentalist forms of religiosity, which emphasize the primary importance of a divine will

(MacDonald, 2000; Saroglou, 2002; 2010).

The second hypothesis—that participants higher in Extraversion and lower in

Neuroticism would narrate their spiritual experiences with greater emphasis on their own agency—did not receive significant support from the correlational data. Neither Neuroticism nor

Extraversion predicted the degree to which participants emphasized their own agency in the S/T scenes. However, Openness to Experience was positively associated with more agentic narration of spiritual experience.

Yet despite the finding that Openness positively predicted NA scores and negative predicted SA scores, Openness was not found to be significant related to SP scores. Thus, the

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 26 third hypotheses—that Openness will predict an inclination to view spiritual phenomena as more omnipresent and related to ordinary phenomena—was not supported by the correlational data.

However, as Table 2 shows, Extraversion was weakly but significantly associated with a greater tendency to view spiritual forces and beings as more proximal to the ordinary world.

Multiple Regression Analysis

In order to better understand the interacting influences of all personality and demographic variables on the narration of spiritual experience, a simultaneous multiple regression analysis was conducted for all three narrative themes. For each test, race, gender, and all Big 5 personality traits were considered as predictors, and the narrative theme was treated as the dependent variable. The first test, which considered whether personality, race and gender impact how much intention participants attribute to spiritual forces, found that 32% of the variance in

SA scores were predicted by these variables (F(7,148) = 9.78, p < .001, R2 = .32). The largest contributor to his relationship was race, and when controlling for all personality variables and gender, Black participants were more likely to emphasize spiritual action and intent (β = .35, p <

.001). When controlling for personality and race, gender also still significantly impacted SA scores, with female participants being more likely than males to emphasize spiritual action (β =

.18, p < .05). Furthermore, lower Openness was the only personality trait to predict higher SA scores, independent of the effects of race, gender, and other personality variables (β = -.22, p <

.01). The reported beta coefficients are standardized to the same unites of measure, so beta coefficients with absolute values closer to 1 indicate stronger influence of the predictor on the prevalence of the narrative themes.

The simultaneous multiple regression analysis also revealed a significant impact of personality, race, and gender on NA scores in the narration of spiritual experience, with these

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 27 variables predicting roughly 13% of the variance (F(7,148) = 3.07, p < .01, R2 = .13). Regardless of race and personality, male participants were more likely than females to emphasize their own agency when recounting spiritual experiences (β = -.18, p < .05). Additionally, when demographic variables and all other personality variables were controlled for, higher

Extraversion did predict higher NA scores (β = .19, p < .05), though it was the only Big 5 trait to do so. Nonetheless this finding does offer some support for the hypothesized relationship between Extraversion and personal agency in the narration of spiritual experience.

Themes of spiritual proximity were also significantly associated with race, gender, and the Big 5 personality traits, which predicted 16% of the variance in SP scores (F(7,148) = 3.94, p

< .001, R2 = .16). Race was the only variable which predicted the prominence of SP themes, with black participants being more likely than whites to describe spiritual beings as accessible and omnipresent regardless of personality or gender (β = .33, p < .001). Overall, it seems an that the ways adults narrate their experiences are influenced not only by personality variables, but also significantly by race, and gender as well.

Discussion

Whereas the study’s main aim was to document associations between personality traits and particular narrative themes in accounts of spiritual experiences, the demographic characteristics of gender and race ended up accounting for much of the variance in narrative themes. According to the multiple regression analysis, men showed significantly higher levels of narrative agency (NA) than women, while African American adults scored significantly higher than their white counterparts on both spiritual action/intent (SA) and spiritual proximity (SP).

With the influence demographics being considered, only Extraversion and Openness proved to

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 28 be significant predictors of narrative themes.  Extraversion was positively associated with NA (as hypothesized), and Openness was negatively associated with SA (contrary to hypothesis).  The traits of Neuroticism, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness were not significantly associated with the narrative themes in the multiple regression analyses.

Spiritual Narration and the Big 5

Personality and the Narration of the Self in Spiritual Scenes

The relationships discovered in this study between personality traits and the ways adults narrate spiritual experiences offer new evidence to the claim that spiritual reasoning is qualitatively different form ordinary autobiographical reflection. Though Extraversion and

Neuroticism were expected to predict how much participants emphasize their own agency since both traits are related to assertiveness and self-confidence (John, 2021), only Extraversion showed the predicted relationship. This finding suggests that the agentic narration of spiritual experiences is not strongly related to emotional stability but is (as hypothesized) positively associated with an upbeat, outgoing, and assertive disposition. Moreover, in the correlational analysis, Openness was also significantly associated with NA.

James (1902) argued that spiritual experiences uniquely push individuals to reflect on deeper, universal truths, and he reported that such reflections are closely associated with questions of morality and personal responsibility. As Openness is the Big 5 trait most closely associated with cognition and intellect (John, 2021), it is plausible that more Open individuals would be more willing to engage with such cerebral questions regarding morality when reflecting on spiritual experiences. Consequently, people higher in Openness may be more inclined to reflect on the moral implications of their spiritual experiences, reflecting more agentic themes like personal responsibility, whereas others may be more concerned with the concrete

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 29 elements of these experiences and consider their concrete influence on real-life events. Consider a response given by one participant high in Openness as she discusses how her connection with

God makes her feel. In her response, she reflects on the observation that strangers seem to find her approachable, and she emphasizes her belief that she can leverage this perception to fulfill a moral responsibility to be kind and supportive of others:

“No, but I -- you know I sometimes when you meet people and you can sense the joy and the sadness if you open to them when they talk to you. […] And people always like to be around me cause I'm always smiling and laughing, so -- even strangers will walk up to me and want to talk to me. I'm like okay, what do you want to talk about? And I'll just listen to them. […] And this one guy, he was strung out but I didn't know that, I was, you know, I been through all that. I just listen to him. And he say I keep trying. I say well you just got to keep trying. And just keep trying, don't give up you know.”

This interpretation is also compatible with the finding that Openness to Experience is strongly associated with quest-religiosity (Saroglou, 2002; 2010), which means that more Open individuals are somewhat more likely to view transcendent experiences within the context of a life-long search for spiritual understanding. McAdams and colleagues discovered that people higher in Openness generally tend to give more elaborative, reflective, and cohesive narrative accounts during life-story interviews (2004). Thus, agentic narration of spiritual experiences might be reflective a more quest-like orientation towards religiosity. The association between

Openness and agency may be driven by a tendency of people higher in Openness to position themselves at the center of their spiritual experiences, emphasizing what they learned from each experience and how it contributed to a life-long search for spiritual understanding. One participant high in Openness narrated his spiritual experience in this way, highlighting his self-

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 30 directed search for spiritual meaning when asked to reflect on what his transcendent experience says about him:

“It says I am a seeker and in my heart a mystic and a non-conformist and, and that has in fact been a problem my whole life and will continue to be […] So, again, but, it reinforced this idea of a seeker, that this, this is really what I'm interested in. And to this day now, since I've had that experience, I don't see the world the same, I just don't.”

Personality and the Narration of Spiritual Elements

With respect to the agency of spiritual forces themselves (the theme of SA in narrative accounts), Openness to experience showed a negative association in the multiple regression analysis. In the correlational results, Neuroticism, was also negatively associated with the tendency to emphasize the presumed agency or intention of spiritual forces. In the correlational analyses (but not in multiple regression), Extraversion, Conscientiousness, and Agreeableness were all positively related to this theme. Given that the majority of religious participants in this sample practiced Abrahamic religions (e.g. Judaism and Christianity), which often characterize spiritual forces as anthropomorphic and deliberate (Kay et al., 2009), it is likely that many of the narrative accounts which attribute intentionality to spiritual phenomena reflect these belief systems. Such an interpretation is consistent with the consistent finding that these two traits—

Agreeableness and Conscientiousness—are strongly related to conventional religious practice and belief (Saroglou, 2002; 2010).

Openness was the only trait associated with the spiritual action/intent theme when all other personality and demographic variables were controlled for. Openness is already negatively associated with more fundamentalist forms of religiosity in previous literature (MacDonald,

2000), so the results regarding Openness and spiritual action/intent probably reflect an

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 31 inclination of more Open individuals to eschew fundamentalist frameworks offered by these religions that imagine the divine as highly anthropomorphized.  People high in Openess may adopt an abstracted and intellectualized form of religion, which might incline them toward less personification of the divine, and less projected agency. For adults high in Openness, religion and spirituality may be more about abstract principles and quests of self-actualization than about the intentional actions of spiritual beings.

Regarding the associations between Neuroticism and Extraversion and the theme of spiritual intent, there is a smaller body of prior research investigating these relationships. Some studies suggest that more Extraverted people are attracted to communal elements of religious worship (Saroglou, 2002; Womble et al., 2013), yet this does not fully account for narrative styles employed by more Extraverted people in this study. Perhaps it is more useful to consider spiritual action/intent’s relationship with Extraversion alongside its negative relationship with

Neuroticism. Many personality psychologists describe Extraversion as a protective factor against mental illness because it is associated with an inclination to experience more positive emotions, whereas Neuroticism is viewed as a risk factor because of its relationship to negative emotionality (Labbé & Fobes 2009; Smillie et al., 2019; Womble et al., 2013). Therefore, the relationship discovered in this study between Extraversion, Neuroticism, and a tendency to view spiritual phenomena as deliberate may actually speak to a profound, positive, and self-affirming emotional quality of adopting such spiritual schemas. In fact, the data shows that an emphasis on spiritual agency may be as or even more strongly connected to emotional stability and self- affirmation than an emphasis on narrator agency in these scenes.

With respect to spiritual proximity (SP), no personality variables predicted this theme once demographic effects were taken into consideration. But in the correlational analyses,

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 32

Extraversion related to the theme of spiritual proximity, suggesting that viewing spiritual forces as deliberate, normative, and omnipresent may be related to more emotionally positive and self- affirming dispositions. This also seems likely when considering that Openness was not associated with spiritual proximity, despite the initial hypothesis. As discussed, Openness to

Experience is more associated with intellect and cognitive styles, whereas Extraversion is somewhat more related to emotional dispositions. Evidently, the tendency to describe omnipresent and accessible spiritual forces is more closely linked with an energetic, upbeat disposition than an imaginative and inquisitive mind. For example, consider the response given by one participant who was relatively high in Extraversion, low in Neuroticism, and average in

Openness compared to the rest of the sample as she describes the feeling of discovering a direct, personal relationship with God:

“I said everything is going to be okay. And it was that power; it was the -- I know it was

[…] God talking to me. A calm.  I was feeling calm.  I was feeling okay. You know, it's okay. Everything's gonna be okay. It was probably one -- another one of those turning points in my life where I realized there were something greater than myself […] I had to rely on that faith. I had to turn to God at that point in my life. And that is the point in my life where everything became not religious but became very spiritual.”

This participant’s response is rife with themes of spiritual intent and spiritual proximity and reflects the profound sense of peace and acceptance that she associates with feeling that her life is in God’s hands. These strong emotional expressions are characteristic of many of the responses given to this section of the LSI, further substantiating William James’s (1902) claim that experiences of divine insight or connection come with their own unique pattern of emotional experiences.

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 33

Spiritual Action/Intent vs. Narrator Agency

Regarding the narrative themes investigated in this study, there is more consideration to be had regarding the relationship between Spiritual Action/Intent and Narrator Agency. While

NA is a long-standing and well-established theme used in life stories research, the SA coding scheme was developed specifically for the purposes of this study. As it turns out, an inclination to emphasize one’s own agency was moderately associated with an inclination to deemphasize the deliberate intention of spiritual beings (see Table 2). On the surface, it seems that NA and SA are mutually exclusive themes, which parallels how psychologists understand locus of control

(LOC). Locus of control refers to whether a person believes control over events in their lives lies primarily in themselves or in external forces such as other people, luck, or nature (Holder &

Levi, 1988). Narrator Agency and LOC do seem to be similar themes, as agentic storytelling does often reflect an internal LOC. Furthermore, more agentic storytelling is associated with mental health benefits (Adler, 2012), whereas an external LOC appears linked to higher levels of anxiety and depression (Holder & Levi, 1988). It seems then, that by extension, having an external LOC would be analogous to SA in the same way having an internal LOC is analogous to more agentic storytelling.

However, I caution against this comparison for a couple of reasons. First, NA is conceptually distinct from having an internal LOC because it also involves describing one’s realized actions and successes, whereas LOC only refers to beliefs about who has potential control over a given outcome (Adler, 2012). Secondly, the finding that SA is related to

Extraversion and low Neuroticism in the correlational analyses actually suggests that including some degree of SA in personal narration is reflective of a more emotionally stable personality profile, rather than one prone to anxiety or depression (Smillie et al., 2019; Womble et al., 2013).

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 34

Indeed, an inclination for a narrative style high in SA may even be a protective factor against anxiety and depression because it offers superior coping mechanisms for stress relief (Berry &

York, 2011; Labbé & Fobes, 2010).

Thus, it seems that SA may be its own, unique complement to NA, and that a balance of the two is ideal for psychological health and existential well-being. Almost all participants in this sample were able to offer a unique spiritual experience, regardless of whether or not they viewed themselves as religious or spiritual. This suggests that with only minimal prompting, all healthy, developed adults are able to engage with ideas of spiritual action and intentionality to some degree, much like how they are able to engage with ideas about their own agency. I propose that further life stories research would benefit from including a spiritually grounded framework that carefully tracks how people make sense of the forces and phenomena beyond their control, and relating it to how humans describe causality, responsibility, and empowerment.

Gender and Race

The results from this study indicate that the demographic variables of gender and race are highly associated with certain ways of discussing spiritual experiences. Men in this study were significantly more likely than women to emphasize their own agency when narrating spiritual experiences, whereas women were much more likely to emphasize the intentional action of spiritual forces. These effects were shown in especially sharp relief when all personality variables and race were controlled for. The multiple regression analysis revealed that race was the strongest independent predictor of narrative styles, more so than gender and any personality trait. Black participants were much more likely than white participants to narrate spiritual forces as actively influencing their lives and working closely with them to achieve their desired outcomes or further their spiritual understanding.

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 35

Developmental research has found that all Big 5 personality traits undergo some degree of change over the course of a life time, with certain stages of life inducing especially strong directional changes in most people (John, 2021). On the other hand, demographic variables like gender and race are typically stable over a lifetime and do not change from birth. Therefore, using correlations to study the relationship between personality and spirituality does little to uncover the mystery of one’s causal influence on the other. However, since gender and race do not change throughout a participant’s lifetime, it seems that these variables precede the development of one’s spiritual beliefs. Perhaps a life time of socialization associated with being male or female, or Black or white, strongly contributes to how participants develop their spiritual beliefs.

As it pertains to gender, some previous studies have found that women tend to report higher levels of religiosity than men. Some researchers have hypothesized that this finding may be driven by a relationship to psychoticism, since women are typically lower in psychoticism than men (Lynn & Martin, 1997; Penny et al., 2015). That women were more likely than men to also narrate spiritual beings as active and intentional further supports the argument that viewing spiritual beings in this way may be reflective positive mental health. Yet, it was men who were more likely than women to emphasize their own agency in these themes, a narrative tendency which has already been shown to be significantly related to positive mental health (Adler, 2008).

Once again, it seems that some mix of both narrative tendencies is ideal from a mental health perspective.

Regarding race, the finding that Black participants seem to employ more concrete and encompassing spiritual frameworks when describing their spiritual experiences is not surprising, considering the previous literature which has documented the profound role of spirituality and

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 36 religiosity for many communities across the African diaspora (Jagers & Smith, 1996). The results of this study are consistent with the findings that Black communities, across the globe, traditionally place very high value in spiritual connection and understanding and tend to view most or all ordinary phenomena as having some spiritual impetus or consequence (Jagers &

Smith, 1996). The results of this study are also consonant with the enduring finding that Black

Americans are the most religiously involved racial group in the country (Blaine & Crocker,

1995). That Black participants so strongly reflected these spiritual beliefs in their narration of spiritual experiences serves as one illustration of how this religious engagement is not only extrinsic, but also deeply intrinsic in nature.

Furthermore, race was not a significant predictor of narrator agency, which strengthens the notion that narrator agency and spiritual action/intent are compatible, complementary themes in autobiographical reasoning. Even though black participants were much more likely to view spiritual forces as active and having infinite agency, this did not necessarily come at the cost of a decreased emphasis on personal agency. This is even further evidence that spiritual reasoning is a profound component of the autobiographical understanding of the self, integrated to varying degrees with other established themes autobiographical reasoning. The strong correlation between Spiritual Proximity and Spiritual Action/Intent observed in the sample further strengthens this notion, as it might be that those who believe spiritual beings to be more omnipresent and accessible are more likely to view spiritual actions as relevant to their own actions. Conversely, those who feel unable to communicate with or understand the actions of spiritual beings may come to view spiritual forces as essentially external, independent, and even conflicting with their own agency. This could mean that the Black and white participants in this

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 37 study demonstrated alternative frameworks for understanding the relationship between spiritual phenomena and one’s own power, agency, and decision making.

Limitations

One of the primary limitations to this study is the narrow population from which this sample was drawn. This study only considered the spiritual beliefs of midlife adults living in the

Midwest, many of whom were slightly more educated than the average American citizen. Further research is needed to see whether these described associations are true of Americans across a wider variety of ages, income and education levels, racial groups, and geographic locations.

Additionally, developmental psychologists have found aging to impact personality variables in a similar fashion across all individuals, especially Conscientiousness and Neuroticism (Hopwood et al., 2011 & Shiner, 2019; Jackson & Hill, 2019), which may obscure subtler relationships between personality and the narration of spiritual belief that may be observable in a younger sample.

Secondly, although initially conceived as separate narrative themes, the spiritual action/intent and spiritual proximity coding systems were highly correlated (see Table 2), meaning that there was significantly more overlap between these themes than initially anticipated. The spiritual action coding system was intended to track how much participants believe spiritual forces intentionally move them towards a new goal or realization, regardless of whether the participant anticipated receiving spiritual aid. The logic of this system was to track how much participants’ descriptions of spiritual forces resemble the popular conception of God shared by many Abrahamic religions as an omniscient, omnipotent, and morally pure entity with infinite agency. Lower scores do not necessarily indicate that participants do not have an extensive and highly developed spiritual worldview. For instance, an individual who views

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 38 spiritual forces as latent reservoirs of power, which can be controlled through means like magic or witchcraft, may narrate their spiritual experience with little emphasis placed on spiritual action or intent. However, this person’s narrative could be high in spiritual proximity if they believed they could access these magical powers at will, at any place. On the other hand, a participant who is not intrinsically religious, but still holds many fundamentalist Christian beliefs may narrate an instance where God acts intentionally to affect change, while also implying that such events are confined to specific religious ceremonies or holy locations. This participant’s narrative would them be high in themes of spiritual action but low in themes of spiritual proximity since he believes God can act independently, but only does so in limited instances.

That these coding systems were highly correlated is likely due to the population of the sample, the majority of whom subscribe to Abrahamic religious beliefs that depict good as highly active and intentional, and highly accessible (Kay et al., 2009). Therefore, for many participants in this sample, both the spiritual action/intent and spiritual proximity themes are likely a part of their spiritual belief systems, so it follows that these themes would be correlated in this study. However, the coding systems for these themes were developed to track what people say, rather than what they believe, since the scenes used for this study do not ask participants to elaborate extensively on the features of their spiritual belief systems. That these two coding schemes are so highly correlated does likely reflect a flaw in the coding system, in that there is too much overlap in the language we used to distinguish high spiritual action and high spiritual proximity. Future research would benefit from revisiting these coding systems and reconfiguring them so that they account for more distinct verbiage.

Furthermore, the data in this study was taken from a short section of a long interview about participant’s lives. More research is needed to understand how participants discuss their

PERSONALITY AND SPIRITUALITY 39 spiritual beliefs in other scenes in the LSI, and how this may differently relate to personality variables and the Big 5. Since this study was designed to be a preliminary investigation of the narration of spiritual experience in the LSI, religious denominations were not considered in data analysis. Future research into the narration of spiritual experiences may benefit from a consideration of how people of different denominations employ different spiritual schemas and narrative tendencies, such as what settings, events, and characters are included in the scene.

Directions for Future Research

In this study, Black and white participants demonstrated two distinctly different ways of understanding how spiritual phenomena relate to one’s own actions and sense of agency. This finding complicates prior research which has investigated the usefulness of spiritual or religious belief systems for promoting positive mental, emotional, and physical health. Perhaps future research could stand to reexamine the ways individuals employ their spiritual beliefs as coping mechanisms with added attention paid to the ways participants conceive of spiritual agency, their own agency, and the accessibility of spiritual forces. Such findings could have significant implications on clinical practices that seek to empower clients and renew their sense of control, responsibility, and agency while also balancing the reality that some events are simply beyond our control.

Additionally, at a social communal level, these findings have strong implications for understanding the ways communities respond to successes, hardships, and collective traumas.

The understood relationship between spiritual power and human agency demonstrated by Black participants in this study offers a glimpse into psychological factors that facilitate collective organizing, healing, and celebration in various communities, even in the face of overwhelming hardships.

Seeing What You Want: Prior Belief Biases Perception of Correlation in Scatterplots Chase Stokes, Cindy Xiong, Steve Franconeri

Background

Balcetis, E., & Dunning, D. (2006). See what you want to see: motivational influences on visual perception. Journal of personality and social psychology, 91(4), 612. Luo, Y., & Zhao, J. (2019). Motivated attention in climate change perception and action. Frontiers in psychology, 10, 1541.

References

295 adults from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk completed a Qualtrics survey with the following sections.

Context variable pairs other than the ones pictured were: Number of people whose names begin with “T”/Number of trees in a neighborhood, and Total amount of rain in the US/Number of US lawyers.

Methods

In predicting error through considering the different between no-context and context correlation ratings of the same scatterplot, no significant effect of condition or topic was found. However, there was a significant effect of belief, as can be observed through the general upwards trend of average difference visualized below. Participants with stronger beliefs in the relationship depicted tended to judge the scatterplots with context as having a stronger correlation than the same scatterplots without context.

So, a real-world application or context on a scatterplot can alter correlation estimation in comparison to the very same scatterplots without said context. This difference may depend on the strength of the belief around the topic, with greater belief showing overestimation. Future work should examine other types of visualizations, as well as investigate more precise impacts of belief on judgment and interpretation of visualizations.

Contact chasestokes@u.northwestern.edu

Data strive to be objective and definitive, but our perceptions and interpretations of them carry bias from our expectations and motivations. A few examples of this have been studied previously (see right).

Could prior beliefs also bias our perception of relations depicted in visualized data? Correlation estimations in scatterplots act as a case study to expand understanding of this process.

Training: Participants received an explanation of correlation and feedback on practice estimations of three scatterplots to improve future accuracy.

No-context Estimation: Participants estimated the correlation of a set of scatterplots with X and Y on the axes, like the training scatterplots (but did not receive feedback or the true correlation).

Distractor Task: Participants reported their first three conclusions after viewing a bar graph.

Context Estimation: Participants estimated the correlation of a set of scatterplots with real-world variable pairs on the axes.

Belief Questions: Participants reported their own beliefs about the relationships between the real-world variables on the context graphs.

Effects of Hearing Loss on Selective Attention from Childhood to Adulthood

Shreya Sriram, Kristi Ward, & Tina Grieco-Calub 1The Roxelyn & Richard Pepper Department of Communication Sciences & Disorders, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL email: shreyasriram2022@u.northwestern.edu

• Crandell, C. C., & Smaldino, J. J. (2000). Classroom Acoustics for Children With Normal Hearing and With Hearing Impairment. Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools, 31(4), 362–370. • Leibold, L. J., & Buss, E. (2013). Children's identification of consonants in a speech-shaped noise or a two-talker masker. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. • Oberfeld, D., & Klöckner-Nowotny, F. (2016, August 31). Individual differences in selective attention predict speech identification at a cocktail party. eLife Journal. • Ruggles, D., Shinn-Cunningham, B. Spatial Selective Auditory Attention in the Presence of Reverberant Energy: Individual Differences in Normal-Hearing Listeners. JARO 12, 395– 405 (2011). • Shinn-Cunningham, B., Best, V., & Lee, A. K. (2017). Auditory object formation and selection. In The auditory system at the cocktail party (pp. 7-40). Springer, Cham.

• Shreya Sriram would like to thank the Northwestern Hearing and Language Lab for the support in data collection and guidance, especially from her mentors Dr. Tina Grieco-Calub and Kristi Ward and members of the lab, especially Natalie Sliskovich. Shreya is incredibly grateful for the opportunity to spearhead this related initiative and for the time and effort of the participants in this study. Lastly, Shreya would like to extend her gratitude to the Northwestern Office of Undergraduate Research for the chance to present her research.

• Listeners have difficulty understanding speech in environments that have multiple sound sources (i.e., background noise). To improve speech perception in these scenarios, listeners must allocate more of their attention to the speech signal and inhibit their attention to the background noise. Thus, the inability to selectively attend to speech would likely further impair speech recognition accuracy.

• This is especially important for listeners with hearing loss, who have difficulty understanding speech even with the use of hearing devices (e.g., hearing aids or cochlear implants). In considering the proposed role of selective attention in speech recognition, it is possible that part of the reason listeners with hearing loss experience poor speech understanding is due to impaired selective attention.

• Previous research has demonstrated this relation in children with hearing loss. However, the extent of this relation in adulthood remains unknown. As selective attention is known to improve with age, the maturation of attentional processes may compensate for differences that are seen in children.

This preliminary study investigates whether adults with hearing loss demonstrate greater difficulty attending to a target stream than adults with normal hearing.

• Future research is needed to delineate these possibilities. Testing this phenomenon with adults with less severe hearing loss or with better aided hearing functionality would allow distinction between audibility and selective attention. • Furthermore, using a larger sample size would allow for more quantitative conclusions to be drawn.

• Stimuli consisted of single-syllable words (ACD; left) or illustrated images (VCD; right). ISI_75 is the amount of time between each presentation of stimuli, a value based on performance in pre-testing.

• Participants were simultaneously presented with two auditory streams (ACD) or two visual streams (VCD). In the ACD task, the two streams were a male voice (F0 = 125 Hz) and female voice (F0 = 200 Hz). In the VCD task, the two streams were a right and left stream.

• Each stream contained standard stimuli (90% occurrence) and deviant stimuli (10% occurrence). Adults were instructed to respond (via keypress) to deviants in the target stream (*), but not the distractor stream (✕). Responses were registered as either a target or distractor hit if within 2 sec of stimuli presentation.

• Deviant stimuli were derived from standard stimuli by transposing the F0 by +3 semitones (ACD) or increasing the saturation of the background by 40% (VCD).

• Performance was quantified by the dependent variables in Figures 2 and 3: • hit rate and speed of responses to deviants in the target stream (% target hits) • hit rate and speed of responses to deviants in the distractor stream (% distractor hits) • relative proportion of responses to deviants in the target and distractor streams (response sensitivity) • responses to non-deviant stimuli (false alarms)

This was a preliminary study in which we did not have sufficient power to execute statistical analyses. Therefore we depended on visual inspection of the data to discuss some early findings:

• We observed differences in the adults’ performance in the ACD task where adults with HL had more difficulty selectively attending to the target stream than NH adults. (Figure 2).

• All adults demonstrated similar ability to selectively attend to the target stream and inhibit the distractor stream in the VCD task. (Figure 3)

• With this limited data set, it is difficult to say whether adults with NH and HL are similarly able to selectively attend to a target stream. Performance on the ACD task in the present study appears to have been influenced by aided hearing sensitivity in adults with HL, which may have resulted in inadequate access to the stimuli’s acoustic characteristics.

• Overall, the ability to selectively attend to the target stream and inhibit the distractor stream in both ACD and VCD tasks is seen to improve from childhood to adulthood. (Figure 2 & 3) This suggests that the developmental trajectory of selective attention is positive, but the present results do not indicate whether these attentional capabilities have matured enough in adults with HL to overcome deficits induced by hearing loss.

• Figure 4 shows the relationship between aided hearing sensitivity and response sensitivity for each task. A relationship between audibility, measured by aided HFPTA, and response sensitivity is only seen in the ACD task. As audibility decreased, the participant demonstrated increased difficulty in selectively attending and responding to the target stream deviants over the distractor stream. Unexpectedly, no relationship between aided hearing sensitivity and performance is seen in VCD.

• Selective attention is a domain-general cognitive resource and, as such, was expected to be reflected similarly in performance across the ACD and VCD tasks. Based on the relations displayed in Figure 4, it is possible that the performance of adults with HL on the ACD task is more reflective of impaired audibility than their selective attention, per se.

• Ultimately, it can be concluded that audibility is a key component in the ability of adults with HL to selectively attend to a target stream and inhibit a distractor stream.

label: Comparing approaches for estimating regional hemodynamic timing differences in BOLD-fMRI data
nurj_title: Comparing approaches for estimating regional hemodynamic timing differences in BOLD-fMRI data
text:
Title: Comparing approaches for estimating regional hemodynamic timing differences in BOLD-fMRI data

Authors: Jingxuan Gong, Molly G. Bright, Rachael C. Stickland Introduction Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is widely used to study neuronal functional connectivity. However, the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) signal demonstrates variable hemodynamic delays throughout the brain that should be accounted for in rs- fMRI analysis. BOLD-fMRI signals are also strongly influenced by carbon dioxide (CO2) [1], a strong vasodilator [2]. There are varying temporal offsets between CO2 fluctuations and BOLD signal changes due to measurement delay, vascular transit times and local vasodilatory dynamics. Previous studies have proposed using this temporal offset to correct for hemodynamic delays in fMRI data [3,4]. There is also evidence that it is easier to estimate hemodynamic timings in BOLD-fMRI data with breathing tasks compared to resting-state data [5,6]. We compare two approaches for estimating relative hemodynamic timings (RHT) in BOLD-fMRI data, with and without CO2 information. These methods are compared for two scans: resting-state only and resting-state preceded by breathing tasks to induce fluctuations in CO2. Methods 9 volunteers (6F; 26±4y) were scanned with a 3T Siemens Prisma and 64-channel head coil. A T1w scan was acquired for registration purposes. Two BOLD-weighted scans (GRE-EPI, TR/TE=1200/34ms; 2mm3; 60-slices, multi-band 4) were acquired: a rest scan preceded by a hypocapnic Cued Deep Breathing (CDB) task and a rest scan preceded by a hypercapnic Breath-Holding (BH) task. A nasal cannula and gas analyzer sampled expired CO2 levels. AFNI, FSL and MATLAB were used for analysis. fMRI scans were motion corrected and brain extracted. Scan data were grouped into 4 segments of equal duration (Fig1): 2 segments (BH+RESTBH, CDB+RESTCDB) included a breathing task followed by rest, and 2 segments included only the rest portion from each scan (REST BH, RESTCDB). The brain was parcellated into 104 regions using FSL’s Harvard Oxford Cortical and MNI atlases transformed to functional space. We compared two methods for estimating RHT between regions. BOLD-xcorr: the average BOLD signal from each region, with motion parameters and polynomial terms removed, was upsampled to 0.3s. For each pair of regions, RHT was measured using cross correlation (max shift ±9s). CO2- BOLD-GLM: HRF-convolved end-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) traces were shifted ±15s in 0.3s increments, then down-sampled to the TR. Multiple linear regression was performed, including polynomial and motion parameters and shifted ETCO2. Voxelwise lag was identified by the ETCO2 shift of the model with the largest R-squared [7]. An average

CO2-BOLD lag was found for each atlas region; RHT was represented by the lag difference between each pair of regions. RHT matrices were compared by taking the squared difference for each subject and averaging across subjects (mean squared error, MSE). Within-method agreement in RHT was assessed separately for segments that included breathing tasks and segments that only included rest. Between-method agreement was compared for each of the four data segments. Results Better agreement in RHT is visualized by lower MSE (Fig2). For the BOLD-xcorr method, RHT matrices agree more between breathing task segments, compared to between two REST segments (Fig2A). For the BOLD-CO2-GLM method, the RHT agreement is similar for both types of data segments (Fig2A). Between-method agreement was better in data segments including breathing tasks compared to REST only segments (Fig2B).

Conclusion Resting-state data show greater variability, both within and between methods, in measurements of RHT. The addition of a breathing task, inducing larger fluctuations in ETCO2 and therefore blood flow, results in better agreement. Further work is needed to understand the influence of single subject variability, partial volume effects and small regions of interest on these RHT estimates, as well as how either RHT measure relates to variation in task-activation hemodynamics.
