Introduction

Large public investment projects are crucial to urban developments. They are the key screw in the urban growth engine. They bring convenience, economic opportunities, improved aesthetics, and leisure amenities to a neighborhood. In order to maximize efficiency in the limited space in an urban area, a good public investment project should hit all criteria mentioned above. The 606 Bloomingdale Bike Trail seems to fit perfectly. It offers another route for people to commute to work; it creates jobs and attracts tourists from

Chicago or even other places; it is no longer an abandoned rail line but an artistic elevated bike trail; it provides green spaces for residents to exercise, walk, and relax. The 606

Bloomingdale Bike Trail would not only be a good infrastructure for the existing residents, but it would be an even greater selling point to attract new affluent residents. On the surface, this whole new development would be a great booster for surrounding neighborhoods. On the inside, however, it induces gentrification through abruptly changing the area’s physical landscapes, causing displacements of the indigenous residents and widening inequality within the community.

Gentrification takes on many forms in urban areas, from transportation infrastructure to environment beautifications and from revitalizing abandoned sites to promoting green spaces. These developments then attract affluent, educated, young, and generally white population to the once disinvested neighborhoods, creating a positive feedback by encouraging more public investment projects into the area. To the indigenous residents (or former residents), they are not only excluded from these amenities and benefits due to various discriminatory reasons (such as income, race, etc.), but they might also face the possibility of displacements.

Nonetheless, without these huge constructions of public investment projects to stimulate growth and create a positive feedback loop in the neighborhood, the community will forever be trapped in the spiral of disinvestments. Thus, the dilemma of whether to welcome and how to welcome these revitalization initiatives remains crucial to a neighborhood. In other words, how could and should developments be planned in order to minimize potential damage from gentrification? The answer would affect the balance between equity and economic developments and the consideration for indigenous residents.

The government, who is normally the core funder of public investment projects and ought to be the gatekeeper of equitable developments, often favors certain side due to various political agenda or simply time constraints.

Some may argue that gentrification is an inevitable outcome of economic development, but research in sociology has shown that institutions often exploit gentrification as a tool to stratify certain groups of people (Zuk et al., 2018). In other words, gentrification helps solidifying existing social hierarchy to ensure the superiority of the dominant group. As a sociologist, I am interested in measuring the degree of inequality gentrification creates in a neighborhood and its mechanism of changes. The degree of inequality would not only reflect on common socioeconomic status indicators, such as household income, property values, tenure status, etc. It would also indirectly influence social factors like racial composition, educational attainment, and residential stability.

In order to examine how large public investment projects can lead to gentrification, this thesis dives into a case study on Chicago 606 Bike Trail from a quantitative approach, namely the difference-in-difference method. The bike trail used to be an abandoned rail line, and the City of Chicago partnered with Friends of the Bloomingdale Trail (an organization formed by local residents) and The Trust for Public Land (a non-profit organization known for raising funds and oversee park constructions) to transform it into an elevated trail

(Rigolon & Németh, 2018). The trail’s groundbreaking was in 2013, and it was made open to the public in 2015. The mixed views since then highlight the unequal nature this project reinforces on the surrounding neighborhoods. In a study by Smith and colleagues (2016), they show that the housing market has surged since the groundbreaking of the 606. However, both Rigolon and Németh (2018) and Smith et al. (2016) studies did not show the 606’s impacts beyond the housing market. Moreover, their main methods⎯interviews, archival research, and Hedonic Price Model⎯ failed to account changes over time. Thus, my study would build on their theory and drill deeper to discuss the overall phenomenon’s social implications. First, I ask to what extent has the 606 Bloomingdale Bike Trail, an example of huge public investment projects, influenced the housing affordability in the surrounding neighborhoods? However, housing affordability is just a number. To make that number significant, I will examine other commonly-studied aspects of gentrification in sociology.

Therefore, my second research question is: what impact does the 606 have on the surrounding neighborhoods’ social composition? My independent variable is the census tracts that are one mile within the 606 Bike Trail versus the non-606 census tracts in the rest of Chicago. My dependent variables are housing affordability, racial composition, educational attainment, percentage of migration, and percentage of renters. By answering these questions through testing these variables, I can evaluate the role the 606 Bike Trail plays and the extent of effect it has in terms of the gentrification process in those neighborhoods.

Literature Review

Gentrification Overview

Definition of Gentrification

Gentrification is an interdisciplinary term packaged with a lot of social factors, including such as but not limited to economic developments, community networks, political regimes, transportation planning, displacements, and racial segregation. The term

“gentrification” was first coined by Ruth Glass (1964), “One by one, many of the working class quarters of London have been invaded by the middle classes – upper and lower. Once this process of ‘gentrification’ starts in a district it goes on rapidly until all or most of the original working class occupiers are displaced and the whole social character of the district is changed.” Sharon Zukin (1987) argues that “gentrification may be described as a process of spatial and social differentiation.” Other scholars highlight the changes in population in a neighborhood, from lower-income residents to more affluent white middle-class newcomers, as an indicator for gentrification. This shift creates a division in social class and status among different social groups (Hackworth, 2002; Redfern, 2003; Lees et al., 2008; Ley, 1996;

Atkinson, 2000) While others may focus more on the socioeconomic status of the neighborhood (Owens, 2012; Davidson & Lees, 2005), some choose to analyze gentrification through a cultural lens and other demographic factors (Llyod, 2006; Hyra, 2017). In short, gentrification can be considered as changes in community spurred by various kinds of urban

(re)developments that are not initiated by indigenous residents, and gentrification transforms the neighborhood characteristics in demographic, lifestyle, and socioeconomic status. The process will continue to divide the neighborhood until the new population replaces the old one completely.

Indeed, defining gentrification is a challenging task itself, but its measurement seems harder to reach consensus (Barton, 2016). Regardless of which definition to center on, gentrification uses urban developments to drive segregation and distrust and hence increasing inequality between residents. With these traits in mind, there are a few ways to identify gentrifications. First, changes in physical landscapes are a common sign for gentrification in a qualitative case study report (Zukin et al., 2009; Hamnett & Whitelegg, 2006). For instance, the ethnic grocery store that were around the corner has suddenly turned into a chained or local high-end coffee shop. Usually, local boutique or chained stores symbolize higher price of consumption, comparing to dollar-stores or subsidized grocery markets. Second, census indicators such as median property values and household income are also a widely-used measurement for gentrification (Laska et al., 1982; Cervero & Duncan, 2004; Smith et al.,

2016) Third, scholars often examine neighborhood migration, both unforced and forced, to determine the extent of gentrification (Zuk et al. 2015; Freeman, 2005; Danley & Weaver,

2018). Since gentrification is such a unique process for each neighborhood in terms of its manifestation (Butler & Robson, 2001; Van Criekingen & Decroly, 2003), the best metric to evaluate gentrification is to study the intersection of its indicators. Ultimately, the goal is to study the changes happen over time, if any.

Neighborhood developments can often lead to displacement and thus gentrification, but it is not always the case. When the government and private developers are willing to listen to the voice of the local people, the neighborhood is more likely to undergo improvements instead of transformations. By assessing the local needs, diversified developments could lead to balanced and more opportunities for the locals to be involved

(Hupp, 2014). In addition, by retaining the ownership of the neighborhood, local residents can minimize risks of being displaced. Therefore, forming partnerships among non-profit organizations, local government, and the residents is the foundation of developments without displacements for community growth.

Types of Gentrification

Scholars categorize their observed phenomenon in different neighborhoods and regions into various types of gentrification, each of which explores a distinctive aspect of community change. There are two key types of gentrification based on past studies: political and cultural. Political gentrification focuses on urban renewal projects initiated by the government, with help from private sectors. Local government implements specific plans to intentionally exclude certain social groups or encourage certain development direction, such as promoting a certain type of business (Owens, 2012). The goal is often to appeal to certain voter groups or attract wealthier tax bases.

Cultural gentrification examines qualitative components that reflect residents’ lifestyle in a neighborhood. These literatures focus more on the character of a city or a community. Richard Llyod (2006) talks about how affordable neighborhoods attract artists, and that leads to a sense of “coolness” around the area. Then, businesses such as cafes move in to cope with the “hippy” style, which is appealing to highly educated young professional.

The outcome of cultural gentrification, which is stated in Zukin’s Naked City (2009), is that gentrification has caused neighborhoods to be identical throughout the city, losing the authenticity of each ethnicity. To the indigenous residents in gentrifying neighborhoods, the amenities constructed associate with other cultural connotations that they do not think they belong to (Danley & Weaver, 2018). The shift in the consumption of urban spaces underscore the privilege of the newcomers, excluding the participation of original residents (Centner,

2008; Lloyd, 2006). As a result, the new pattern of spatial practices catalyzed by newcomers encourage a specific urban lifestyle that causes the vibrant cultural diversity to be forever lost.

Modern U.S. Gentrification: A Combination of Everything

Sociologists in the past have tried but struggled to study gentrification due to its complexity and the gentrification indicators they use. In the most recent review by Brown-

Saracino (2017) on gentrification, she points out that depends on how gentrification is defined and which variables are chosen to use in their project, the conclusion drawn can be totally different. In qualitative studies, scholars might study how the residents “feel” and

“think” about the neighborhood after developments. Sharon Zukin’s (2009) Naked City and

Richard Lloyd’s (2006) Neo-Bohemia focus on the subjective aspects of economic developments. On the other hand, research that takes a quantitative approach examine statistical data to broadly observe the trend of gentrification.

Regardless of which approach scholars take, consensus on the effect of gentrification and its extent is rarely reached. For one, gentrification might manifest itself differently at each site, and the nuances will lead to different insights for the researchers (Maciag, 2015;

Brown-Saracino, 2017). Furthermore, various stages during the gentrification process can also affect the researcher’s perspective. This characteristics makes comparative studies across cities difficult and therefore is hard to generalize results. Secondly, the path each scholar chooses to define gentrification will encourage them to focus on one particular area of gentrification. Due to this collective uncertainty, scholars often drill deeply into one outcome they think is resulting from gentrification. While this does help readers to conceptualize some consequences of gentrification such as displacements, racial segregation, or educational inequality, often time this strategy neglects other important counterparts of gentrification.

Worst of all, gentrification in modern American cities affects every outcome all at once.

Essentially, it is a hybrid form of past gentrification trends. Below I explore literature in each gentrification outcome to demonstrate how each sector is correlated. This association contributes to the evolvement of gentrification into cases like rail-to-trail projects, which are rehabilitation initiatives to turn abandoned rail lines into multi-purposeful bike trails.

Displacements, being one of the most notorious consequences of gentrification, are a common measurement of gentrification. What is displacement? Some argue that displacements occur when indigenous residents can no longer afford housing prices and are forced to move elsewhere (Atkinson, 2000; Newman & Wyly, 2006; Centner, 2012; Ding et al., 2016). Newman and Wyly (2006) point out that urban housing markets have been polarized, and decision-makers selectively de-regulate some policy to dismantle resistance to gentrification. In Ding and colleagues (2016) report, they use a longitudinal dataset to analyze the mobility rate in Philadelphia, and they state that vulnerable residents move, not because of gentrification but due to their likeliness to move. These quantitative aspects of displacement, though have documented observed phenomenon, are likely to miss out minute details. Other researchers argue that displacements can happen in the cultural and political realm (Brown-Saracino, 2009; Hyra, 2014; Zukin, 2009). Instead of being physically removed from the neighborhood, residents can feel the loss of neighborhood authenticity.

Displacement, in both quantitative and qualitative fields, is easily identified and multi- dimensional; thus, researchers often rely on displacements in a neighborhood to measure the damage caused by gentrification.

Damage from displacements is especially severe if it comes from political initiatives.

For instance, transit-oriented developments that enhance residents’ mobility are very likely to lead to higher property values (Kahn, 2007; Lin, 2002; Barton & Gibbons, 2017). Local governments may use transportation projects to connect targeted areas for future investments.

Another example would be rising urban green space as a result of the high demands over healthy urban lifestyle. The culture draws affluent newcomers, encouraging the government to launch more green projects to increase tax base. As a result, affordability will decrease, and residents would feel a sense of displacement pressure (Danley & Weaver, 2018). In addition, indigenous residents are often excluded from the planning process (Rigolon &

Németh, 2018; Curran & Hamilton, 2012). Thus, converting confined and fragmented spaces into local parks is a common strategy for the government to act as a gentrification agent.

Some might argue that as long as the developments are locally rooted, displacements are not going to happen. One counterexample is the surging amount of local arts. Although the artworks are perhaps built by local artists, the residents are often outsiders because white affluent people are demanding more artistic elements when choosing places to live (Brown-

Saracino, 2009; Zuk et al., 2018). Artworks may not have high logistical function, but they can contribute to community attractions and call for local and other regional tourists. In essence, the effect artworks have on gentrification process is more indirect, and they will reshape people’s perception for the community and increase people’s desire of the neighborhood’s properties.

Besides displacements, sociologists also love to investigate racial tension in gentrifying neighborhoods. Neighborhoods with people of color are predominantly disinvested, with fewer community attractions. Indeed, public amenities appeal more to relatively well-off residents, but racial composition is one consideration for people when deciding where to live

(Bader et al., 2015). In other words, neighborhoods with higher proportion of people of color hardly attract white residents. At the same time, white residents are usually more educated and affluent. The lack of presence of the wealthier group gives no incentive to the government or private developers to invest in the area. This negative spiral is exacerbated when racial preference of a neighborhood is systematically biased (Krysan et al., 2017). On the other hand, when white young professionals do move in, tensions between racial groups heighten (Hwang & Sampson, 2014). Governments would even intervene by demolishing public housings in order to initiate redevelopment plan (Goetz, 2011). Last but not least, racial segregation is hard to break; when black and white communities undergo gentrification, people still move into the place of their color (Solari, 2012; Timberlake &

Johns-Wolfe, 2017).

A sized portion of sociological research predict gentrification through education, as literature has shown that people who have higher income to afford more affluent neighborhoods often have higher educational attainment. Young professionals, usually college graduate, desire neighborhoods that are close to work and provide community attractions. In the long run, people who have higher educational attainment will be able to fund more resources to local schooling. This type of developments, just like displacements and racial composition, creates a positive feedback loop because the invested school districts can now attract more young and affluent homebuyers (Varady & Raffel, 1996, Keels et al.,

2013).

By focusing on each individual outcome of gentrification, sociologists have gained insights on how developments are turned into gentrification and how gentrification exacerbates existing segregation and economic inequality between new and former residents.

These outcomes of gentrification⎯displacements, race, and education⎯are very important when assessing and predicting gentrification. However, these social factors are highly correlated with one another. For instance, white people are more likely to be well-educated, affluent, and therefore become the initiators of gentrification. If the studies only emphasize on any particular one, the picture of gentrification would only be partial. Essentially, modern- day gentrification is not all or none; it is rather a combination of everything. For example, a public investment project is both a transportation infrastructure and an urban green space, so simply focusing on residents’ mobility will ignore the cultural meaning behind having a park.

The same project is sprinkled with local artists’ mural design to increase the “human warmth” and “authenticity”. More factors have to be considered and thus complicate the whole analysis process. Race is likely to influence educational attainment and thus the school districts, and these changes will either increase or decrease property values, hence physically and mentally displacing indigenous residents. Therefore, only focusing on one particular outcome  is not enough to capture gentrification comprehensively. Depending on the level of development a neighborhood has, there could be many potential spurious variables, which is why modern gentrification is often a hybrid form of developments, affecting social outcomes all at once. This is exemplified in this thesis’s main subject: the 606 Bloomingdale Bike

Trail.

The 606 Rail-to-Trail Public Investment Project: A New, Contemporary Form of Urban

Gentrification

Modern urban public investment projects are multi-purposeful; they provide many functions and improve a neighborhood in many ways. For one, less space is available, so projects have to be more “efficient” to satisfy the demands of the community. Two, every development is interconnected with each other. For instance, transportation infrastructure might attract high-rise buildings because of the convenience it brings. To the city government and private developers, public investment projects can shape a neighborhood both physically and culturally in the most direct way, and they can help the government achieve the political agenda in the shortest amount of time. This is because massive public investment projects usually attract more housing developments and businesses. An underserved neighborhood may suddenly be seen as an ideal living space that contains high and loft condominiums and proximity to transit and amenities (Quastel et al., 2012). Building multi-purposeful public investment projects often encourage other strings of investments such as real estate, commerce, or tourism (Rigolon & Németh, 2018). In this way, the projects are not only going to increase property values, but they are also transforming the whole culture and demographic of the community. Paradoxically, underserved neighborhoods are less likely to attract infrastructure investment (Flanagan et al., 2016). Therefore, locations become very important. Abandoned sites are the most convenient because some forms of infrastructure already exist, and they can utilize the space and revitalize the surrounding regions. For this reason, a lot of abandoned rail lines were transformed into bike trails, such as Beltline in

Atlanta, Highland in New York, and Bloomingdale in Chicago (Rigolon & Németh, 2018;

Lang & Rothenburg, 2017; Immergluck & Balan, 2018).

The rail-to-trail projects demonstrate recent trend in such initiatives. They demonstrate the hybridity of American urban developments in the 21st century, and they can hardly be categorized into any specific type of gentrification since they pertain to a particular lifestyle, improves transportation, and creates urban recreational spaces. Furthermore, they are sustainable and environmentally friendly, and they generate jobs and attract tourism.

These investments rarely consider the need of a poor neighborhood. Instead, the planning committee often team with private developers so that they can use the new urban green spaces to market the neighborhoods with depressed property values (Rigolon & Németh,

2018; Immergluck, 2009; Roy, 2015). The issue is further complicated when racial components are introduced. First, parks echo different meanings to Blacks and Hispanic than white people, and this gap already creates the first layer of stratification (Danley & Weaver,

2018). To Blacks and Hispanic people, parks have a connotation of gangs and crimes, while in the eyes of white people, parks are often associated with family and socialization. Second, developers prefer lower racial diversity in an urban renewal project because racial stigma would lower the desirability of the neighborhood. The nature of these rail-to-trail projects is inherently exclusive, and this type of public investments is the best fuel for inequality.

In the case of the rail-to-trail public investment project in Chicago, the 606 Bike Trail is 2.7 miles long and 17 feet above the ground, and it runs between Ashland and Ridgeway

(“Bloomingdale Trail Facts”; “Getting There”).  The origin of the 606 Bike Trail dated way back in the 19th century, when railroads were the motors of American booming economy, especially in the cities. The rail line built along the Bloomingdale Road then was part of

Chicago and Pacific Railroads’ (C&P) huge plan to connect Chicago down the Mississippi

Banks, but the plan was put to a haul due to the company’s financial burdens. When C&P later merged with Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railroads (CM&StP), Chicago, the rail line’s origin, also turned into a populated, industrialized city. Unfortunately, the reliance of trains in a dense urban area also led to more accidents along the rail roads. Residents demanded measures to improve their safety, so the city responded by elevating a part of the rail (2.7 miles in total) above street level, which was finished in 1915. Over time, rail roads were less used due to developments of highways and other transportation methods. Plus, City of Chicago rezoned the area to residential use, intending to drive out factories. However,

Bloomingdale Trail still continued to operate with limited number of passengers and cargos until the operation completely ceased in 2001 (“Bloomingdale Trail History”).

The discussion of turning the Bloomingdale Line into a public space had since been a vital topic for local residents and the city government. For one, the area was heavily underserved. The dialogues precipitated into the formation of Friends of the Bloomingdale

Trail in 2003, a non-profit organization consisting of local residents. In 2006, the

Bloomingdale Trail Project was promoted by Local Initiatives Support Corporation’s (LISC)

New Communities Program, which proposed the construction of greenway along the former rail line. For instance, in the Logan Square Quality of Life Plan, the Friends of the

Bloomindale Trail reached out to The Trust for Public Land, a non-profit organization to raise funds for public parks, to raise public awareness (particularly the eyes of the local government). As for the engineering and design of the project, the Friends of the

Bloomingdale Trail contacted Chicago Department of Transportation (CDOT). Since this project fell under the category of parks, Chicago Park District also offered their supervisions, feedbacks, and, more importantly, some funding. The partnership between the locals, non- profit organizations, and the government ensured each side had representations to speak their minds. The project eventually spent 95 million dollars, which came from federal, state, local, and private donations (“FAQ: The 606”, 2020). The project broke the ground in 2013 and finished in 2015 with great efficiency because Mayor Rahm Emmanuel promised to finish the construction within his first term.

The enthusiasm from the local government and a small group of residents definitely accelerated the planning and construction of the 606 Bike Trail. The lack of time and consideration for other groups of residents turned the whole public investment project into a community asset that benefited specific groups of people. Studies in urban planning have shown that different government planning policy can lead to different results of gentrification. Baker and Lee (2017) study 14 U.S. cities with light rail transit and find that the ones in San Francisco are gentrifying but not the ones in Portland. Indeed, light rail transit developments are not like rail-to-trail projects. Yet, they both are in the realm of transportation. In the 606 planning process, many residents felt excluded, and their voices were silent (Rigolon & Németh, 2018). Unsurprisingly, these people were more likely to be either people of color or vulnerable residents.

When considering the 606 Bike Trail as a transportation infrastructure, only a specific group of people are using or able to use the bike trail to commute. The 606 Bike Trail is only

2.6 miles long; therefore, unless the person’s job is very close to where they live (which is one characteristics of developed and expensive neighborhoods), it is unlikely for the residents to use the bike trail to commute to work or travel. Admittedly, the 606 is not the most efficient way to travel. One can argue that it may be the most environmentally friendly, but it certainly cannot be counted as a rapid transit. The means of transportation, bicycle, entails the cultural connotation the 606 carries. Cycling ridership appeals to more affluent population because it symbolizes a type of privileged lifestyle (Flanagan et al., 2016). The perceptions of biking give great social values to such action as they belong to a higher social status. In other words, the 606 provides such a forum for people of that status, and, coincidentally, they are usually wealthier and will bring more investments with them to the area. Eventually, gentrification will continue to happen.

From an environmental perspective, the 606 is advocating for urban sustainable development, but it is also driving the housing affordability down in the surrounding community. The 606, as a park, is advertised as a selling point for realty groups. However, there was no consideration of creating buffers such as public housing or rent control when planning the 606 Bike Trail (Newman & Wyly, 2006; Rigolon & Németh, 2018). The dominant institutional ideology of “sustainability” and “sustainable development” is instead strengthening and solidifying the status quo of social inequalities (Gunder, 2006). When the local government does not intervene and even advocate for this growth of the real estate market, other people who are against of such superficial eco-developments will rather lose their voices. In return, agents of gentrification can continue to develop the neighborhood in their desired direction (Quastel, 2009). The effort to redevelop underutilized urban spaces so that the neighborhood is presented as “active living” and “walkable” is not only a straightforward green space initiative but also a forceful driver of local property values

(Immergluck & Balan, 2018). From a city government points of view, a rail-to-trail park project would greatly increase the property tax base. In short, the 606 is a wolf in sheep’s clothing, calling the name of sustainability and urban revitalization initiative but truly an advocate for gentrification underneath.

Not only did the city government and developers portray a functional (as in transportation) and recreational (as in parks) image of the 606 Bike Trail, they invited artists to decorate the bike trail, intending to raise its value culturally through beautifications effort.

In summary, the art spaces should reflect local social condition and provide a platform for local youth and multi-generational citizens to exhibit their artworks. The main planners of the

606, the City of Chicago, The Trust for Public Land, and Chicago Park District, will also invited their desired artists. The system basically insulates any opposition voice while deepening the gap between wealthy and poor residents. Firstly, the artworks should be locally recognized, which will increase the “authenticity” of the bike trail. This “authenticity” is rather another mechanism to attract new and affluent residents. Secondly, the agencies can basically censor what kind of artworks and messages they want to exhibit on the 606 through choosing their partners and artists. As a result, the division within the community is widened since opposition voice is silenced. Segregation is reinforced, and the whole gentrification process is exacerbated.

The 606 is not just a part of transportation infrastructure, urban green spaces, and artworks but a combination of all three of them. Each individual section already enlightens sociologists about the nature, mechanism, process, and consequences of gentrification. Yet, the intersection part is yet to be studied. Although the literature on gentrification is with traditions, comprehensive examination over recent urban development initiatives is quite a young one, especially studies over rail-to-trail projects. It is because this type of projects only emerges in the last decade. However, these projects are actually the newest form of gentrification, demonstrating its evolving and chaotic nature. Two studies specifically on the

606 have demonstrated the negative impacts the trail has on the neighborhoods’ housing markets (Smith et al., 2016; Rigolon & Németh, 2018). Smith and colleagues (2016) compare the median property values between the west and the east side of the trail, and they conclude that there is a division in terms of price increase between the two sides. However, the study falls short in terms of analyzing other demographic factors such as migration or racial composition. The method it implements, Hedonic Pricing Index, can only relate housing prices and capture the residents’ willingness to pay, but they cannot consider potential social factors. The other study takes a mixed methods approach to investigate the planning process of the 606 (Rigolon & Németh, 2018). They record several census factors such as median income to provide descriptive statistics of the area, and they conduct interviews with 16 key actors to obtain information and perception on the planning. However, their qualitative method overly emphasize the significance of the planning while neglecting important variables (Brown-Saracino, 2017). Overall, although there are already two existing studies on the 606, their methods are inadequate to explain the social implications of the phenomenon.

Additionally, their research only scratch the surface by reporting their observed data, without analyzing the data with consideration over gentrification’s social effects. Therefore, my research fills the gap by looking at the housing affordability and the surrounding neighborhoods’ social composition after the trail made public since time is an important variable for gentrification. This project also contributes to the relatively young literature in sociology on modern hybrid form of public investment projects and its relationship with gentrification.

Theory and Hypothesis

In this study, I built my definition of gentrification on top of Glass’s definition. I defined gentrification as the process of replacing and displacing indigenous residents through urban development or revitalization initiatives until the culture and population is completely changed. Urban developments can take many forms, from public investment projects to private developers and private funding to residents’ personal initiatives. As indicated in the

Rigolon and Németh’s (2018) research, the partnerships among the City of Chicago (and

Chicago Park District), The Trust of Public Land, and the Friends of the Bloomingdale Trail exactly form this triangle relationship that reinforces gentrification and marginalize vulnerable and financially deprived residents. The marginalized residents eventually face threats, or at least the pressure, from displacements. In Marcuse’s theory on displacement, residents are either directly forced out of the neighborhoods when landlords drastically increase the rent or heightening displacement pressure through visible and foreign economic and community changes (Marcuse, 1985). Examples of displacement pressure would be a high-end and locally owned boutique store that indigenous residents cannot afford. Although they are still living in the neighborhood, these buildings rise an invisible wall and block them from their community power. This displacement pressure will not necessarily dislocate indigenous residents, but it will widen the segregation within the community.

Given that the 606 Bike Trail is a hybrid form of gentrification for being transportation infrastructure, urban green space, and local art works, I theorized that it would lead to gentrification based on the past findings discussed in the literature review section. To assess the effect of these mechanisms on the surrounding neighborhoods, I investigated the gentrification outcomes mentioned earlier.

The dominant group that reinforces displacements is usually whiter, more educated, and more affluent than the inferior party. A lot of past research in sociology has documented the social composition of gentrification, especially on race (Bader et al., 2015; Krysan et al.,

2009; Hwang & Sampson, 2014). In these studies, residents of color have attempted to resist developments in their own areas, but they are eventually displaced as the living cost has become too high for them. Eventually, the population is transformed into a white space.

Danley and Weaver (2018) further expands on this theory of white space; it creates a sense of unwelcomeness for residents of color and pledges to a specific type of lifestyle that can only be afforded by affluent population. Therefore, the first hypothesis is as follows:

Hypothesis One: 606 encourages more white, affluent, and educated population to move in, while displacing or segregating people of color or indigenous residents.

This study on the 606 will not only focus on the social compositions of the bike trail’s surrounding neighborhoods but also the housing affordability in the areas. Zuk and colleagues (2018) indicate that desired public investments such as transit could lead to higher rents and living expenses in their reviews of public investment and gentrification. The 606, being the new community attraction, will drive the housing demand up, but the supply still remains the same. In addition, private developers could demolish old buildings in order to rehabilitate into appealing single town-homes. Consequently, the neighborhood might lose affordable housing and low-income residents while blocking lower socioeconomic status residents from moving in. One study has shown demonstrate that the housing prices on the both sides but particularly the west part of the trail went up after the groundbreaking of the project (Smith et al., 2016). My second hypothesis built on their conclusion to study the results from a different timeframe and method so that it could be further validated. My second hypothesis is as follows:

Hypothesis Two: The 606 public investment project will lower the housing affordability in the surrounding neighborhoods.

Nevertheless, not all neighborhoods exposed to the 606 would experience the same amount of influences. In other words, gentrification is the most apparent at margins. It affects the disinvested neighborhoods that are undergoing initial redevelopment process the most.

Lees and colleagues (2008) argue that in order for a neighborhood to experience residential gentrification, it must be an underserved neighborhood. The introduction of the 606 to already-gentrified neighborhoods (such as West Town in this case) will not have a great effect since the social composition already matches with the one mentioned in Hypothesis

One. Thus, my last hypothesis argue:

Hypothesis Three: The impacts of the 606 would be greater in disinvested neighborhoods than already-affluent and developed areas. If my findings matched with my three hypotheses, I would identify a steep growing trend on both housing prices and proportion of white, affluent, and educated people in the study site. I expected more people of color moving out after the trail was made open to the public. If the displacement effect is not significantly strong, I might notice exacerbated segregation within the neighborhood, which can be seen by comparing the growth and declines in property values and demographic changes between already-affluent neighborhoods and the disinvested ones.

Methods and Data

The main goal of this research project was to examine the changes in social composition and housing affordability in the surrounding neighborhoods of the 606

Bloomingdale Bike Trail using census tracts from 2010 to 2017. One issue with the former studies (Smith et al., 2016; Rigolon & Németh, 2018) and especially the one done by Smith and his colleagues is that the Hedonic Price regression model can only calculate housing prices. It also assumes every buyer has full knowledge on the market and power to choose what they prefer, if given enough resources. These calculations cannot reflect social changes happened throughout 2010 to 2017, during when the 606 was planned, constructed, and made open to public. Therefore, a regression model that can encompass social composition variables is essential for this project. Hence, I selected the difference-in-differences model.

The basic structure to achieve this goal was to divide the census tracts into two groups: one with the treatment of the 606 Bike Trail and the one without. The two groups were then compared with time series and other independent variables. The coefficients acquired at the end would provide insights of the question: to what extent has the 606 Bike Trail socially influenced the surrounding neighborhoods?

This study took a quantitative approach because it was best to examine changes over time. My methodology enabled me to comprehensively gather empirical evidence and hence minimizing potential spurious variables and alternative explanations. Of course, I could rely on ethnographic studies and anecdotal evidences. Nevertheless, gentrification happening in the surrounding neighborhoods complicates the process to track down indigenous residents since they might already be displaced. A lot of residents also recently moved in to the area, so using qualitative evidences would potentially be less accurate.

Data Collection

Quantitative longitudinal data collection for this study contained census tract level data between 2010 to 2017 from American Community Survey via the portal of National

Historical Geographical Information System (NHGIS) in Integrated Public Use Microdata

(IPUMS). American Community Survey is a yearly report based on an on-going survey to estimate different demographic information of Americans. Also, there were seven indicator variables created manually: whether the tract is exposed to the 606 within a mile, whether the observation is made after the 606 made open to the public, the interaction of the 606 and time, whether the tract is considered as non-affluent, the interaction term between being non- affluency and the 606, the interaction term between being non-affluency and time, and the interaction term of all three together (which will be further discussed in the section below).

To construct my master dataset, I first imported my data and shapefiles into ArcGIS

Pro. Since the census tract shapefiles covered the entire U.S., I cross-compared with the city boundary of Chicago (also a shapefile) and selected the tracts within the boundary. Then, I joined my tables of data with the designated census tract shapefiles based on a system- generated series number called GISJOIN. The series number was different for every tract in every year, so the process was about matching and merging. Once the data was joined, I exported the attribute table to obtain files that I could work with on Microsoft Excel and

Stata. The same process was repeated for every year. I merged the each year’s dataset in

Microsoft Excel, creating a master dataset. I started by sorting tract numbers from the least to the greatest. Then, I imported individual data to the main dataset. Fortunately, the census tracts did not change from 2010 to 2017, so I did not have to reallocate data entries. After the master dataset was done, I recoded the variable names (please consult Appendix A for the data codebook). However, the tracts within a mile around the 606 were buried in the master dataset, blocking me to select the treatment group. I solved this problem by using “Select by

Location” in ArcGis Pro, and I extracted the ones within a mile around the 606. The exported census tracts were compared with the master dataset. Eventually, I was able to isolate and separate the treatment and control groups.

Chicago is known for its distinguished neighborhoods, so census tracts will provide the most detailed data possible. This is useful when examining the nuances within a neighborhood. On the other hand, a block group might be divided in half between two community areas in Chicago, and the result will not be accurate enough.

Model

I built a linear regression model using the difference-in-differences method to examine the relationship between the 606, a massive public investment project, and gentrification on social composition and housing prices while considering the division between affluent and disinvested areas. The reason for choosing this analysis method is its intuitive visualization and the ability to obtain a causal relationship. In addition, the absolute values in the dataset do not matter since the model only cares about changes over time, not the actual observed datapoints.

The difference-in-differences model records the average change over time in the treatment group (which is the census tracts around the 606 in this case) and the control group

(the census tracts that are not around the 606). It then calculates the effect of the “treatment”, which is the 606 Bike Trail (Angrist, 2009).  One challenge when answering my research question is the uncertainty of the causal relationships between variables. For instance, although property values went up around the 606 from 2015 to 2017, it was actually due to the whole rising real estate market in Chicago. Difference-in-differences method accounts for this uncertainty. It already considers the existing difference between the treatment and control group, so the effect of the treatment can be isolated. According to Angrist (2009), the most critical element to determine the validity of this model is whether it follows Parallel Trend assumption. Essentially, the treatment group and the control group would share a similar trend until the “treatment” is introduced, and the observed group will deviate away from the parallel path, presumably.

The exact linear regression function is listed below:

Variables

Dependent Variables

In order to examine my hypothesis that the 606 Bike Trail public investment project would indeed lead to gentrification, my key dependent variables are the housing affordability and social composition of the surrounding neighborhoods. The housing affordability is measured with median property values. Since this is already the median, it is resistant to outliers and extreme values. Thus, it does not to need to be weighted with the number of properties in a census tract. Although the difference-in-differences method is only interested in changes over time, the median property values are not calculated into percent change.

When analyzed with the regression model, it will show the exact change in numerical form, which can then be considered with inflation and interest rates.

The social composition outcome variable is consisted of racial composition, education attainment, residential stability, and the percentage of renters. Racial composition is divided into white and Latino. The reason is to distinguish the ethnic factors within racial composition. Education attainment accounts for percentage of people with a Bachelor’s degree or higher in a census tract. Migration is obtained through dividing the number of people who live in a different house than last year by total population in the census tract. It measures the residential mobility within a census tract. Percentage of renters examines the tenure status; it is simply the proportion between the number of renter-occupied housings and the number of owner-occupied housings. The social composition variable is all about percent change from 2010 to 2017, and the obtained value is multiplied by “100” in order to intuitively evaluate the coefficient later acquired from the regression model. By calculating the changes in percentage, I would be able to identify the trend, instead of just observing the numerical value.

Independent Variable

My independent variable is the treatment of the 606 Bike Trail to the surrounding census tracts. Difference-in-differences method depends on separating two groups into the treatment and control group, and it observes the changes in two groups over time. It not only comprises of the treatment and the time variable but also their interaction term. The independent variables therefore have to be dichotomous, also known as indicator variables.

First, I separated Chicago census tracts by dividing them into two groups: the ones that are within a mile of the 606 Bike Trail and the ones that are not. The independent variable is called “606_MILE”. In this way, I set up the difference between the treatment and control group. As for time series variable, I set 2015 as the dividing point since it was the year when the bike trail made open to the public. The variable is named as “POST_606”. Although

Rigolon and Németh (2018) show that the planning process is crucial for the development of a public investment project (in that case, I would have set 2013, the groundbreaking year, as the dividing point), this project measures the impact the 606 Bike Trail after it was built.

My third hypothesis predicts that the gentrification would worsen disinvested neighborhoods more than already-affluent neighborhoods. To test this hypothesis, I divided census tracts into “affluent” and “non-affluent” to create a treatment of “non-affluency”. In order for a tract to be considered as “affluent”, this tract’s median household income must be

1 standard deviation above the average from 2010-2017 and vice versa. One caveat is that inflation might affect the exact amount of dollars, but the number is only marginal and thus would not be affect the results in a statistically significant way. I then crossed this independent variable with both the 606 and time variable, essentially creating an interaction term that has all three independent variables.

The goal is to use these independent variables to predict the dependent variables and extract the coefficients from the linear regression model. The coefficients of the interaction terms will show the changes over time. Nonetheless, the “606_MILE” or “POST_MILE” variable is still crucial to set the base number. The base value will be used to compare with the interaction term.

In terms of social composition around the 606, there is no clear trend of changes in both Latino and white population. The values fluctuate throughout 2010 to 2017, with the maximum numerical change of 5 percentage in white-only population. The percentage of

Latino slowly declines from 2010 to 2015 but experiences a surge of 4% in 2016, almost increasing the population one-third more. Non-606 tracts have a relatively stable percentage of Latino, but the percentage of white population has a big jump in 2016. In terms of education, although both groups are both growing each year, the 606 experiences a faster increase, averaging around 1% per year. This trend, if considered together with the percentage of migration, indicates that more educated are more likely to move into the area each year (i.e. in 2017, 19% of new residents and 51% of population has a Bachelor’s degree). The 606’s percentage of people living in a different house than the previous year is roughly 3 to 4% higher than the rest of the Chicago, and this is also true in terms percentage of renters. The difference is consistent from 2010 to 2017, and this means that the region has lower residential stability. People are less likely to be homeowners and would move around more frequently around the 606. There is a handful of insights from this descriptive results table. Firstly, the trend of both Latino and white people is unclear. Secondly, other dependent variables around the 606, education, migration, and percentage of renters, are already higher than other Chicago tracts before the bike trail was made open to public in 2015. It is hard to determine whether the difference is due to the 606 Bike Trail or the neighborhoods are already better off than other Chicago neighborhoods at the beginning.

Table 5 presents the difference-in-differences regression analysis of gentrification around the 606 Bike Trail. The goal is to see if the variable changes follow the parallel trends assumption mentioned in the previous section. The interaction term 606 Tracts  Post 606 accounts for the shift in the dependent variables after the bike trail was built, which is 2015 and onwards. The interaction term’s coefficient regresses the parallel trend assumption’s validity.

It appears that census tracts around the 606 are already more gentrified than other neighborhoods in Chicago before the bike trail was built because the coefficients of the key dependent variables are mostly higher. The property value is around $13,000 higher  on average than the rest of Chicago, and the residents fit the young, educated professionals profile, who are known as common gentrification agents. However, white population is actually lower than the city average, showing that the area may be a racially diverse one before the bike trail was built. Indeed, population of other races can also move in if their income and capital are able to afford the living cost. Based on Smith et al. (2016; 2020)

report, housing prices vary a lot around the neighborhood. In this way, people of color might still reside in the disinvested areas within the neighborhood, while white people are living in the wealthy and more developed regions. This is perhaps why the 606 has lower white population from 2010 to 2014.

After the 606 finished construction, residential stability decreases, given the statistically significant coefficient 1.7213. Around 1.7 percent more migration happens around the 606 neighborhoods, whether emigrating from other places and migrating internally. Comparing to other Chicago areas after the 606 was built, which the amount of migration has declined, 606 areas have lower residential stability. This trend is supplemented with the percentage of renters, where it is already higher prior to the bike trail. While other

Chicago neighborhoods also have more renters after 2015, the percentage is still lower than the ones around the 606. Statistically, it is hard to determine whether 606 has fewer renters after it is built. However, these two variables indicate that residents are constantly renewing and thus are catalysts for changes.

Property values, different than the results the from descriptive statistics, are around

$9,200 higher around the 606 after the bike trail was finished than the ones in other Chicago areas. While the overall Chicago housing market declines after 2015, the neighborhoods around the 606 does not show that sign. The interaction term 606 Tracts  Post 606 is not statistically significant, and it is unsure whether there is a change materially. In other words,

Chicago housing markets may be declining, but the regions around the 606 are decreasing at a lower rate, showing signs of stagnating and resistant housing price. Hence, housing affordability around the 606, comparing to other Chicago areas, is lower. This difference can be explained by the variability in housing price data within the neighborhood, supporting

Smith et al. (2016) findings. Some census tracts may have higher property values, while other areas still remain the same. On the other hand, although $9,200 is not a significant amount in terms of real estate values, the amount is still impressive given that Post 606 only accounts for three years.

No simple and decisive conclusion can be drawn in terms of the changes in social composition. To being with, the 606 Bike Trail had fewer white or Latino population prior to

2015. The proportion in both 606 and other regions in Chicago remain unchanged after the bike trail was done. Therefore, white population around the 606, instead of displacing indigenous residents, are perhaps reinforcing segregation because the overall population does not increase significantly while property value has gone up other social factors does change.

Besides from racial composition, the trend in educational attainment is unclear. Indeed, residents are already much more educated around the 606 than other Chicago citizens before

2015. The whole Chicago’s educational attainment is around 2% higher before and after

2015, while the 606 increases around 2.5% (not statistically significant). Insofar, no significant difference regarding the 606’s education can be proven with this regression model. There are also fewer renters in general, meaning people are buying more homes and condominiums around the 606 after 2015, even though home ownership rate in Chicago itself is declining. Residential stability actually decreases around the 606 after 2015, given that the rest of Chicago increases after 2015. In this way, the flow residents is higher.

The results in Table 5 supports the hypotheses regarding gentrification effects on the social composition and housing affordability around the 606 Bike Trail. Since there is limited amount of urban space for housings within the neighborhood, having more white people means more people of color are being replaced by the newcomers. This claim is supplemented with the lower residential stability around the 606. More people are either moving in or out of the neighborhood. This two-way transaction signifies that either the poor are being displaced internally (or elsewhere into other neighborhoods) or wealthy people are moving in to the 606. Either way, it is a sign of displacement or at least displacement pressure within the neighborhood, indicating gentrification is fermenting in the area. The robust migrating underscores a high number of new residents, which answers the

“…indigenous residents” part in the first hypothesis.

Nevertheless, some may argue that the changes are minimal and are not statistically significant. Indeed, based on this model, there is a possibility that these shifts may just be

“noises” throughout the years. However, one cannot deny that the 606’s presence is shaping the neighborhood’s appearance, given that the neighborhoods are already better off than other

Chicago neighborhoods at the beginning.

Discussion

By aggregating census data over 8 years, my findings suggest that changes in property values and social composition are happening around the 606, but whether the agents of changes fit the initial impression is unclear. In addition, my findings show that gentrification is actually creating more divisions between neighborhoods around the 606, instead of exploiting the potential of further gentrifying disinvested areas. The inequality is therefore exacerbated, even though there seem to be no significant changes over the course of study timeframe.

Gentrification has always been considered as a mechanism to transform a neighborhood into a more homogenous, economically well-developed, and culturally identical place. The key characteristics of “changing” is in the core of gentrification. In this thesis project, however, the “change” is actually being resistant to other changes. For instance, I hypothesize that housing affordability will go down after the 606 was finished.

While the housing price did not show any changes, housings were not more affordable when compared with other real estate in Chicago. From this perspective, I argue that the 606 Bike

Trail builds a social moat to resist drastic changes throughout the years. One interesting note is the 606 initial social composition status in 2010. Residents were already whiter, more educated, and younger (given there were more renters) than other Chicago areas. Essentially, some parts of the neighborhood were already gentrified, and having the 606 was just fortifying, if not worsening, the existing inequality. If a neighborhood is already affluent or gentrified at the beginning, more development projects would solidify and preserve that status, blocking any social groups that do not match with the specific profile. At the same time, the surrounding non-affluent areas may not necessarily undergo the gentrification process due to such projects. They would not be converted or transformed into a homogenous space like their affluent neighbors, like Glass and Zukin suggest. The distinction between affluent and non-affluent areas would rather be more significant.

From another perspective, gentrification is not an endless journey but a temporary phase. Neighborhoods that are initially poor may present as gentrifiable because there are a lot of potentials to develop. Therefore, having a massive public investment project would definitely drive up property values and displace indigenous residents. However, if the public project is introduced in an already-gentrified neighborhood, then the neighborhood has surpassed the gentrifiable period. While the project may not necessarily continue to increase living costs, it will certainly protect the areas from or at least slow down the economic downturns, should there be any.

On the other hand, it is possible that the creation of the 606 Bike Trail is spurred by the existing wealthy and advantageous groups in the neighborhood. As the literature mentioned, gentrification can encourage more gentrification. Thus, having a public investment project that appeals to a certain lifestyle of a specific social group in an already- gentrified neighborhood would actually add fuel to the gentrification engine. As a result, regions with high white percentage continue to expand its population, whereas poor neighborhoods are welcoming Latinos and other people of color. Since education is highly correlated with racial composition, same logic can be applied here. The polarization, supplementing with low residential stability and high renting status, continues to engrain segregation into the neighborhood. In the 606, more people come and go, and fewer people own a home. Thus, the demographic is constantly changing, forcefully displacing the indigenous residents.

My findings adds a new piece of discussion to the literature of gentrification by focusing on the resilience part of gentrification. The whole project compares changes in two different groups throughout time. Unlike other gentrification initiatives, the 606 is consisted of transportation infrastructure, urban green space, and art works. Because of these explicit characteristics, the 606 should be generating growth in the surrounding neighborhood based on what the literature shows. However, if only look at the descriptive results, one can easily identify that the numerical values do not show a clear upscale growth. While other parts of the city are deteriorating or declining in markets, the 606 public investment project may not necessarily skyrocket neighborhood growth but maintain its situation. In other words, hybrid form of gentrification such as the 606 could be served to increase segregation and attract certain group of people. This form of gentrification will typically appear at the ending phase of gentrification, where residents have enough tax bases to afford it. Although it may be in the ending stage, my difference-in-differences regression model shows that changes are still present. Since the project is implemented by the advocates of gentrification, it excludes disadvantageous groups and continue to polarize the neighborhood. On the contrary, a classic gentrification example (such as the one in Neo-Bohemia) may argue that gentrification is about attracting young, poor professionals, and they will slowly transform the neighborhood.

In those cases, developments can be more single-function because they will spark large growth regardless. In the case of the 606, the project is more hybrid in terms of functionality and thus is more efficient in terms of space.

The results also have a few policy implications. Local ownership is the key to combat gentrification. Although the bike trail is currently overseen by The Friends of the

Bloomingdale Trail, the board members mostly share similar social profiles. Having diversity in such organization will welcome more voices to the planning process, and residents can reach compromises that serve the best interests for all, ideally. Secondly, since the bike trail is a public investment project, government plays an essential role through the planning phase to daily operations. Therefore, careful and comprehensive assessments from all perspectives

(economical, urban planning, sociological) have to be considered in order to reach the balance of equity and efficiency. Last but not least, the gap between affluent and non-affluent tracts can be shortened with appropriate amount of incentives such as housing subsidies.

Financial injection may start the long-stalling wheel of growth in disinvested neighborhood, and this may initiate positive feedback loop that attracts more equitable and thoughtful developments for them.

Limitations

Difference-in-differences method evaluates whether an intervention or treatment over time has created a difference in whatever subjects being studied. I use this method to examine if the 606 Bike Trail is contributing to gentrification in the surrounding community. One important factor is the study timeframe, as it is directly related to the comparison of the two groups. Since gentrification never happens at an exact rate, it is hard to determine what is the best cutoff point between two groups. This study I chose 2015, when the project was finished, as my dividing point. However, there is a possibility that gentrification might already has happened during the planning process or even earlier. Furthermore, 8 years in total is not a very long time in terms of studying social changes. If I were to retrieve more historical data in the 2000s, perhaps the findings will show a different result. In short, the study design is limited in terms of the data availability, and the results may be altered depending on the deciding point for the control and treatment group.

Another flaw in this study design is the lack of consideration over distances to the 606 in this project. I simply divided Chicago into two groups: one being a mile around the 606 and vice versa. However, the data is highly correlated with each other (please address

Appendix B for the bivariate correlation table). As a result, the dependent variables may be co-mingling with each other. For instance, education, racial composition, and property values are not independent from one another, and the possible collinearity among some categories might possibly blur the results presented. This perhaps is the reason causing some of the interaction terms to be statistically insignificant in the regression model.

Additionally, difference-in-differences method fails to consider the proximity to the bike trail and variability within the treatment group. It assumes that the intervention has a uniform effect over the treatment group. As other literature indicated, the area is highly divided, even down to each census tract. Simply creating an affluent and a non-affluent group would not document the nuances. However, my methodology does demonstrate that a difference is presence between the control and treatment group, but to what extent does the difference impact the community and its composition are unclear. Hence, further research on this matter using spatial regression would be a good building block for this literature.

Conclusion

This study aims to use the 606 Bloomingdale Bike Trail to build on the relatively new literature on rail-to-trail public investment projects under the gentrification umbrella. From a quantitative approach, I am able to collect census data on a mass scale that examines the whole Chicago city. By comparing the property values and the social composition in the surrounding community between two timeframes, I have successfully found that the bike trail does have an effect on social factors in those neighborhoods. Moreover, gentrification is actually creating more divisions and exacerbating segregation in the community; the wealthy areas create an invisible wall that only welcomes a certain type of residents while the poor ones remain to be disinvested.

In the modern hybrid form of gentrification, gentrification no longer has a prominent effect on one single social factor. Instead, it combines every aspect of development and complicates the change process as investment projects build on one another. The wrestle between economic prosperity and equity is therefore a never ceasing debate. Certainly, developments are important for the local’s livelihood and for sustainable growth.

Nevertheless, the returned profits should not be excluded from the indigenous residents as they are the ones defining the authenticity community. Thus, it is important to conduct more research to encourage a robust yet considerate economic development in the future.
